#5541. Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September

Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals’ operations took another dip in September amid a slew of ongoing headwinds including weakened payer mix and rising costs, healthcare advisory firm Kaufman Hall reported alongside warnings of a “historically large portion” of the nation’s hospitals running on negative or near-zero operating margins.

The firm’s latest monthly benchmark report, released Tuesday, showed a calendar year-to-date operating margin index of 1.4% and a single-month operating margin index of 2.4% in September, the latter of which was a decline from August’s 3.0% operating margin (all including health system allocations for shared services costs).

The performance decline wasn’t for want of patients. Daily discharges and adjusted discharges both rose 3% from August to September, and are generally above the numbers from last year. Operating room minutes per calendar day also rose 6% from August—an encouraging sign for hospitals whose surgical slowdowns had hamstrung acuity—but remain 1% below September of last year.

The increased foot traffic also grew revenues, with daily net operating revenue rising 4% from August and 6% year over year while gross operating revenue rose 4% month to month and 8% year over year. Much of the increase came on the outpatient side, where daily revenue increased 5% from August and 10% compared to September 2025. Net patient service revenue per adjusted discharge was more mixed, rising 2% from August but remaining 1% below September 2025.

However, hospitals’ margins are being challenged by persistent bad debt and charity care burdens, Kaufman Hall’s data show. Daily bad debt and charity care may have remained flat from August, but is 17% higher than September 2025 and 16% higher when comparing both years’ first nine months. As a percentage of gross operating revenue, they’re 6% higher than Sept. 2025 and 8% higher year to date.

On the spending side, daily total expense rose 3% from August and is 5% higher than September 2025, primarily reflecting the heightened volumes even as hospitals held their average length of stay flat month over month or 1% shorter year over year. The expenses were more pronounced on the non-labor side, where increases on a per adjusted discharge basis were higher than labor’s per adjusted discharge decline.

"Hospitals continue to operate in an environment marked by significant financial variability," Erik Swanson, managing director and Data and Analytics group leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. “Many organizations continue to face mounting pressure from uncompensated care and rising expenses, underscoring the importance of proactive operational and financial strategies that build long-term resilience."

Another amplifying market trend is the “bifurcation of hospital performance” often highlighted by the firm and others that monitor multi-organization financial trends, such as credit rating agencies.

"The margin gap between higher and lower-performing hospitals has widened to 19 percentage points, with a historically large portion of hospitals operating at negative or very thin margins,” the report reads. “Even slight revenue reductions threaten organizations, which face increasingly difficult decisions on future operations, care delivery, and expense control.”

The firm encouraged hospitals to take “deliberate, proactive steps” to strengthen their financial situations, particularly as macro reimbursement trends stiffen and the site of care delivery shifts from the hospital to outpatient settings.

Kaufman Hall’s hospital reports pull data from more than 1,300 nationwide hospitals as collected by parent company Strata Decision Technology.

Accompanying the monthly hospital benchmark was also Kaufman Hall’s quarterly numbers on more than 200,000 employed physicians and advanced practice providers, which painted a much rosier picture for health system and hospital employers.

It showed, for the first time in five years of data collection, that healthcare employers’ investment/subsidy per provider and per physician has declined year over year (by 1%), and “across every cohort, including primary care, medical specialty, surgical specialty and hospital-based specialty.”

Kaufman Hall attributed the rare turnaround to revenue growth and sustained productivity increases that together outpaced expenses.

"Medical groups made meaningful performance improvements this quarter, achieving gains in revenue, productivity and thoughtful workforce management," Matthew Bates, managing director and Physician Enterprise Service Line leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. "The growing utilization of [advanced practice providers] and ongoing focus on operational and team effectiveness are helping organizations manage financial pressures while increasing access to care.”

#5539. At SC26, Nvidia debuts new Rubin HPC chip, scientific research libraries

Nvidia Corp. today introduced a set of offerings designed to speed up scientific research across a range of fields.

The lineup is headlined by Rubin HPC, an upcoming graphics card with significantly more cores than the company’s current flagship chip. It’s joined by more than a half-dozen software tools geared toward scientists and engineers. The technologies made their debut at the SC26 high-performance and supercomputing conference in Chicago.

Nvidia’s flagship Rubin graphics processing unit features 898 Tensor cores, transistor clusters specifically optimized for large language models. It also includes over 28,000 CUDA cores. Those circuits can run not only LLMs but also other workloads such as scientific simulations.

The Rubin HPC (pictured), the upcoming chip that Nvidia previewed today, will feature more than 50,000 CUDA cores. It will also ship with a new iteration of NVLink, the interconnect that Nvidia’s GPUs use to exchange data with central processing units. The current version of the technology can move 3.6 terabits per second per graphics card.

Nvidia stated that Rubin HPC will also include a “sparse data acceleration” feature. Sparse data is the technical term for datasets that contain a large number of zeros. Many scientific projects generate such data, particularly in fields such as biology and astrophysics. A telescope, for example, might use zeros to represent sections of space without any visible stars.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

Nvidia plans to ship Rubin HPC in 2028. In the meantime, customers can speed up their scientific workloads using the software tools that debuted alongside the chip today.

Nvidia ships its GPUs  with a collection of libraries called CUDA-X that is designed to ease scientific research projects. The company’s SC26 announcement introduced several new additions to the suite.

Astrophysicists are gaining access to cuPhoton.xBeam, a library that makes it easier to analyze data from the Event Horizon Telescope network. It’s a collection of observatories used study black holes. According to Nvidia, cuPhoton.xBeam can perform data analysis tasks that historically took a month in eight minutes. It’s rolling out alongside cuPhoton.xLens, a library for simulating the plasma that fusion reactors use to generate electricity.

On the biology research side, Nvidia is open-sourcing cuSpa. It speeds up cell polygon calculations, which are used to study the structure of cells and the manner in which they interact with one another. Plus, an existing cellular analysis tool called rapids-singlecell is now available to Nvidia users in a containerized format.

Nvidia’s new biology research tools are joined by an AI bundle called Nemotron for Science. It’s built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open-source LLM the company introduced last month. The model features 124 billion parameters and activates about a 10th of them at any given time. It’s partly based on Mamba-2, a more hardware-efficient alternative to the ubiquitous Transformer model architecture.

Nemotron for Science pairs the LLM with a set of pre-packaged post-training workflows. Researchers can use them to optimize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specific scientific tasks. Additionally, Nvidia has added in nearly 50,000 chemistry-related questions. They can be used to post-train AI models and evaluate the capabilities of models that have already gone through the process.

“Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries,” Buck said.

Quantum computers rely on a conventional processor to manage their qubits. Nvidia provides a set of software tools called CUDA-Q that makes it easier to link quantum hardware to its GPUs and CPUs. The company today expanded the suite with new building blocks for developing quantum software and an algorithm that can mitigate qubit errors.

Nvidia is teaming up with IBM Corp. and the U.S. Energy Department’s Fermilab to create a “modular quantum codesign platform.” It will combine the chip giant’s DGX B200 systems with quantum hardware from IBM. According to the companies, the goal is to create an environment that researchers can use to develop new qubit error correction algorithms and other quantum software.

#5537. A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

Researchers have identified a protein that may play an important role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising new target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

The protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance

Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

To investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising New Direction for Diabetes Treatment

Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

The study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment."

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?

Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan plans to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore new strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he said. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution."

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

#5536. HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: Oura, Counsel Health CEOs talk $625M acquisition; Why DJ Steve Aoki is investing in innovative science

HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: Oura, Counsel Health CEOs talk $625M acquisition; Why DJ Steve Aoki is investing in innovative science" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Fierce Healthcare team is on the ground at HLTH 2026. Stick with this news tracker to catch all the highlights from the show floor, and click here for additional coverage from the conference.

DJ and music producer Steve Aoki told the HLTH audience that his father's passing was the catalyst for his interest in healthcare.

Learning more about what caused his death, and if it could have been prevented, drew him to the impacts of dementia and cancer. And in exploring that, he said he decided he wanted to invest in the people who are pursuing the "science fiction concepts" in healthcare, and support cutting edge innovation.

Aoki said that his celebrity status made it easier to get into a room with people leading the charge on innovation, and learn as much as he could.

"I was just as intrigued as working with a big artist in the studio or playing a big show," he said.

It was with that learning that he established Aoki Foundation, an organization he said is dedicated to bringing back the science and investing in what's next.

"People are excited about science fiction, about the possibility of doing things that are impossible," Aoki said. "And I feel like the superheroes of our time are like right right in our midst, and it's about it's about highlighting their journey and giving them a spotlight."

On the HLTH show floor, you may have noticed a theme.

Las Vegas is abuzz with the upcoming Formula 1 race, which is taking place on Saturday, Nov. 21. The city has been preparing for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which is on the Strip, for weeks, and HLTH is taking place at one of the hubs for F1 excitement, The Venetian.

So at this year's conference, each of the stages is themed around racing: the Velocity Stage, the Ferrari Stage, the Monacco Stage. And each breakout track is referred to as a "circuit." In the conference livery, HLTH mascot Petunia is show driving a race car.

Activations on the show floor also play into the F1 theme. A racing simulation game is set up for attendees near the Pharma Force stage, and swag giveaways allude to the race.

Panelists at a HLTH session discussing the uptake of ICHRA — scratch that, CHOICE — faced a challenge around the nomenclature.

Individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRAs, represent a growing area of interest for employers and insurers participating in the individual market. But on Sept. 3, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that it would instead refer to these models as CHOICE, which stands for Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense.

In these models, an employer offers enrollees a stipend to purchase coverage on the individual market rather than securing a traditional employer-sponsored plan. ICHRA (or CHOICE) has gained traction with employers that may otherwise struggle to offer health coverage.

Moderator Joseph Mercer, senior managing director at Marwood Group, joked that the panelists had all agreed to call these plans CHOICE rather than ICHRA. But throughout the session, slip-ups drew a chuckle.

Even the panel's title made reference to the evolution of the name: "The ICHRA (CHOICE) Debate."

Healthcare platform Simple HealthKit announced Tuesday a partnership with Waters Corporation to expand access to at-home cervical cancer screening.

The collaboration aims to expand access to BD’s Onclarity HPV Self-Collection Kit, which is tested with the BD Onclarity HPV Assay  and Simple HealthKit's artificial intelligence-powered direct-to-patient-provider platform.

"We envision a future where personalized, world-class healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of where they live,” said Sheena Menezes, Ph.D, Simple HealthKit CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “Our AI-powered direct-to-patient and provider platform brings that vision to life by connecting people with the right education, intelligent personalized engagement, and clinical care at every step.”

Menezes continued, “Through partnerships with innovators like Waters Corporation, we are empowering individuals to take charge of their health while making seamless, personalized care accessible at scale.”

Oura CEO joined Counsel Health CEO and founder Muthu Alagappan Tuesday morning to discuss the wearable company’s recently announced $625 million acquisition of the virtual primary care company.

Hale said Oura selected Counsel as a partner after reviewing the landscape, and “uptake” from customers was “very positive.”

“We started talking seriously about taking that partnership,” Hale said. “And while we had been dating for a while, we thought maybe it was time to get married.”

Hale said the agreement was “really driven” by Oura customers using Counsel in “really novel and interesting ways.”

Alagappan said one of the most exciting aspects of the partnership is the potential impact of AI-fueled access to physicians on preventive care, adding the daily engagement of wearing Oura rings struck him.

“The buy-in from almost all users is tremendous, and so you enable primary care with the thing that has always been missing, which is engagement,” he said. “And now we have a way to incentivize, motivate patients to make the changes that actually prevent disease, alongside the screenings and lab tests that are also very important.”

During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason said HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the issue to “remove friction from the patient experience.”

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient,” she said.

Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.

“The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason said. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”

Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her company looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.

Jain said women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.

“Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain said. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”

To bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain said.

Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.

And, Jain said women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.

“I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain said. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”

Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp said the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.

Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently nominated to serve as Deputy Secretary at HHS and is a rising star in the White House.

He said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.

But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp said.

In addition, he said the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.

"Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he said. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it quickly becomes the most important thing to you."

"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp said.

Houston Methodist announced Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.

Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton, which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.

The vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.

“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find new ways to extend the positive impact,” said Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. By thoughtfully extending this model into new care settings, our goal with this program is to demonstrate how our system’s existing technology and clinical expertise can strengthen access and improve outcomes in rural communities.”

Loewy added the expansion is an opportunity to “explore how the capabilities of a major health system can be shared across geographic boundaries.”

While 72% of health tech startups lead with “AI-powered” in their descriptors, zero surveyed venture capitalists in a new report from HLTH and SolComms said the phrase increased their confidence.

Independently surveyed health tech reporters also ranked “AI-powered” as one of the most overused phrases in pitching–in addition to “revolutionizing/transforming” and “disrupting.”

Alongside these survey responses, researchers compared–and scored–the messaging of 72 U.S.-based, venture-backed health tech startups at series A to series C for the “Healthtech Attention Economy Report.” Startups’ messaging across their website and social media was scored on four main dimensions: clarity, differentiation, proof and policy awareness.

SolComms Vice President of HealthTech Isabella Morreale said in a statement the companies that will get attention within the next year “are leading with proof, not adjectives.”

“That means speaking to clinical data, measurable outcomes, and validation from third parties,” Morreale said. “Founder-led storytelling will also continue to stand out. Among the data, one common through-thread for investor and reporter interest was founders with a real point of view on the industry.”

Morreale continued, “Reporters don't need another company description; they need a source who can help them explain what's happening in healthcare.”

Less than half (42.2%) of patients say communications from healthcare providers “often” or “always” feel relevant to their needs, a new report from Lirio found.

Analysts at the behavioral science and AI-powered behavioral intelligence platform polled 1,500 adults across the U.S. for the survey. While 58% of respondents report communications not consistently feeling relevant to their needs, 55.6% rate overall communication experiences with healthcare organizations as “good” or “excellent.”

When asked why healthcare communications are ignored altogether, respondents report generic or irrelevant content (24.4%), too many similar messages (21.8%) and confusing, jargon-filled messages (18.8%) as top reasons.

Nearly half of respondents (47.9%) report the potential value of more personalized, better-timed messages as an “8, 9 or 10” for how much it could help them make better care decisions and stay engaged.

Lirio Chief Behavioral Officer Amy Bucher, Ph.D., said in a statement patients “are not rejecting healthcare communications outright.”

“They are telling us, in specific and measurable terms, that the system is talking at them instead of to them,” Bucher said. "The instinct in healthcare has long been to solve engagement with more outreach - more emails, more reminders, more portals. This data shows that volume is not the problem. What is missing is relevance — content and timing designed for where a specific patient is in their own health journey, rather than a single message broadcast to an entire population.”

Bucher added the healthcare organizations that close the communication gap will be “the ones that use behavioral data to determine the right message, the right channel, and the right moment for each individual patient, which is the model Lirio was built to deliver."

Community-based specialty palliative care provider Vynca is expanding its reach into four more states.

Patients will now be able to access Vynca’s services in Georgia, Hawaii, New Jersey and Texas. Vynca is one of the first practices approved to provide services under New Jersey’s Community-Based Palliative Care Medicaid benefit, launched in April, according to the Nov. 16 announcement.

Founded in 2013, the company’s hybrid care model combines in-home visits with virtual clinical support and predictive technology, and executives say it has shown 43% fewer emergency department visits and 52% less hospital stays within six months of enrollment.

“Health plan and government program leaders understand the value of community-based palliative care for people with serious illness,” said Darren Schulte, M.D., Vynca CEO, in a statement. “Our expansion in four key states reflects growing momentum to expand specialty outpatient palliative care outside of hospices. The key is to broaden access and convenience for the entire eligible population by offering home-based options. Too often, patients are limited to seeking palliative care when available in the community, at hospital-based clinics and facilities.”

#5535. Agricultural Visionary: Stefan Soloviev's Path to Innovation

Entrepreneur Stefan Soloviev has created an indelible impression in the global agribusiness landscape. Known for his innovative approach and dedication to sustainability, his journey provides essential insights into successful entrepreneurship in this challenging yet rewarding industry.

Breaking Ground: Stefan Soloviev's Foray into Agribusiness

When talking about Stefan Soloviev, one cannot ignore his impressive transition into the agribusiness sector. He recognized the immense potential in this industry, which is evident in his ownership of Crossroads Agriculture, managing more than 70,000 acres of farmland from New Mexico to Colorado1. His entrepreneurial spirit and strategic foresight have enabled him to cultivate success in this multifaceted industry.

Nurturing Sustainability: Soloviev's Cornerstone for Success

In the world of agribusiness, sustainability isn't just an option; it's a necessity. Soloviev's commitment to sustainability is clearly reflected in his farming practices. The integration of advanced technology and sustainable farming techniques has not only driven growth for Crossroads Agriculture but also underscored Soloviev's dedication to preserving the environment for future generations2.

Leveraging Technology: Innovation in Agribusiness

Stefan Soloviev's innovative approach has been a significant driver of his success in agribusiness. Leveraging cutting-edge technology, Soloviev has been able to increase productivity while also promoting sustainable farming. #5533. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

Materials provided by Cell Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

HLTH 2026: Teladoc Health's weight care program lets employers partially contribute to GLP-1 costs" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Teladoc Health is expanding its Comprehensive Weight Care program with a new option that allows employers to contribute to GLP-1 costs outside of traditional pharmacy benefit designs.

Through the new offering, employers can give access to medications from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk—accompanied by support from licensed professionals, personalized lifestyle coaching, artificial intelligence-enabled food logging and more.

With each plan year, employers will set a fixed payment per employee per fill that applies consistently across covered medications, the company said. Employees then pay the remaining balance for each fill. Teladoc manages eligibility, program oversight and consolidated invoicing.

Pharmacy claims are administered on a 100% pass-through basis, including eligibility verification and audit-ready claims documentation.

Moreover, employers can opt in to tie contributions to program engagement, using metrics like food logging and regular weigh-ins, executives say.

The offering is available now, with initial contracted clients slated to launch programs for their employees beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

“Employers want to provide benefits that help their workforce achieve their health goals and need flexible strategies that work for their organizations,” said Kelly Bliss, Teladoc Health U.S. Group Health president, in a statement. “We are helping employers meet the needs of their employees while providing greater predictability and transparency around healthcare spending. Importantly, we give people a trusted path to high-quality care and affordable access to FDA-approved, authentic medication for meaningful, sustained health outcomes.”

Alongside the announcement, the company also unveiled new research examining two years of weight-loss outcomes among nearly 23,000 members enrolled in its programs.

Results indicated “clinically meaningful weight loss” increased over time, with 47.7% of members achieving at least 5% weight loss by 24 months. And among those who lost weight during their first year, 53% continued losing additional weight during the second.

#5531. NIH’s infectious disease unit has a new head at last

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Good morning and happy Tuesday! Today’s newsletter includes good news for international students, bad news for the makers of signs proclaiming “zero tolerance” for violence in hospitals, and mixed news for children with rare brain disorders. Read on!

No branch of the NIH has faced more scrutiny than the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. For nearly four decades, the institute was run by Anthony Fauci; it’s since become a major focus of Republicans looking to re-litigate the Covid pandemic.

The institute has been without a permanent director since Jeanne Marrazzo was forced out in 2025 for objecting to grant terminations. Now officials have announced that acting director John Powers III will take the lead role.

Powers is a physician-scientist who’s worked at NIAID in several clinical research positions. He has run the institute in an acting capacity since June. Earlier this year, he co-authored a paper with NIH director Jay Bhattacharya that argued NIAID should move away from its focus on HIV and pandemic preparedness, instead prioritizing broader categories of infectious disease and immunology.

Read more from STAT’s Anil Oza, including Powers’ response to questions about health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s position on vaccines.

One of the key tenets of Alcoholics Anonymous is surrender to a higher power. There, and in other organizations, faith-based addiction recovery can serve an important role in supporting people trying to stay sober.

But experts warn the Trump administration’s full-throated embrace of these programs will result in federal grants to centers that don’t always provide evidence-based treatment. As STAT’s Theresa Gaffney explains, some faith-based addiction centers don’t allow participants to use drugs like methadone, which is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for opioid use disorder.

Kennedy also has expressed support for unconventional (and scientifically dubious) approaches to treatment, including “wellness farms,” where people reside in nature and engage in manual labor. Read more about the tricky balance experts hope Kennedy can strike.

That’s the share of women who provided care to a friend or family member with a health problem in the past 30 days, according to a new analysis of 2025 data from the National Center for Health Statistics. Women were about 32% more likely than men to have provided care, offering a real world data point to back up the viral Saturday Night Live sketch about the gendered dynamics of caregiving (which makes it sound much less funny than it is! Give a watch here).

Last year, researchers thought they’d had a breakthrough — they finally engineered a virus to ferry gene therapy to the brain. Experts were hopeful this innovation could cure Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and slew of rare diseases.

Then the first person to undergo treatment with this new technique — a 3 year old — died of brain swelling 65 hours later, sending fear and uncertainty through the industry. Nearly a year later, researchers have unveiled how the process can be shored up for the future, with ideas for new tests and trials to ensure safety. Read more here.

A proposal by the Trump administration to cap the amount of time foreign students and scholars can spend in the country has been struck down in court. In a decision Monday, a federal judge said the rule was “arbitrary” and “capricious,” writing that the government did not sufficiently consider the ramifications of the new policy.

In his story on the ruling, Anil Oza breaks down why this matters: “International researchers make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates and around 60% of postdoctoral researchers. About 40% of American Nobel laureates in the sciences are immigrants.” Read more.

Violence against doctors and nurses has jumped in recent years, due to an ugly swirl of understaffing, overcrowding, and pandemic-era stress that hasn’t quite faded. In response, many hospitals have started to hang signs declaring “zero tolerance” for violence or other bad behavior from patients.

The problem, according to three professors, is that these signs don’t actually help protect workers. Instead, they signal to families that care is something that can be withheld. The signs often include long lists about things that patients shouldn’t do, without a similar standards for nurses and doctors.

“The content of the signs sends clear messages to patients and families about their tenuous status and value in the institution,” they write. Read more.

#5529. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5528. Manhattan’s Top 2 Sales This Week Go Under Contract After Price Hikes

The top-two sales in Manhattan last week were in signature luxury buildings that have seen very strong sales and were able to raise their prices from initial launch.

The No. 1 contract, a 17th floor unit at 1122 Madison Ave., is pending with an ask of $38.75 million, a bit over its original ask of $38 million in January.

The next highest contact, Penthouse B at The Henry on 211 W. 84th St., went under contract with an ask of $28.75 million, a hefty bump over its August 2024 price tag of $24.95 million.

Both units were sponsor sales in new construction, and are full-service luxury buildings with renowned architects and designers. The buildings essentially look at each other from across Central Park, one on the upper east side, one on the upper west.

"This is a sponsor strategy," says luxury broker Michael Reisor, of the Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team in Manhattan, who is familiar with both locations. "It's escalating pricing based on absorption."

Escalating pricing can create a sense of exigency in the buyer, offering a strong incentive not to dilly-dally with an offer, as the price will likely increase over time.

"The initial release pricing will always go up as the market absorbs apartments," he says. "This gives people the urgency of, 'If we don't act now and secure the apartment, then it's just going to get more expensive.'"

However, the early release strategy "doesn't always work unless buildings are this in demand," the broker says of the two top sales. The strategy is obviously successful, as the first building has only one unit left, and the second has only four.

Both complexes have highly desired locations as well being architecturally significant with bold names attached: Studio Sofield for 1122 Madison Ave. and Robert A.M. Stern Architects (RAMSA) for The Henry.

Nor did either development spare expense on finishes, materials, appliances, or amenities. (There is one key difference, however: The Madison Ave. building doesn't have a parking garage.)

Additionally, both are boutique buildings with a controlled number of residences: 26 for the first, and 45 for the second. With buildings like this, says Reisor, there usually is no downward negotiation on pricing.

"If you're selling really well, especially on a certain line, developers are always looking to maximize what they can get," agrees Manhattan broker Lisa K. Lippman of Brown Harris Stevens, who is familiar with both buildings.

She says that once The Henry sold its penthouses quickly, it was off to the races in terms of price.

In February, the 1122 Madison building's penthouse duplex went under contract for $89.5 million, setting a record for a condo on the Upper East Side, and also giving leeway for the building to raise prices.

Lippman, who heads up sales at another Stern building, 200 W. 88th St., has just raised prices on its A line due to its popularity, thanks to it being a corner line with four-bedroom layouts.

"We sold so many of them that we felt we could raise prices there," she says.

"When a building launches and signs a significant number of contracts in a relatively short period, the sponsor may recognize that the remaining inventory is worth more than originally anticipated," agrees Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman, who has shown clients in both buildings.

She notes that there is a strong pricing difference between new development and resale, saying, "On the resale side, it's generally less common for sellers to raise an asking price once a property is already listed."

The 1122 Madison Avenue full-floor condo comes with five bedrooms, five bathrooms, two balconies, a powder room, a library, a home office, and a laundry room. Then there's the sweeping Central Park and Metropolitan Museum of Art views from the great room, library, eat-in kitchen, and primary bedroom suite.

Despite being built in 2026, the building has a convincing prewar look. The unit boasts European white oak Parquet de Versailles-inspired flooring in the entrance hall and entertaining spaces, and quarter sawn European white oak plank flooring in all living areas, as well as soaring 11-foot high ceilings.

The impressive amenity suite contains two floors of leisure and wellness spaces, with a squash court with a retractable basketball hoop, a fitness center programmed by The Wright Fit, a private training studio with Pilates reformer, a spa with a steam room, sauna, and cold plunge, and a sports simulator.

On the lower level is a drawing room, a residents' lounge with bar, private dining room, billiard room, media room, game room, and children's playroom.

All but one unit is sold out, yet the complex won't be completed until fall of 2027.

Griffith says the building is doing particularly well because it's a boutique, brand-new condo in a neighborhood that is "largely defined by older co-op buildings."

The sales agent, Cathy Franklin of Corcoran, told Realtor.com she not wish to comment.

Across the park at The Henry, Penthouse B offers a full-floor with six bedrooms, 6.5 bathrooms, a living room, library, and formal dining room, chef's kitchen with an eat-in area and a large pantry, and terrace with the ultimate perk of Central Park views.

Designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects, the building showcases the high quality work the atelier is known for, including "a classic facade of Indiana limestone and hand set brick," along with prewar-style touches such as "terrace setbacks, bay windows and decorative detailing—emblematic of the best Stern buildings."

The week ending Nov. 15 saw 34 luxury (over $4 million) contracts signed, 11 fewer than the week before, according to Olshan Realty. As usual, condos out sold co-ops, but at 17 condos versus 12 co-ops, the gap had slimmed considerably since the week before.

Experts say that co-op sales, which often come with an arduous board-approval process, are increasing to due to a lack of inventory.

However, there will always be those who prefer an older building with a classic New York feel. The two top buildings this week managed to convincingly create that prewar (pre-1939) feel while being newly constructed.

#5527. Open AI hit with lawsuit in California over Hugging Face rogue agent incident

California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced the state has launched a lawsuit against OpenAI Group PBC after the company’s AI agents earlier this year went rogue and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc.

The 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, claims Open AI has engendered the public and put institutions at risk by developing products without suitable safeguards. Bonta likened Open AI’s behavior to being a “public nuisance,” asking the judge to order the company to change its practices while imposing financial penalties for any money the company made from the high-risk areas of its business.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta said in a statement at a press conference. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

Bonta believes that without external pressure, the scope and frequency of such attacks will increase in the future. “In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company,” he added.

The “unprecedented” rogue attack in question occurred on July 21 this year when one of Open AI’s agents escaped what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment — a sandbox. To break out of their restricted environment and access the internet, the AI models exploited a previously unknown security flaw in OpenAI’s systems. From there, they gained access to other parts of the company’s network, stole login credentials, and exploited further security weaknesses to break into Hugging Face’s servers.

In response to the lawsuit, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said he believes the company has been singled out when similar challenges have been faced at other major AI firms. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” he told media, adding that the company will continue to work with the state and share information to ensure public and institutional safety.

Nonetheless, Bonta has expressed skepticism about Open AI’s willingness to conform to safety practices, writing that through a “lack of transparency and misrepresentations” the company has continued to develop dangerous models with the ability to deceive and engage in malicious behavior.

Open AI is already facing lawsuits in eight states over a number of incidents. The company stands accused of developing technologies that have harmed the public by providing dangerous medical advice or steering people to make bad, sometimes harmful, decisions that threaten their safety.

#5526. Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected new weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.

The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.

The research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.

Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.

According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.

One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.

The researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies."

Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.

A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results

The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.

To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.

The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.

The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments.

With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.

Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive

One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.

The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.

Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.

In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.

Importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.

Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?

The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.

"Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.

Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.

For now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.

If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.

Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

Other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.

This work was supported by NIH (grant 5-R01-HL 107904-13 awarded to Henry Daniell), the Academic Senate Grant of David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (the Surgical Education Research program), and National Cancer Institute Cancer Center (Support Grant P30 CA168524).

New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye could miss the rest of the 2026 season after injuring his ankle against the Detroit Lions in Munich.

#5523. U.S. loses measles elimination status, marking embarrassing stain on its public health record

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Andrew covers the biopharma industry, scientific research, and public health across the continent. You can reach Andrew confidentially on Signal at drewqjoseph.71.

International health officials said Tuesday that measles is no longer considered eliminated in the United States, a finding that was widely expected but that marks an embarrassing and avoidable backslide in the country’s basic public health standing.

The announcement, made after a meeting of a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional World Health Organization body, is a largely symbolic recognition of transmission that’s already occurred. But it could have political ramifications, with resurgent Democrats already attacking the Trump administration — in particular, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — for not responding forcefully to recent outbreaks and for mixed messaging around the benefits of vaccination.

Health authorities in 2000 determined that the U.S. had eliminated measles, a milestone victory. But the country almost lost the designation after outbreaks in 2019, and has been experiencing far bigger outbreaks in the past two years than in the decades prior.

“Losing measles elimination status is a tragic loss for our country,” Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer for the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, told reporters Monday. The announcement formalizes what public health departments have been seeing on the ground across the U.S. in recent years, she said. “Measles has taken a hold in our country.”

Officials bestow the measles elimination designation on a country that prevents persistent spread of the virus. Cases can still occur, when people infected outside that country import the virus, and limited transmission can take place from those infected people. But if those chains of spread are not stopped within a year, measles is considered to be endemic again.

“Elimination must be continuously protected,” Jarbas Barbosa, the PAHO director, said at a news briefing.

This year, the U.S. has reported more than 5,000 measles cases for the first time since 1991, a figure that’s widely presumed to be an undercount. Last year’s total of 2,289 cases was at that point also the highest number seen since 1991, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The overwhelming majority of infections — 96% — are in unvaccinated people or people whose vaccination status is not known.

The PAHO commission’s review focused on a period starting in January 2025, and depended on establishing that a series of cases continued for at least 12 months.

“It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles,” said Noel Brewer, a public health expert at the University of North Carolina, who chairs the group that provides data on the measles landscape in the U.S. to PAHO.

“We need a plan,” Brewer said last week during a briefing for reporters. “We need to have a concrete and integrated measles elimination plan that allows us to either sustain the gains we’ve made in the past or to return to a state where measles is no longer stalking children in their schools, in grocery stores, and in their churches. The United States is no longer a safe place for children with respect to measles. It is not as prevalent as some other diseases. At the same time, it is a fully preventable disease.”

The U.S. has seen 10 measles-associated deaths this year, according to state data, though the CDC’s website currently lists six deaths. Some recent deaths reported by states have yet to be added to the CDC’s count, but federal officials have also squabbled with Pennsylvania over its tally. New York and Wisconsin recently reported their first measles deaths in at least 30 years. Last year, there were three measles deaths.

Experts fear that measles deaths — practically unheard of in the U.S. for over 20 years — could become regular events going forward, even if they are not expected to occur nearly as frequently as in the pre-vaccination era, when some 400 to 500 people died every year from infections.

Doctors are also reporting an increase in complications — both maternal and neonatal — from measles infections in pregnancy.

In a statement Tuesday, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the U.S. is “focused on stopping outbreaks.”

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” she said. “We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” she added, referencing funding the CDC has recently distributed to areas facing outbreaks.

The CDC recommends that children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, with the first shot at 12 months and the second at 4 to 6 years. Some doctors offer the first dose to younger babies if they live in an area where the virus is spreading. The CDC’s statement Tuesday said “we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

While Kennedy has at times acknowledged that the best way to prevent measles infections and spread is the MMR shot, including in a social media post Tuesday, he also has a long history of attacking vaccines with false arguments. As health secretary, he has downplayed the severity of outbreaks, overstated the risks of the vaccine, and pointed to unproven treatments as possible solutions for infections.

Public health experts have criticized the federal government for not doing more to address measles even as infections mounted and as it became clear in recent months that the country’s elimination status was well on its way to being lost. On Tuesday, Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.) called on Schwartz to resign after the PAHO decision was announced.

“The fact that the flag was raised, and it was not heeded, is to me the most alarming thing,” said Maia Majumder, a computational epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital, who co-authored a Lancet paper in May about the at-risk elimination designation. U.S. health officials are “not interested in doing the things that are necessary to maintain our measles elimination status,” she told STAT.

Kennedy, meanwhile, has argued that other countries have also seen more measles cases.

Canada lost its elimination status last year, and PAHO’s reverification commission also determined this week that measles had returned to endemicity in Mexico and Bolivia. A number of European countries — including the U.K. and Spain — have also lost their designation.

The U.S.’s susceptibility to measles has been building for years. Vaccination rates within certain regions and communities have slipped for any number of reasons: a rise in vaccine skepticism, the spread of misinformation online, failures of public health campaigns, or the perception that measles doesn’t pose a threat. Adults have made up sizable portions of infections in some recent case clusters, a sign that it’s not just a nascent retrenchment of parents not immunizing their children that’s allowing for transmission.

But for a long time, unvaccinated people were generally protected from the highly contagious virus because they were surrounded by so many others who were vaccinated, increasing the chances that any burgeoning outbreaks would be quickly snuffed out. (The CDC defines an outbreak as three or more linked cases.) Now, though, pockets of susceptible people, both adults and children, have grown so large that the virus can circulate among them for extended periods. Plus, more measles spread in other countries increases the likelihood of imported cases.

While vaccine coverage of 95% of people is considered sufficient to keep a lid on measles transmission, the vaccination rates for kindergarteners has dropped below 90% in nearly 20 states. Looking at local levels can reveal alarmingly low vaccination rates within individual counties and school districts.

Brewer noted that the CDC has quietly been supporting states in their outbreak responses, including with the recent funding. But the fact that top U.S. officials, whether Kennedy or Schwartz, aren’t regularly encouraging vaccination, as would’ve happened under previous administrations, including the first Trump presidency, has created a vacuum for rhetoric that undermines vaccination to fill.

“We need leadership to step up,” he said.
