#5504. Inside the Properties James Bond Has Made Famous as Robert Pattinson Gears Up to Play 007

It’s official: Robert Pattinson is stepping into the role of James Bond.

The news comes after years of speculation surrounding who might succeed Daniel Craig—who was the sixth actor to bring 007 to life, and portrayed the British spy in five films, ending with 2021’s “No Time To Die.”

The official James Bond X account shared a first look of Pattinson donning the infamous tux for the role, captioned “Identity Confirmed.”

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Director Denis Villeneuve alluded to the search for the next Bond in the statement.

“I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” the “Dune” director said. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007.”

Dozens of potential candidates have been floated as possibilities since Craig’s reign came to an end, including Idris Elba, Jacob Elordi, Callum Turner, and John Hardy.

Bond first walked onto the silver screen in 1962, when Sean Connery brought the iconic book character to life in the first film, “Dr. No.” There have been a whopping 25 Bond films so far, with Pattinson suiting up for the 26th.

After seven films, Connery ended his run in 1983 with “Never Say Never.” In 1969, George Lazenby became the only actor to star in a single film in the franchise, with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.”

Roger Moore held the role from 1973 to 1985, also impressively holding the gig for seven titles. Next up was Timothy Dalton, who starred in two films between 1987 and 1989.

Pierce Brosnan reinvigorated the franchise when he became Bond in 1995, holding the job until 2002. In 2006, Craig ushered in a new era, tackling 007 with a more rough-and-tumble edge.

Perhaps even more impressive than the scale of actors who have taken their martinis shaken, not stirred, is the sheer number of filming locations the franchise has made its mark on for over 60 years.

Hunting Bond, a fan site that tracks the locations, has identified nearly 600 filming spots across the world. While the James Bond universe is certainly action-packed, it’s also quite aspirational, and has often provided viewers with rich backgrounds and fascinating properties that became characters in their own right.

It would be nearly impossible to rank all of the lavish homes Bond has stepped foot in over the years, but there are definitely a handful that stand out in memory.

Even without a connection to one of the Bond films with the strongest pop culture staying power—”Diamonds Are Forever,” of course—the Elrod House in Palm Springs, CA, is an incredible dwelling.

Perched on a hillside overlooking Coachella Valley, the 8,900-square-foot home was designed by modernist architect John Lautner for interior designer Arthur Elrod.

The fascinating structure has a concrete dome-shaped roof, a circular living room, and a half-moon swimming pool that Connery’s Bond threw an enemy into during a heated fight scene.

Villa Sylva is a picturesque Greek estate that’s appeared in a handful of movies, including Moore’s “For Your Eyes Only”—although in the film, it assumed the role of the Madrid home of hitman Hector Gonzales.

The 12-bedroom luxury villa boasts unobstructed views of the Ionian Sea and is perched on an idyllic 10-acre property. Today, it can be rented as a wedding venue or a vacation home sleeping up to 18 people.

Given Bond’s important role at the UK-based M16, it only makes sense that at least some of the locations had to be local. The sprawling Luton Hoo Estate was a location in Brosnan’s 1999 film, “The World Is Not Enough” and Connery’s 1983 return for “Never Say Never Again.”

It’s also been featured in dozens of other projects, including “Downton Abbey.”

Built in 1903, the property is about an hour’s drive from London—a journey that would probably be cut in half when Bond is behind the wheel. The historic English country estate spans more than 1,000 acres and has a handful of structures—most notably, a five-star hotel and an exquisite mansion.

Craig’s Bond debut in the 2006 film, “Casino Royale,” was set in the breathtaking Ocean Club in the Bahamas.

The luxury resort has a number of sea-view villas for rent, including one that served as the perfect backdrop for a romantic scene between the spy and Solange Dimitrios, the wife of villain Alex Dimitrios.

Although Bond was just a visitor, the Ocean Club does have “67 turnkey oceanfront residences” available for ownership. The ultraprivate oceanfront abodes are available in a variety of sizes between two- and five-bedroom. Pricing begins at $7.5 million, according to the Ocean Club’s website.

It’s never been captured on screen in a Bond film, but 007 creator Ian Fleming built a bungalow called GoldenEye in Port Antonio, Jamaica.

The private estate is where the prolific author wrote all 13 of the original James Bond novels. Eventually, it was sold and turned into a resort, which is still called GoldenEye today. The property has been vastly expanded in the decades since Fleming, who died in 1964, lived there. It now includes lagoon cottages, villas, beach huts, and a spa.

The 25th Bond film, “No Time To Die,” provided a nod to the character’s birthplace. According to Architectural Digest, there’s a replica of Fleming’s desk in the opening scene of the film. Like the writer, Bond lives in a Jamaican bungalow in this installation, but it was built from scratch solely for filming.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5503. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

Materials provided by Semmelweis University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5502. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#5501. Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s “AI Leadership Symposium”

Moving enterprise AI workloads into production introduces practical challenges for chief information officers. Those challenges include managing costs, scaling enterprise AI infrastructure and establishing governance models to keep agents in check and data secure.

Cost and control were major themes of discussion at Dell Technologies Inc.’s “AI Leadership Symposium.” Expanding AI workloads can drive up infrastructure and model costs, while deploying autonomous agents introduces new questions about security, oversight and data access.

At the same time, organizations are exploring different ways to run AI, from private cloud environments to models operating directly on devices. That is creating demand for enterprise AI infrastructure and partnerships that can accommodate a wider range of deployment needs.

“No one is asking whether to adopt AI; that’s pretty much a done deal,” said John Furrier, executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “They’re asking who controls it, where it runs and whose law it operates.”

Furrier spoke with industry experts from Dell, Deepgram Inc., Singulr AI Inc., MisaLabs Inc. and Intel Corp., among others, during the AI Leadership Symposium. The interviews covered the infrastructure, partnerships and computing power needed to scale AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete keynote analysis from John Furrier:

Cloud token bills remain a major pressure point on enterprise AI budgets. That’s leading some businesses to look for ways to relieve that pressure, according to Helen O’Sullivan, AI business development manager and solutions specialist at Dell.

“A lot of our customers I support in the Bay Area, they’re dealing with this real immediate struggle of running through their token budget in a matter of weeks that they had allotted for months,” she told theCUBE. “You still use those frontier models, but you use the open source and infrastructure on-prem to at least eliminate some of the token stress and token maxing going on right now.”

Organizations can also make better use of existing data center capacity when evaluating enterprise AI infrastructure investments. Dell and Intel are helping customers evaluate those options, according to Tim Wood, sales director for the Northwest region at Intel, who joined O’Sullivan during the discussion.

“A lot of enterprises already have [central processing units] in their data center,” he said. “There may be existing resources and headroom in the infrastructure they already have that’s capable of doing some of these next-generation apps and workloads.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Helen O’Sullivan and Tim Wood:

As companies deploy more AI agents, they need better ways to monitor what those agents actually do and ensure their actions align with company policies and intentions. That means introducing runtime governance that can assess AI agent behavior during execution, according to Shiv Agarwal, co-founder and chief executive officer of Singulr AI Inc., who spoke alongside Sri Viswanath, founder and chief executive officer of Sycamore Labs Inc., and Victor Jakubiuk, co-founder of MisaLabs Inc.

“[It’s] as simple as an action where it reaches out to the internet to get some data or sends out an email to a private account or something,” Agarwal told theCUBE. “That could be deeply hidden inside an agentic action.”

Good AI governance also means setting boundaries around where models can access data and how they process it. CIOs often prefer virtual private clouds to keep sensitive information within a controlled environment, according to Viswanath.

“They’re also trying to architect in a way that all of the data stays there,” he said. “They don’t trust sending it outside because then we don’t know where it goes.”

The pace of AI development complicates those governance efforts. Companies need to ensure their systems behave as intended even as AI capabilities evolve, according to Jakubiuk.

“AI has no limit to the speed of development, speed of progress,” he said. “As an enterprise, as that AI lead, you want to be able to take the latest and greatest and stay on top.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Victor Jakubiuk, Shiv Agarwal and Sri Viswanath:

Deepgram is working with Dell and Fortanix Inc. to bring its voice AI models beyond the cloud and onto customer devices. Potential applications range from interactive voice response systems for small businesses to AI-enabled laptops for students, according to Nick Mann, staff technical program manager at Deepgram.

“I want our models on those, on the hardware, to run natively,” he told theCUBE. “Air-gapped. That’s where we want to get to. That’s where AI as a whole needs to start meeting people where they are and how they’re going to use it.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Nick Mann:

Deepgram’s plans reflect a broader push to develop AI solutions tailored to how customers want to build and deploy the technology. In Silicon Valley, where technically sophisticated buyers often prefer building their own solutions over buying packaged products, Dell is expanding its partner ecosystem to help meet that demand, according to Sean O’Connor (pictured), regional manager of ENT West, large enterprise and acquisition, at Dell.

“For us, that notion of ecosystem is starting to change,” he told theCUBE. “Today we’re here with Intel [Corp.], we’re here with SHI [International Corp.], we’re here with Microsoft [Corp.]. But that ecosystem also now is starting to bleed into private equity and venture capital.”

#5500. Aging Parents and Empty Nests Force Homeowners To Rethink Layouts Years Before the Move

Most homeowners know their homes may need updates to accommodate their changing needs as they age.

Some, however, are thinking even further ahead.

Instead of waiting until those changes are necessary, they’re investing in renovations years in advance to prepare for aging parents who might eventually move in after their children leave the nest.

Angi’s 2026 State of Home Spending Pulse study found that 66% of homeowners plan to make a major home investment within the next five years. And the 2027 Home Trends To Watch report predicts that 2027 will be the year they take a proactive approach and focus on creating a home that grows with them.

If you own your home, experts agree that you should anticipate how your needs could change in the next five to 10 years and use that information to guide your long-term home improvement goals today.

By doing so, you can make the most out of your renovation budget, avoid costly last-minute adjustments, and ensure your home comfortably adapts to the different stages of life.

Matt Plaskoff, CEO and founder of One Week Bath in Los Angeles, is seeing this proactive, multigenerational "future-proofing” trend among his clients.

“It comes down to people having heard stories of it going the other way. Mom falls or receives a diagnosis, and suddenly the family is trying to put in a walk-in shower and grab bars on short notice while suddenly incurring more costs with doctors and insurance,” says Plaskoff.

Multigenerational living is also at an all-time high, and the recent National Association of Realtors® Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers report reflects this shift. It found that 17% of homes purchased last year were intended for multigenerational households.

And when adult kids leave, there’s suddenly more space that makes it easier to create a home that works well for both aging in place and aging parents.

We can’t forget the housing affordability crisis forcing families to rethink the homes they already own.

“The house may no longer fit the household, but buying a better-fitting home can mean a higher price, a higher mortgage rate, and higher monthly expenses,” says Jon Brooks, co-founder of Momentum Realty in Jacksonville, FL.

Plus, it's more cost-effective to future-proof your home when you plan properly and actually have the funds to support your projects.

“The worst time to remodel is when you don’t have the budget for it. You make decisions that should take time and careful planning under pressure and may just accept whatever contractor can show up ASAP, even if it means you have to pay more,” says Plaskoff.

If you're already opening up walls for a bath remodel, for example, adding blocking for future grab bars, widening a doorway, or adding a curbless shower will be faster and cheaper than if you were to come back later and redo finished work.

Experts agree that a strong universal design features a functional yet beautiful bathroom with a wider doorway, good lighting, lever handles for knobs, a walk-in shower, and slip-resistant flooring.

“If done right, it feels more like a spa than a hospital, and that’s what matters most to those who are using it every day,” Plaskoff explains.

You might also consider adding a second structure to your backyard like an accessory dwelling unit or tiny home.

“For families with the space, an ADU is one of the best solutions we see. It gives an aging parent true independence, with their own kitchen, bath, and front door, while keeping them close enough for daily connection and support,” explains Michelle Squire, designer and principal at Studio SQUARE in San Francisco.

If long-term resale is important to you, be sure to consider what buyers value in your neighborhood. This way you can determine where to make permanent changes and where to keep things flexible.

“If you’re overimproving for the area, just understand you may have a harder time recouping that money if you choose to sell,” says Christina Rordam, real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando, FL.

At the end of the day, prioritize flexibility, try not to over improve for the neighborhood you’re in, and most importantly, consider what works best for you and your family.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5498. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5497. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5494. SiMa.ai’s Palette 3.0 runs many AI models on one chip and lifts throughput up to 3.5 times

Physical artificial intelligence chip startup SiMa Technologies Inc. today released Palette 3.0, a new version of its Palette software suite intended to allow many AI models to run concurrently on one chip.

According to the company, the release, which builds on the Palette Neat agentic development environment launched in June, can raise model throughput by as much as 3.5 times.

Developers building drones, robots and other autonomous machines, which need to run AI models on the device rather than in a data center, are a primary focus of the release. SiMa.ai argues that while industry incumbents rely on adapting legacy data center technology, it builds its software and silicon exclusively for physical AI.

Leading the new capabilities in Palette 3.0 is improved concurrent model execution on SiMa.ai’s Modalix MLSoC. Maintaining what the company describes as a low-power profile, a single chip can handle complex reasoning and multimodel workloads at the same time. The platform can also run separate Docker containers on the chip. Supported workloads include large language models and vision-language models.

Perception, depth and reasoning models used by drones and robots are also said to run faster on the new version. Working with ecosystem partners, SiMa.ai has added unified sensor fusion, dense neural depth fields and closed-loop digital twin simulation to the platform. The goal of the additions, SiMa.ai says, is to remove the integration and validation bottlenecks that slow down autonomous development.

Performance figures for those models are published in a new Model Registry, which SiMa.ai says measures every result within real-world power constraints. The company is offering competitive benchmarking details on request.

Also new in the release is a set of open-source capabilities for generative AI application development. Behind the 3.5-times throughput figure is speculative decoding, using the EAGLE3, DFlash and Gemma 4 MTP algorithms. Support has also been added for large mixture-of-experts models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-OSS-20B, which can now run on the Modalix MLSoC 16GB system-on-module.

Developers are free to adapt the open-source code, which is available on GitHub. Documentation for Palette 3.0 is provided through SiMa.ai’s Developer Center.

Founded in 2018 by Chief Executive Krishna Rangasayee, SiMa.ai offers a platform that combines purpose-built silicon with software for AI on physical devices. Notable customers and partners include Robert Bosch GmbH, Emerson Electric Co. and Synopsys Inc.

SiMa.ai raised $150 million in a Series C round at a $1.45 billion valuation in September. Fidelity Management & Research Co. and Amplify Partners co-led the round. The company has raised $500 million to date.

#5493. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5492. The Homeownership Gap Between Young and Old Americans Has Doubled—These Cities Reveal Why

The homeownership gap between younger and older Americans has more than doubled over the past four decades, with some of the nation's most expensive cities seeing the sharpest increases, according to a new report.

The analysis, from the Urban Institute, finds that nationally just 43% of households headed by adults aged 25 to 35 owned their homes in 2024, compared with 79% of those headed by adults 65 and older. The 35.8-percentage-point difference is more than twice the 17.5-point gap recorded in 1980.

But that divide pales in comparison to the gaping chasm in some of America's most expensive metropolitan areas. Between 1980 and 2024, the homeownership gap grew by 29 percentage points in Denver, 23 points in New York City, and 22 points in San Francisco, compared with 18.3 points nationally.

But those widening gaps also expose a deeper economic trade-off: The cities offering young Americans the greatest opportunities to earn more may be the very places preventing them from building wealth through homeownership

"The cities with the strongest labor markets tend to be the least affordable, so some will take the better job and rent indefinitely, giving up equity accumulation," explains Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Others will pass up higher-paying roles or move to cheaper, lower-opportunity markets in order to buy."

In 1980, younger households in Denver were nearly as likely as their older counterparts to own a home.

At the time, 55% of households headed by adults aged 25 to 35 owned their homes, compared with 67% of households headed by adults 65 and older.

By 2024, the younger group's homeownership rate had fallen to just 37%, while the older group's rate climbed to 78%, expanding the divide from 12 to 41 percentage points.

But the decline in young homeownership may reflect something besides worsening affordability: Denver's success in attracting young workers.

"Two things are likely at work. One is the affordability decline itself. The other is Denver’s growth as an economic hub that appeals to young workers, many of whom arrive as renters," says Jones. "That adds renters to the mix and dilutes the young homeownership rate, even for people who never intended to buy."

There, younger households were already far less likely to own homes in 1980, when their homeownership rate stood at 28%. By 2024, it had slipped only slightly, to 26%.

Older New Yorkers, meanwhile, saw their homeownership rate climb from approximately 43% to 63% over the same period.

"In New York, homeownership has always been expensive and out of reach for most young households, so there was little room to fall," Jones explains. "Young homeownership slipped only slightly, which suggests the current rate is close to a floor."

She suggests low COVID-19 pandemic-era mortgage rates may have helped some older households that had been waiting to purchase finally enter the market.

And regardless of how the divide developed, entering homeownership later can carry lasting financial consequences.

Separate research from Realtor.com, co-authored by Jones, found that purchasing a home by age 30 was associated with 22.5% higher net worth—approximately $119,000 more—by age 50, compared with buying in one's 40s, even after accounting for income, education, and marital status.

Those advantages can extend across generations, too. Children raised in homeowner households were 18.4 percentage points more likely to become homeowners themselves by age 35, the same research found.

One of the Urban Institute's most striking findings concerns a milestone that comes before homeownership: establishing an independent household.

In 1980, young adults in high-cost metropolitan areas were slightly more likely than their counterparts nationally to head their own households. By 2024, that relationship had reversed.

Just 41% of young adults in expensive markets were household heads, the lowest share among the study's housing cost categories.

Instead, more are living with parents, other relatives, or roommates. Research from Realtor.com backs this up, finding that a third of young adults lived with their parents across the country in 2025.

Yet expensive cities haven't lost their appeal. The share of young households living in high-cost markets actually edged up from 28% in 1980 to 31% in 2024, partly reflecting a broader shift toward urban areas.

What's changed is their housing tenure. In those markets, the homeownership rate among younger households fell from 40% to 32% over the same period.

So young adults are continuing to pursue opportunities in expensive cities, but fewer are establishing households of their own once they get there. And another finding suggests that rapidly rising prices may be changing the age composition of metropolitan areas, regardless of how expensive those places were to begin with.

Between 2014 and 2024, metropolitan areas experiencing faster home price appreciation generally saw declines in young adults' share of the population, the Urban Institute found.

The relationship held across high-, moderate-, and low-cost markets. But Jones cautions that the findings don't necessarily mean young people are being priced out.

"That can come from young people leaving, older people moving in, or both," she says. "Florida metros on the included chart may be an example. Their older populations are large and grew significantly during the pandemic, which could erode the young share on its own."

Indeed, the relationship between home prices and demographic changes could run in either direction.

"Young people may be fleeing places where costs are climbing, or older, more financially equipped buyers may be moving in and competing for homes," Jones says. "That pushes prices up, and the newcomers then make up a larger share of the population."

Determining whether younger residents are actually leaving would require examining changes in the number of young adults, not just their share of the population.

Still, other economic research suggests that housing costs can constrain where workers pursue employment.

A May 2025 analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond found that geographic mobility has declined across all age groups since the 1990s. Among the contributing factors, researchers identified restrictions on housing supply in economically productive cities, where high costs can discourage workers from relocating to pursue better opportunities.

The researchers also identified another potential obstacle: Older homeowners have become less responsive to rising local housing costs, making them more likely to stay put even as prices climb. In supply-constrained markets, that can make it harder for newcomers to move in.

Meanwhile, a February 2026 analysis from the St. Louis Fed found that home prices had risen approximately 207% from 2000 to 2024, outpacing the roughly 155% increase in per-capita incomes.

Together, the findings suggest that the costs of entering high-opportunity housing markets could affect younger Americans' earnings prospects as well as their ability to build wealth.

There may be a way around that trade-off for some.

"Remote work may be loosening the link between where people live and where the jobs are, which could enable more households to achieve homeownership without giving up job opportunities," Jones says.

But that flexibility is not available to everyone. Workers whose jobs require them to be physically present may face a more difficult choice between buying a home where they can afford one and pursuing careers in the cities where their skills command the highest wages.

And unlike the wealth accumulated by longtime homeowners, the career opportunities they pass up may be difficult to recover later.

#5491. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

#5490. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5489. Exclusive: Cogent Security’s DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents

Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today launched DefenseOS, an operating system designed for artificial intelligence agents that carry out defensive cybersecurity work inside the enterprise.

Arriving with DefenseOS are two new capabilities, Agent Policies and Agent Automations. The first is designed to give Cogent’s AI agents a deep understanding of the enterprise environment, while the second puts recurring security work on an automated schedule.

Cogent is pitching DefenseOS at security teams that are struggling to keep up as AI speeds up the discovery of vulnerabilities. In October, Microsoft Corp. fixed more than 1,400 security flaws in a single Patch Tuesday release, more than it fixed in all of 2025. The window between disclosure and exploitation has also shrunk, by Cogent’s count, from months in 2024 to only hours this year.

Prioritizing at that pace requires context such as which assets are business-critical, which are exposed to the internet and who owns them. According to the company, that information is spread across documents, teams and tribal knowledge, and most organizations see only a fraction of it.

In its role as the context engine for Cogent, DefenseOS ingests data from scanners, business systems and other security tools. Once the data has been normalized and deduplicated, DefenseOS encodes how the enterprise functions to deliver accurate risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The platform serves as the AI harness that sets the working environment and limits for Cogent’s agents.

The first of the two new capabilities, Agent Policies, is described by Cogent as creating a context layer that builds and grows via agents, turning how an enterprise works into rules. Those rules then shape how the Cogent platform handles asset context, risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The company claims the feature strips out much of the operational overhead that enterprises formerly had to put into running a vulnerability management program.

The second, Agent Automations, acts as the execution layer within DefenseOS. Using it, security teams can build agentic workflows that run automatically to generate alerts and reports, investigate vulnerabilities and deliver remediation guidance on a consistent basis.

Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Geng Sng said recurring reports, known investigations and routine alerts take up a large share of a security team’s week. With Agent Automations, he said, teams can “define that work once” and have Cogent’s agents run it on their schedule.

“Every enterprise runs its security program differently, and moving at machine speed means grasping those differences,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti. “DefenseOS unifies the context of an enterprise environment, surfacing rules into Agent Policies that a customer can codify, and creating the runtime environment for continuous cyber defense led by AI agents.”

The launch follows the release earlier this month of VR-1.1, a new version of Cogent’s frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

DefenseOS and Agent Automations are available now to all Cogent customers. Agent Policies has launched in beta for new Cogent deployments ahead of general availability at a later date.

Founded in 2025 and staffed by former researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal AI Inc. and Coinbase Global Inc., Cogent says Fortune 500 security teams using its platform have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%. The company has raised $53 million to date, including a $42 million Series A led by Bain Capital Ventures in February.

#5488. Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle

A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.

At issue is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.

The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.

As the nation confronts a shortage of 4.03 million homes and an aging energy grid, supporters argue that reducing regulatory hurdles will accelerate infrastructure development. But preservation advocates warn the changes could leave communities with less influence over what gets built—and what gets lost.

"Preservation is not a hindrance to progress," Heather Veneziano, director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, told Realtor.com® during a recent walking interview through Bayou St. John, one of New Orleans' oldest neighborhoods.

Rather than keeping neighborhoods frozen in time, she argued, preservation can help communities determine how they evolve.

"Keeping things static is impossible," Veneziano said.

New Orleans provides a particularly salient standpoint from which to understand Veneziano’s perspective.

The city is home to 26 nationally recognized historic districts encompassing more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area, according to the city. Indeed, its architectural heritage is so extensive that it became the only entire city included on the World Monuments Fund's Irreplaceable America list.

Veneziano helped lead the nomination, informed in part by the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and the connections to place that could not be rebuilt elsewhere.

"You lose all your really strong ties and connections to place, but also to people," she said of the communities uprooted after the devastating 2005 superstorm. "And places don't matter without people."

But Veneziano sees the buildings themselves as part of what makes those communities viable.

"It's an economic driver for the community, it's housing at a basic level for the community," she said. "Those are the containers for all of the services that happen in your community."

Along Bayou St. John, Veneziano pointed to the Pitot House, built in 1799, as an example of another kind of value older buildings retain.

Its elevated living quarters reflect a time when residents built knowing water would eventually come, while its surviving materials offer lessons in constructing homes suited to Louisiana's flood risks.

Yet, those lessons might have been erased had preservationists not found a way to accommodate another pressing community need.

In 1964, the religious order that owned the property needed land for a girls' school. Rather than allow its demolition, preservationists raised money to move the house 220 feet down the street on flatbed trucks.

The compromise allowed both the school and the house to continue serving the community. And today, the deal serves as a reminder of how preservation can accommodate development rather than prevent it.

Not every historic property can be relocated, however, and the expense of finding alternatives can test even the most committed to protecting a neighborhood's housing resources.

In March, Jane Place Neighborhood Sustainability Initiative, a community land trust dedicated to permanently affordable housing, sought permission to demolish a century-old shotgun house in Mid-City.

The nonprofit argued that rehabilitation would be prohibitively expensive and higher-density construction would better serve the property.

Preservation authorities disagreed, finding insufficient evidence that the house was beyond repair. Jane Place eventually withdrew its appeal without a finalized replacement development plan.

The spat concerned local demolition rules, not Section 106. But it exposed competing interpretations of how best to protect a neighborhood's housing resources: Preserve an existing home or make room for more?

Veneziano acknowledged that unclear local requirements can frustrate homeowners trying to maintain or renovate their properties.

"If your municipality doesn't have their act together and isn't clear about what their guidelines are," she said, "it can be very challenging to homeowners."

In a city facing an estimated shortage of 44,000 affordable rental units, the case for preserving old buildings can be difficult to reconcile with the urgent need for new homes. But elsewhere in the Big Easy, a long-vacant public building offers another approach.

In September, a century-old firehouse reopened after decades of vacancy, transformed into seven affordable apartments above an early-childhood education center.

The mixed-use redevelopment cost approximately $8 million, including $1.35 million in state historic tax credits and $725,000 in federal disaster recovery funds.

"The Louisiana Avenue Firehouse shows us that demolition of historic buildings is not always the answer," Louisiana Housing Corporation Executive Director Kevin Delahoussaye said.

But the very public investment that helped save the building also triggered Section 106 review—and that additional requirement is what housing advocates argue can make federally assisted developments more expensive and difficult to finance.

Their argument is simple: More reviews take more time. More time costs more money. And combined, that can make a project not worth it.

YIMBY Action, which supports the proposed Section 106 exemption, estimates that at least $10 billion annually in federal housing and community development funding could move faster under the broader permitting package, citing delays that can jeopardize financing or discourage developers from accepting public money altogether.

Veneziano emphasized that preservationists aren't simply trying to "save this fancy house." Their work, she explained, is "really community engagement"—helping residents recognize and protect histories that might otherwise be overlooked.

That concern brought hundreds of preservationists, civil rights advocates, and tribal representatives to the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9 to oppose changes to Section 106.

"Our sacred places are living places of prayer," Harry Antonio Jr., governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in New Mexico, told the crowd.

The Senate proposal would narrow consideration of certain effects on historic places, including noise and visual impacts, raising concerns about the protection of sacred landscapes, burial grounds, and other culturally significant sites.

Veneziano pointed to a conflict farther upriver in Wallace, LA, where federal scrutiny exposed problems with a developer's assessment of a proposed grain terminal.

There, descendants of enslaved residents opposed the project, which would have been built near historic plantations, burial grounds, and their predominantly Black community.

A ProPublica investigation revealed that an archaeological consultant's original findings about potential harm to historic sites had been stripped from a report prepared for the developer. The Army Corps of Engineers subsequently rejected the assessment as insufficient and demanded further investigation.

In April 2024, the Corps determined that noise, light pollution, and the terminal's industrial appearance would adversely affect Wallace's historic character—precisely the kinds of impacts the Senate proposal would subject to a narrower standard of review.

The company behind the terminal abandoned the project later that year, blaming prolonged permitting delays. Residents celebrated the outcome as a victory.

Such lengthy reviews, however, may be the exception rather than the rule.

An October analysis by Virginia's Department of Historic Resources found that 85% of nearly 9,900 projects completed Section 106 review within 30 days. Just 6% took longer than 90 days, primarily because they required additional surveys or involved potential harm to historic properties.

Those figures aren't necessarily representative nationwide, nor do they establish whether reviews actually delayed construction.

"If you're trying to get a project through, yeah, it's annoying," Veneziano acknowledged.

Still, Section 106 doesn't prohibit development. It requires agencies to consider the consequences and potential alternatives before proceeding.

And as Congress weighs how to accelerate construction, lawmakers will also confront a more fundamental question: Who gets to determine what a community can afford to lose?

Veneziano posed a question of her own: "How do we take the best of what we have, and build upon it into the future?"
