#5465. Sellers Vastly Outnumber Buyers as Top Metros Shift Further: Report

Buying house, real estate deal and investment. Tiny woman carrying money in shopping cart to buy family home, agent or broker giving building model and apartment key cartoon vector illustration

Sellers have largely had the upper-hand in the housing market since the pandemic as home prices reached new peaks, giving sellers max equity to see large returns on their investments. Now, as the market is observing some shifts, a new report from Redfin found that seller’s markets are losing ground.

Homebuyers have gained more negotiating power across the country, as Redfin data estimated there were 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October. This was the biggest recorded gap seen since 2013, as well as the sixth month in a row this measure has reached a new record.

Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan said that sellers are “increasingly competing for buyers’ attention,” which has led to more “price reductions, concessions and other savings.”

“First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle—but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate,” he continued. “With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting—and can afford today’s costs—may have an opportunity to make a move.”

Looking at the 50 most populous metros in the U.S., only three were seller’s markets in October. Redfin used “proprietary” data on buyer behavior and MLS listings to estimate the balance of buyers and sellers.

Notably, all three of the seller’s markets were located in the Northeast, where home prices remain higher than other regions. These three markets saw home prices rise 3.3% year-over-year in October, compared to prices increasing only 0.3% in buyer’s markets.

The top of the three seller’s markets was Nassau County, New York, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers, a gap that actually shrank from 28.3% the month prior. The other two markets were Newark, New Jersey (14.3% fewer sellers, down from 17.6% the month prior) and Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (12.1% fewer sellers, down from 20.1% the month prior).

Another difference from September’s data was the loss of a fourth seller’s market—Milwaukee, Wisconsin, which is now balanced between buyers and sellers.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

#5464. Beyond Beauty: Kitchens That Work as Well as They Look

A kitchen at Skyline by Toll Brothers in Summit at Orchard Hills in Irvine, California.

Gena Kirk had a couple of non-negotiables when she renovated her Southern California kitchen: a Moroccan door that would open to the pantry and a touchless faucet that she “couldn’t live without.” Turns out, Kirk’s design decisions are in lockstep with many homeowners today who prioritize multifunctional kitchens that are inherently personal.

“Home buyers are less afraid of taking some risk and making their kitchens more curated to feel like it’s their own,” says Kirk, vice president of KB Home Corporate Design Studio.

In fact, today’s more nuanced kitchen is reflected in the 2027 National Kitchen and Bath Association’s Kitchen Trends Report, released in October. Among the findings are expanding kitchen floor plans with more clearly defined zones and a growing preference for personalized gathering spaces over bland, impersonal kitchens designed with resale in mind.

A kitchen at Toll Brothers at Thornebrook in Bulverde, Texas.

“While the kitchen has always been the ‘heart of the home,’ that idea has taken on new meaning,” said Bill Darcy, global president and CEO of NKBA, commenting on the report. “We’ve entered a new era of what the kitchen can do for homeowners—solving real problems … and elevating the way we live.”

We ask more of our kitchens today. Beyond meal preparation, they serve as gathering places for everything from homework and family dinners to entertaining. As their role expands, so does their connection to surrounding spaces. Mudrooms, pantries, and back kitchens are becoming more common, along with dedicated coffee and beverage stations, baking centers, and pet areas.

“[Kitchen] design is becoming more intentional to reflect how people cook, entertain, and connect,” says Lisa McClelland, senior vice president of the Toll Brothers Design Studio. “The emphasis is on creating spaces that feel open and welcoming while providing distinct areas for preparation, dining, and conversation.”

According to the NKBA report, kitchen footprints are expected to continue growing over the next three years. Yet even as kitchens get larger, their layouts are becoming simpler, “with less clutter and a more spacious feel,” the report states. The traditional kitchen work triangle remains important, along with multifunctional features that support a wider range of activities.

“People are thinking about how they operate in their kitchen,” Kirk says. She also predicts continued growth in products designed to simplify everyday tasks, such as motion-activated faucets, workstation sinks that combine a cutting board and built-in strainer, and countertop cabinets and drawers to store small appliances.

“It’s really about form and function,” Kirk says. “People want to be organized so everything is in one place versus spread throughout the kitchen.”

A kitchen at KB Home’s Primrose community in Lancaster, California.

Kitchen islands have evolved beyond their strictly utilitarian roots, too, becoming larger and more central to everyday living. Features such as “thoughtful seating, storage, and room to work” enhance their role as gathering spaces, McClelland says. “The goal is a kitchen that feels effortless, whether you’re making breakfast or hosting a large celebration with family and friends.”

Although kitchens are working harder, homeowners want them to look as good as they cook. Furniture-like cabinetry, layered lighting, and handcrafted, artisanal details help seamlessly bridge kitchens with the rest of the home.

“Faucets, cabinet hardware, and lighting can coordinate without matching exactly, creating a layered, collected look that feels personal rather than overly designed,” McClelland says.

Kirk notes a marketplace shift toward using more natural materials, including quartzite countertops and backsplashes and woods such as walnut that show natural graining. The NKBA report highlights this shift, with quartzite and quartz as the top two countertop materials that will be a key design feature in the coming years.

“Consumers are more interested in natural products, period. Not only in what they’re putting in their mouths, but what they’re putting around them,” Kirk says.

A kitchen at Toll Brothers at Sedona in Sedona, Arizona.

Lighting is emerging as a key design element, as well. “Good kitchen lighting gives you useful choices, and placement is critical, especially at work surfaces,” lighting designer Nathan Orsman notes in the NKBA report. Layered lighting designs include undercabinet, task, and decorative lighting, all part of the recipe that helps “shape a space that feels both practical and inviting throughout the day,” McClelland says.

Layered lighting designs include under-the-counter and built-in cabinet, task, and decorative lighting, all part of the recipe that helps “shape a space that feels both practical and inviting throughout the day,” McClelland adds.

Mixed metal hardware and plumbing fixtures that blend finishes, from brushed brass and gold tones to matte black, nickel, and stainless, are another way homeowners are expressing their individual styles, McClelland says. Likewise, she adds, “blending natural wood tones, creamy neutrals, and rich textures creates spaces that feel both refined and welcoming.”

Beyond the visible design elements, technology and wellness features are playing an increasingly important role in kitchen design. Solutions that enhance natural light, improve ventilation, and filter water are helping create healthier, more comfortable spaces. Multifunctional appliances are also gaining traction as homeowners look for greater convenience and versatility.

“Consumers are looking for convenience, form, and functionality,” Kirk says.

A kitchen at KB Home’s Gateway community in El Cajon, California.

According to the NKBA report, top appliance features include ovens with air-frying and steam-cooking capabilities, dedicated beverage units, and refrigerators with zoned storage that supports healthy habits.

“Manufacturers are getting smarter about the products they are producing that follow the health and wellness trends the consumers are after,” Kirk says.

Kitchens have long commanded a significant share of homeowners’ design budgets. More and more, though, their influence extends well beyond the kitchen itself, shaping design decisions throughout the home.

“We’re building the kitchen first, and then that’s leading to the rest of their home design,” Kirk says.

Although design preferences vary by region, the desire for kitchens tailored to homeowners’ lifestyles remains consistent. “The common thread is a desire for kitchens that feel warm, functional, and highly personalized,” McClelland says. “Buyers want spaces that support everyday living while still delivering the craftsmanship and luxury details that make a home special.”

#5463. Job Growth Slows Nationally, but Some Local Markets Tell a Different Story

Job growth is one of the most important signals for home builders, as employment security helps shape consumer confidence, household formation, and the willingness to make a major purchase. And right now, the latest employment picture is a mixed one for the housing industry.

While employment growth remained positive, the U.S. added just 29,000 positions in September 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Meanwhile, unemployment edged up to 4.2%. The slowdown fits a broader pattern of relatively modest hiring rather than a sharp deterioration in the labor market.

The composition of growth is equally important. Education and health services remained the strongest employment engine, expanding 1.7% from a year earlier. Information employment, by contrast, fell 4% year over year, while financial activities declined 1.1% over the same period.

These differences matter for builders. Two markets can add a similar number of jobs but generate different levels of housing demand depending on the industries driving growth and the incomes associated with those positions.

The national slowdown also masks significant geographic variation.

Salt Lake City led the major markets tracked by Zonda with 2.8% year-over-year employment growth in September, followed by Raleigh at 2.1% and Las Vegas at 1.9%.

The picture changes when looking at the number of jobs created since last year. Dallas added 36,200 positions despite employment growing a more modest 0.8%. New York City added 29,800, Los Angeles 28,600, Houston 25,100, and Phoenix 24,400.

That distinction is also important: percentage growth can identify accelerating economies, while absolute job creation provides another measure of the potential scale of household demand.

At the other end of the spectrum, Washington, D.C., lost 66,800 jobs and employment declined 2% since September 2025. Indianapolis fell 1.1%, Portland 0.9%, and Atlanta 0.3%. Still, several markets with declining employment have not experienced unusually high unemployment rates, suggesting builders should avoid treating negative job growth as a standalone demand signal.

For builders making multiyear land decisions, the outlook through 2031 may be even more important. The strongest projected employment gains cluster in Texas, the Mountain and Desert region, and the Carolinas, per Moody’s. Raleigh is forecast for 9.9% total employment growth from December 2026 through December 2031, followed by Austin at 9.7%, Orlando at 8.4%, and Las Vegas at 7.9%.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s Apartment Outlook subscription.

#5462. LanceDB raises $57.5M to accelerate AI model training with multimodal data platform

LanceDB Inc., the developer of database technology designed to speed up artificial intelligence models, today announced it has raised $57.5 million in early-stage funding to bring a multimodal lakehouse to researchers, model builders and platform teams.

Bessemer Venture Partners and Innovation Endeavors led the Series B round. Other investors in the round included Theory Ventures, Dimension, Swift Ventures, CRV and Y Combinator, bringing the company’s total funding to $98.5 million.

AI is making it easier to create and interpret increasingly complex forms of data, but creating it also brings an infrastructure problem. LanceDB is tackling this problem by providing a unified multimodal data lakehouse, giving researchers, enterprise outfits and AI agents a unified way to access, find, prepare and train on that data without spending weeks managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Typically, research teams have to put different parts of their dataset in different places, and they lose weeks or months getting a whole training dataset ready for that single training run at the end of the day,” co-founder and Chief Executive Chang She told SiliconANGLE in an interview. “There’s a missing data layer for AI today, and that’s what we’re trying to build.”

LanceDB’s technology is built on Lance, an open-source data format designed for AI workloads that combines structured information with images, video and other large files. Unlike traditional analytics formats optimized for processing entire tables, Lance supports the rapid retrieval and modification of individual records, making it particularly useful for searching and preparing massive training datasets.

The company built this format into a large-scale data lakehouse for retrieval, which is needed for the sheer scale of information needed to train modern AI models. A lakehouse combines the flexibility of a data lake, which can store enormous amounts of raw information, with database-style capabilities for organizing, querying and managing that data.

“Part of what makes multimodal data different and more difficult is the size of the data,” She explained.

By bringing multimodality to the lakehouse format, LanceDB brings different forms of AI training data into a single platform, allowing developers to search, organize and prepare their datasets without maintaining separate systems for each data type. It can connect directly to customers’ existing cloud storage, where the data remains, while distributing computational workloads across the infrastructure required to process it.

Multimodal AI involves more than combining text, audio, images and video. Autonomous vehicles, robotics and world models also involve three-dimensional sensor information, geospatial coordinates, time-series data and annotations that explain what the sensors are detecting.

For example, a self-driving car doesn’t merely capture an image. Its sensors might produce a three-dimensional representation of the surrounding environment, which then needs to be associated with information that identifies roads, pedestrians, vegetation and other objects.

The sheer amount of data included in lidar 3D clouds, images, video, audio and more can take up, on average, 10 to 20 petabytes of data in a single table for many large training workflows, with some becoming even larger – potentially approaching 80 to 100 petabytes. Researchers and model builders may maintain huge pools of data across different systems because conventional platforms weren’t designed around the requirements of multimodal AI.

Researchers must then assemble, reconcile and store different components of a training dataset to enrich it for training. The curation itself can take weeks or months just to move, prepare and process. LanceDB’s answer is to manage the infrastructure itself without ever copying or moving data from enterprise or research storage, giving it a single unified access point.

“The data stays in place,” She explained. “It remains yours. We don’t need to copy it.”

In short, LanceDB isn’t simply introducing a new way to store data; the objective is to provide a way to access the data less often, without needing to copy, convert or move it through network infrastructure. This greatly speeds up what She refers to as the “AI flywheel,” which is currently driven by feeding AI models good data as quickly as possible to mint and roll them out.

“The faster we can make that spin, the faster research teams can get to higher quality models and allow us to make even more interesting AI applications,” She said.

Notable customers include Runway AI Inc., which adopted LanceDB’s enterprise platform as its AI training needs expanded. Netflix Inc. built a media data lake on the technology for content creation. And Microsoft Corp. uses the platform as a data layer for training models on tens of billions of rows of image and code data. The platform lets these organizations consolidate data management, search, curation and feature engineering into a unified workflow, helping researchers prepare training datasets at petabyte scale without juggling separate infrastructure systems.

“A training example at Runway doesn’t stay still,” said Runway Chief Technology Officer Kamil Sindi. “It starts as a video and a prompt, then we add embeddings, resolution and duration metadata, whatever the next experiment needs. We first started using the Lance format in 2024 because it was the only option that handled unstructured data, column appends, distributed reads and ad-hoc SQL all at once. We’ve since become a LanceDB Enterprise customer.”

She said LanceDB intends to use the new funding to expand its multimodal data platform and accelerate the AI model development cycle, particularly by improving large-scale data curation, feature engineering and data loading to keep thousands of graphics processing units supplied efficiently during training. The company will also deepen its support for emerging AI workloads, including video generation, world models and robotics, where researchers must manage growing volumes of first-person sensor data, synthetic data and other multimodal information.

#5461. Shoppable Model Homes Bring New Convenience to Buyers

Homeowners are becoming more practical in nearly every aspect of homeownership. This pragmatic mindset is also influencing the model home experience. For today’s home shopper, inspiration has greater value when buyers can actually put it to use.

Although buyers are drawn to the blank-canvas opportunity of a new build, decision fatigue is real, and tools that build confidence and save time are a welcome relief.

“We are seeing a lot of interest in making models actionable through features like the shoppable model home,” says Ali Richert, enterprise sales, head of home builder at Wayfair Professional.

In addition to shoppable models, furnished homes are popular too. A Zonda survey showed that 73% of buyers would be open to buying a furnished or partially furnished home.

With affordability still a challenge, buyers are looking closely at the overall value of a new-home purchase, including what builders can offer beyond the home itself.

“Regardless of why someone is buying a house, most home buyers will have one thing in common after getting the keys. They will need to furnish the home,” says Richert.

“Historically, the relationship between a builder and buyer ended at closing. Now builders are asking how they can help make the full journey easier.”

“This is one of the ideas that drive innovations like our shoppable model homes or even alternative closing incentives, like home buyer Wayfair gift cards. Instead of furnishing a model to inspire buyers, builders are beginning to view furnishing as an extension of the home buying experience itself,” she says.

In shoppable models, features like scannable QR codes, product links, online storefronts, or other purchasing arrangements simplify the process and bridge the gap between inspiration and real-life functionality, a pragmatic benefit that saves time and builds confidence when envisioning what life will look and feel like at home.

Various buyer groups see benefit in these features, explains Richert.

Investors may need to furnish a whole home quickly to go to market. A second-home buyer might want their home furnished immediately, so that vacations can be taken. First-time and move-up buyers may not have enough existing furniture to fill a space.

But regardless of why you are buying a home, “having a turnkey option for furnishing solutions can remove time, stress, and uncertainty from a process that can seem overwhelming,” she says.

“For a lot of buyers, especially after the long process of choosing a builder, a lender, a community, finishes, cabinets, flooring, and countless other decisions, the appeal of having to skip another major project full of decisions can be incredibly appealing.”

Love the look and the vibe of the model? Model home merchandisers make it look easy, but the aesthetic and the experience are the result of a highly curated, researched process that requires training, talent, and access to products.

Model homes not only display the latest trends and demonstrate how to make the best use of various spaces, but their design details are also selected to appeal to the target market. It’s no wonder that buyers find the aesthetic compelling.

“We focus heavily on purposeful merchandising and thoughtful space planning, showing buyers how each room can function, including multifunctional spaces and ideas they can realistically incorporate into their own home,” says Megan Calmes, director of sales and marketing with Creative Design.

“Additionally, we think about the buyer’s journey beyond the purchase. We want the model to feel aspirational, but also attainable.”

Models aren’t like generic furniture showrooms. The specifics of the floor plan guide the selection of furnishings, which means buyers are seeing pieces chosen for the very spaces they may soon call home.

For example, a buyer might choose a sofa on their own for the new living room, but that’s only a small part of the overall design. Accents like tables, rugs, and artwork matter too. The model demonstrates how these pieces work together, both aesthetically and within the room’s dimensions.

The model shows you how to assemble a look, not just admire it.

A flex room has a ton of potential, but will various uses work comfortably in real life? A model can demonstrate the size and placement of furniture and accents to support a particular purpose, or even multiple functions, within the available space.

Having shoppable tools, or the option to purchase the home furnished as demonstrated, can make those possibilities easier to recreate.

The vast majority of house hunters aren’t designers, so having access to professionally selected furnishings and decor gives buyers a practical head start.

Personalization is always possible, of course. Buyers might purchase the larger anchor pieces, such as a sofa, rug, and dining table, then bring in their own artwork, textiles, or accessories to make the space their own.

This article was originally published on NewHomeSource.com.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5460. Builder Sentiment Falls to 14-Year Low in November

Builder confidence fell sharply in November as higher mortgage rates, persistent affordability challenges, and rising construction costs continued to weigh on the new-home market, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB).

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell four points to 25 in November, its lowest reading since April 2012. The index stood at 29 in October. Any reading below 50 indicates more builders view market conditions as poor than good.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” says Bill Owens, chairman of the NAHB. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

All three components of the HMI declined during the month. The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, while the component measuring sales expectations over the next six months declined two points to 30. Prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, its lowest level in 15 years excluding the onset of the pandemic in 2020.

In response to weaker demand, builders continued to rely heavily on incentives and price reductions to attract buyers. The share of builders cutting home prices increased to 46% in November, the highest level of the post-Covid period. The average price reduction remained at 6% for the eighth consecutive month.

Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high. November marked the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders reported using incentives. That represents a further deterioration from October, when 43% of builders reported cutting prices and 65% used incentives.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” says Robert Dietz, NAHB chief economist. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence, and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

On a three-month moving-average basis, builder confidence declined in every region. The Northeast fell four points to 34, the Midwest declined five points to 35, the South dropped three points to 27, and the West fell three points to 23.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

The tree makes an appearance on the cover, as well, shining alongside the statement-making picture-frame windows and rustic checkerboard flooring that make the Gaines home so recognizable.

#5455. Red Hat and Microsoft bring OpenShift virtual machines to Azure

IBM Corp. subsidiary Red Hat and Microsoft Corp. are expanding their longtime engineering partnership to enable enterprises to run virtual machines on Microsoft Azure using Red Hat’s OpenShift Virtualization platform, providing an alternative to traditional hypervisors and what Red Hat called a path to modernizing legacy applications.

The collaboration, announced today, involves changes to Azure’s underlying computing architecture to connect it natively with Linux through Microsoft direct virtualization. That’s an Azure feature that gives performance-sensitive workloads near-bare-metal access to underlying hardware components.

Red Hat said this provides a direct pipeline between key hardware such as graphics processing units and isolated workloads. The companies are also working to give Linux-based workloads more direct access to Azure’s hardware resources, including graphics processing units.

Separately, Red Hat said it’s making its Lightwell Network vulnerability remediation service available through Microsoft’s Azure Marketplace.

The virtualization initiative addresses growing enterprise concerns about hypervisor licensing costs, hardware availability and the complexity of managing virtual machines alongside newer containerized applications. Red Hat said those pressures have intensified as organizations seek to accommodate AI workloads without abandoning existing applications.

Virtualization market leader Broadcom Inc. recently took aim at the same issue by open-sourcing its software for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same protocols that the Kubernetes container orchestrator uses. At the center of the effort is Microsoft’s direct virtualization, which lets Linux-based and cloud-native platforms running on Azure virtual machines access the same virtualization and hardware capabilities available to Azure-native services.

Red Hat said it will be the first commercial Microsoft partner to support the technology through OpenShift Virtualization on Azure Red Hat OpenShift, the jointly engineered and managed Kubernetes service offered by the two companies.

The agreement includes collaboration on several upstream open-source projects, including KubeVirt, LibVirt, QEMU and the Linux kernel. KubeVirt enables organizations to manage virtual machines and containers using Kubernetes tools.

Microsoft has extended KubeVirt beyond the Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine hypervisor by adding support for its own hypervisor. That allows OpenShift Virtualization to run on Azure virtual machines using Microsoft’s direct virtualization technology.

The approach is designed to let organizations consolidate traditional virtual machines, containerized applications and AI workloads on a common platform. Red Hat said its migration toolkit for virtualization will help customers move workloads from existing hypervisors.

The companies said the architecture will also improve resource utilization by supporting CPU and memory overcommitment, enabling more workloads to share available infrastructure. Kernel-level isolation is intended to protect sensitive workloads without compromising performance.

“Enterprises shouldn’t have to choose between managing rising hypervisor costs and accelerating their IT roadmaps,” Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer, said in a statement. He said the collaboration would provide a common foundation for modernizing existing virtual machines and running AI workloads.

The companies did not announce a general availability date for the new virtualization capabilities.

Red Hat also said Lightwell Network is immediately available through private offers on Azure Marketplace, allowing customers to obtain remediated versions of vulnerable open-source software dependencies.

Lightwell addresses a persistent application security problem: correcting vulnerabilities in third-party software without forcing upgrades that could disrupt production applications.

The service provides version-specific fixes through secured repositories, accompanied by signed software artifacts and supporting provenance, software bills of materials and vulnerability information where applicable.

Customers can incorporate those fixes into existing development and deployment pipelines without replacing their vulnerability scanners, artifact repositories or build systems. Findings can surface in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, while Azure Policy provides governance controls.

Customers can purchase Lightwell subscriptions through Azure Marketplace and apply eligible spending toward their Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitments.

#5454. U.S. Chamber Backs Capital Gains Tax Exclusion Bill Aimed To Reduce Taxes on Profits From Home Sales

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has announced support for reducing taxes on the profits homeowners make on the sale of their home, saying it could stimulate more home sales.

Raising the capital gains tax exclusion—something hundreds of members of Congress and a number of real estate groups have pushed for this year—is one key lever that Washington, DC hasn't yet pulled. It could have major implications for the housing market, the Chamber said.

"Capital gains taxes tend to distort housing choices by discouraging individuals from selling their homes because of changing family or health circumstances," the group said. "And the taxation of capital gains in excess of exemption caps creates inequities between homeowners with different job circumstances and those living in different parts of the country."

The most visible effort in Congress comes from the More Homes on the Market Act, sponsored by Rep. Jimmy Panetta (R-CA), which would double the current exclusion. Realtor.com® has reached out to his office for comment.

Both the Senate and the House have versions of the bill, which are almost identical. The Chamber said that bill offers a "reasonable, cost-effective solution" to spur more home sales.

The two versions have picked up 186 sponsors and cosponsors in Congress, including large numbers of Democrats and Republicans. Earlier this year, Panetta acknowledged the push faces resistance. A congressional analysis from last year estimated such a change could deprive the government of $46.4 billion in tax revenue. Even a more targeted approach, like raising the exclusion only for people over 55, could still cost $4.9 billion.

The National Association of Realtors® also champions the bill to change the tax scheme, because it could allow more people to sell their homes without incurring a punishing tax bill. Kevin Brown, president of NAR, lobbied for the law as he spoke to a panel in Congress in June.

Congress set the current capital gains scheme in 1997. Sellers can exclude up to $250,000 in profit if single, or $500,000 if married and filing jointly, when they sell a primary home, with few strings attached.

But the law didn't include adjustments for inflation. As home prices have appreciated in the years since, homeowners see a mounting impact. The longer the value of their home appreciates, the larger the cut the federal government can take as a capital gains tax when they do sell.

Oftentimes, these might be older Americans whose lifestyle might support downsizing. But they're "locked in" to their homes thanks to high mortgage rates.

That causes large tax bills, especially for those who have stayed in their homes the longest. Or, those who live in areas where home prices have grown the fastest. NAR has estimated that nearly 13 million homeowners would face a tax penalty if they sold their homes today. Brown argued that raising the exclusion limits would help free up housing inventory at a time when the country is facing a major supply crunch.

"Capital gains indexing has huge bipartisan support," Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance told Realtor.com. He brought up the possibility that it might appear in the next Congress in the form of a reintroduced bill or as a part of a reconciliation package.

"It would certainly unlock a number of homes immediately and free up their owners to do something else once they retire, and help families looking to make that next move," Allen said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5452. Chainguard goes self-serve with free Starter plan and $500-a-month Team plan

Software supply chain security company Chainguard Inc. is now offering its products on a self-serve basis, with the launch today of a free plan called Chainguard Starter and a paid Team plan priced at $500 a month.

The free plan covers nearly all of Chainguard’s products, with usage limits set at a level that fits a personal project or a small team. According to Chainguard, users can sign up, pull an image, connect their package manager to its screened libraries and place coding agents in a sandbox in one sitting, with no credit card or sales call required.

The launch comes after Black October, the name given to a run of supply chain attacks and critical vulnerability disclosures in the third week of October. With incidents like those, a team may have only until the end of the day to deal with a bad dependency, according to the blog post in which Chainguard announced the plans. In such cases, the company wrote, “nobody is going to wait on a purchase order.”

Until now, access to Chainguard’s products has typically required a conversation with its sales team first. One exception was Catalog Starter, a free beta plan offered earlier this year that was limited to five container images. Chainguard says the sales-led model, designed around large companies with procurement processes, works far less well for a team that needs a hardened base image ahead of its next deployment.

In most cases, moving a service onto Chainguard requires changing only a single line in the file that defines its container image. Security engineers can also put Chainguard’s images and libraries through their own scanners before signing anything, according to the company.

Starter includes five container images from Chainguard’s catalog of more than 3,000 minimal images, which are claimed to have near-zero known vulnerabilities, with downloads of up to 100 gigabytes a month. A software bill of materials and signed build provenance are provided for every image.

Also part of the plan is Chainguard Libraries, which provides malware- and greyware-scanned dependencies for JavaScript, Python, Java, Go and .NET with a limit of 50,000 pulls a month. Under a fixed seven-day cooldown, newly published versions are held back for a week, which the company says allows a compromised release to be caught before it reaches a build.

Starter also comes with 500 hours a month of virtual CPU time on each of Chainguard Checks and Chainguard Workspaces, which launched in beta at the company’s Assemble London event in October. Checks is designed to provide hardened runners for continuous integration, with Workspaces providing hardened sandboxes for coding agents.

Other features on the free plan include hardened replacements for GitHub Actions, more than 1,000 hardened agent skills, community support and 100 gigabytes of private artifact storage. Starter users also get 1 million tokens a month for Guardener, Chainguard’s artificial intelligence agent, which inventories the GitHub Actions and container images in a customer’s repositories and opens pull requests to swap in the company’s hardened versions. Each Starter account is limited to five users.

The paid Team plan, which is billed to a credit card, includes everything in Starter with higher limits, such as unlimited users, 1 terabyte of image downloads and 1 million dependency pulls a month. Team customers also get base, application and AI images at their latest versions on top of their five chosen images, along with 1,000 hours a month each of Checks and Workspaces, 5 million Guardener tokens and 500 gigabytes of private storage.

Features reserved for Team include backported fixes for known vulnerabilities across five remediated versions, zero-day patches on the day of disclosure, ticketed support and managed policies that set rules for what is pulled and what is blocked. Chainguard says the usual reasons for upgrading include a sixth person needing access, a project outgrowing the usage limits and a team needing a patch for a version it cannot yet move off.

According to Chainguard, the upgrade takes a few seconds from the console that flags which limit a user has hit. Nothing has to be migrated, since the account, images and session all carry over. Customers can cancel at any time from the same console. Storage beyond Team’s included 500 gigabytes will be metered starting Jan. 1, 2027, according to Chainguard’s documentation.

The Enterprise offering is unchanged and still starts with a conversation with the company’s sales team. Enterprise provides companywide use of Chainguard with no usage limits, along with service-level agreements, enterprise compliance features and integrations. Starter is available now.

Chainguard says it has raised $892 million since its founding in 2021. Its most recent round, $280 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund, came in October 2025.

#5451. Exec: Time for Banks to Reclaim Mortgage Biz From Non-Bank Lenders

Mortgage rates recently reached 7.51% on the 30-year fixed, almost a full percentage point higher than last year. Despite that, the CEO of Chase Home Lending plans to aggressively expand its mortgage business to reclaim market share from non-bank lenders.

In a recent report on CNBC, Sean Grzebin noted that while banks had to recover consumer confidence following the great financial crisis of 20-some years ago, he thinks that’s a done deal.

“The non-banks are all very formidable competitors, and I think they’ve had an advantage while the banks were distracted through several decades,” he said. “Now you’re starting to see the resurgence of banks. A lot of banks are actually going to grow their mortgage business through this.”

Some of the major non-bank lenders in the U.S. include Rocket Mortgage, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), PennyMac Loan Services, loanDepot, Better Mortgage, to name a few.

Non-banks currently dominate originations with a 66.3% share by dollar volume, up from just 27% before the 2008 financial crisis, according to CNBC. However, large banks with $50 billion or more in assets are now increasing originations by 34% annually, outperforming competitors.

“We’re going to hire a bunch of lending advisors across the United States,” said Grzebin. “We’re going to focus on areas where we haven’t had a lot of coverage, but there’s a lot of mortgage activity and transactions taking place. And it really matches the expansion that we’re having within the branch network on the consumer bank side.”

Non-banks had a 66.3% share of originations by dollar volume in the first half of this year, an increase over all of 2025, according to Inside Mortgage Finance. That compares with just a 27% share in 2000 before the financial crisis. But large banks, those with $50 billion and more in assets, are now increasing originations by 34% on an annual basis, outperforming both competing banks and non-banks.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5450. Alex Trebek’s Former 578-Acre California Ranch and Winery Heads to Auction for $6.45 Million

A sprawling California ranch where Alex Trebek helped run a winery is heading to auction, giving buyers a chance to purchase nearly 578 acres of the Central Coast once owned by the longtime “Jeopardy!” host.

Known as Creston Manor, the property in San Luis Obispo County near Paso Robles is listed for $6.45 million.

In a press release shared with Realtor.com®, Concierge Auctions revealed bidding is scheduled to open on Dec. 4 and conclude live on Dec. 16 at The Dominick in New York City, where the ranch will be offered as part of the company’s year-end sale.

Lindsey Harn of Christie’s International Real Estate and Mike Goldfarb of Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company are working with the auction house on the sale.

Creston Manor is the second former Trebek property in the area to come up for auction through the company this year.

Earlier in 2026, Concierge Auctions sold Windfall Farms, a nearly 724-acre property in nearby Paso Robles, for $16.9 million. The auction house said it marketed that property for 39 days before the sale.

Creston Manor was established in 1900, decades before Trebek became a partner in Creston Manor Vineyards and Winery in 1987.

According to the auction house, the game show host used the property primarily for ranching and wine production.

One vintage detail from the auction announcement ties the ranch to Washington, DC. Concierge Auctions says wine from the estate was served at President George H.W. Bush’s inauguration.

The vineyard and winery are still operational, according to the sale announcement.

The estate also retains parts of its ranching history, including a preserved blacksmith shop and the original Highway 58 bridge.

Those structures sit on the same property as the barns, stables, and livestock facilities that support its current agricultural use.

The ranch covers approximately 577.65 acres, with rolling pastureland and mountain views. Livestock pens are set up to accommodate cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs, and the stables provide dedicated space for horses.

The existing agricultural facilities are a central part of the offering, particularly for buyers who want to continue ranching or producing wine on the property.

Beyond the agricultural buildings, the property has five residences and a separate private suite. Together, the living quarters span approximately 7,550 square feet and contain 14 bedrooms and 14 full bathrooms.

According to Concierge Auctions, the estate can accommodate more than 30 guests.

Harn pointed to the combination of housing, winemaking facilities, and equestrian infrastructure as a distinguishing feature of the property.

The ranch is in Creston, a community in northern San Luis Obispo County with agricultural ties of its own. Goldfarb highlighted the estate’s seclusion and its proximity to Paso Robles, where the surrounding wine region is home to more than 200 wineries.

Paso Robles also has a downtown dining scene and the Tin City tasting district. Nearby Santa Margarita Lake offers kayaking, fishing, and hiking.

Concierge Auctions is handling the sale through its division focused on wineries, vineyards, and other wine country real estate.

Creston Manor brings those uses together on a single property, with the working winery and vineyard sharing the acreage with livestock facilities and multiple homes.

Chad Roffers, the auction house’s CEO and co-founder, said the company hopes to draw international bidders to Creston Manor, just as it did when it brought Windfall Farms to auction earlier this year.

The auction house also says a closing will trigger a contribution toward building homes for families in need through its Key for Key program, a partnership with Giveback Homes.

#5449. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5447. Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home

Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers—if you can actually find such a property.

Properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers. They certainly have become all the rage on TikTok, with influencers snatching up properties left and right and sharing their renovation journeys.

Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside. (There might actually be laws against that!)

An abandoned property is usually a property whose original owner is no longer in possession of the home. Due to the owner's financial difficulties, the house is typically run-down and in desperate need of repair. If the law in your area allows you to claim this type of home and you're handy, it might be worth investigating.

However, some abandoned homes for sale can turn out to be in good condition, with the owner hoping to unload the property before foreclosure. This could provide the right buyer with an opportunity to purchase the abandoned property or unclaimed home at a discount—and possibly a significant return on investment if you later flip it.

Purchasing an abandoned or unclaimed property involves following the same procedures as buying any other piece of real estate. Before setting out on your journey to find an abandoned home, review your financial situation.

Remember, there will be additional expenses over and above the original sale price of the property. A pre-qualification from your bank or lender will help you estimate what mortgage amount you qualify for. Many banks also require pre-approval letters, so you can make quick decisions on the property you wish to purchase.

Most abandoned homes for sale are on their way to foreclosure, but the bank has not yet initiated the process. Various lists of abandoned properties or unclaimed properties are available, or you can search for abandoned foreclosures or pre-foreclosures online.

Check for listings of homes for sale with certain phrases that might indicate an abandoned property, such as "immediate possession," "must sell," "below market value," or "under appraisal." Don't forget to add "near me."

Real estate agents will usually have valuable knowledge of abandoned properties in the area and the law relating to claiming them, and can provide you with a selection of homes about to be foreclosed on by the bank.

Some properties might look abandoned but are not listed for sale. You might also check into the laws regarding unclaimed property and whether there is a statute of limitations on its return.

If you find an interesting unclaimed property like this, visit your county clerk’s office. It will have information about the homeowners, the home's current appraised value, liens, or tax problems.

You could then try tracking down the owners and asking them to sell their property. If the property has had liens or tax problems, the owners might be more willing to sell.

Abandoned homes will almost always have issues. Due to months (or years) of neglect, a lack of maintenance, and overall aging, vacant homes are far from pristine. They are often sold as is, which means what you see is what you get.

One major risk? Abandoned homes usually have had their utilities turned off. With no way to check the water, electricity, gas, heating and cooling systems, or appliances, even a professional home inspector will be unable to thoroughly evaluate the house. There could be wiring problems, water leaks, or gas leaks—any of which would be extremely costly to repair.

It might be possible to have utilities turned on temporarily, but that requires paying a deposit and putting the utilities in your name. Even if utilities are turned on, you'll likely have to accept some elements of the abandoned home as is. But remember, forgoing major system inspections is a huge gamble.

A second major risk factor is the deferred maintenance involved with the purchase of a property that's been left to the elements. If previous owners abandoned the home or lost it to foreclosure, they probably didn't pay attention to routine maintenance tasks. Costly repairs will crop up sooner than expected, and you'll have to budget for future repairs.

And to top it off, obtaining home insurance on an abandoned home is difficult. Most insurance agencies won't insure a vacated house without an inspection from one of their agents. And that agent might require you to make costly repairs before issuing a policy.

If the insurer issues a policy, premiums for an unoccupied structure will likely be significantly higher. Because no one has watched over the home, it's more likely to have suffered vandalism or fire damage. Vacant homes often have broken pipes or leaking roofs with resulting water damage, stolen copper wiring, mold, pest issues, and damaged appliances.

Assuming you have found a potential abandoned property for sale and been pre-approved, you will want to factor in costs that will be needed to get the home into solid condition. Get a thorough maintenance inspection performed on the property, and note what needs to be fixed and how much it will cost.

Claiming a property like this also involves adding in the cost of the appraisal fee, pest and lead inspection fees, title insurance, closing costs, and other legal fees.

Crunch the numbers before you consider a bid. A real estate agent can also accompany you to the abandoned property for sale and point out the extra expenses you will incur after the purchase of this property. The agent can also help you figure out how high your bid should be. Look for the right opportunities, and you might find a home that is just right for your budget.

Angela Colley writes about real estate and all things renting and moving for Realtor.com. Her work has appeared in outlets including TheStreet, MSN, and Yahoo.

#5446. Zillow Launches Four Tools to Narrow Down Homes, Agents and Affordability

To help renters and homebuyers answer questions, Zillow has announced the release of four new tools to help users rent or buy with more confidence.

According to a release, Zillow’s Home Loans’ BuyAbility℠ tool allows users to answer the question: How much can I afford? The Home Loans’ BuyAbility tool can help keep a buyer’s home budget more current and accurate.

Buyers can link to Experian—the credit reporting company—once to verify their credit and debt, and their target home price will update automatically each month based on any changes. BuyAbility is also refreshed daily with updated interest rates from Zillow Home Loans, Zillow notes.

Because the Experian integration is built on a verified credit score, the release notes that Zillow Home Loans can estimate what buyers can afford more accurately, so they can search with more confidence from the start.

Buyers can also plan for and track their progress toward homeownership as they pay down debt and improve their credit. The BuyAbility tool is free, has no impact on credit scores and doesn’t obligate buyers to use Zillow Home Loans.

“Moving is a series of important decisions, and each one gets easier when you have clear information in front of you,” said Cynthia Taylor, Zillow’s senior vice president of product. “These tools give both buyers and renters clarity at every step, and connect homeowners with local experts if they’re ready to sell.”

Zillow’s Regional Insights page addresses the questions of: Where should I live? The release says that it can also describe what it’s like to live in cities and neighborhoods across the U.S., so renters and buyers can weigh neighborhood tradeoffs and compare prices early in their search.

The “compare homes” module further narrows down lists of homes for buyers. Now, buyers and renters can view their top homes side by side, with photos, financial information and key details in one place. They can start a comparison from search results, listing or their “favorites,” and stop toggling between multiple tabs.

For the final new tool available, the release states that for off-market homes, Zillow now displays a curated list of Zillow Preferred℠ agent partners who recently sold similar homes nearby, allowing homeowners to compare and contact local listing agents who may be a good match.

All four tools are live on Zillow, with availability that varies according to the tool and the user’s platform, such as the web, iOS or Android.

For more information, visit https://www.zillow.com/product-releases/fall-2026/.

#5445. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5443. Arista takes aim at the next AI network battleground: distributed inference

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Awareness of the network’s role in artificial intelligence has steadily increased, with much of the focus on the back end – larger clusters, faster ports and scale-across fabrics that stitch graphics processing units together across data centers. Arista Networks Inc. has seen continued, accelerated growth and has been one of the biggest winners of that buildout.

This week at SC26, Arista announced a shift in focus to the other side of the network. The company also announced a new set of Etherlink R4 routing platforms designed for what it calls distributed inferencing, along with a pluggable optical line system for data center interconnect. The lineup includes:

All are based on Broadcom’s Jericho and Qumran silicon, designed to deliver up to 60% lower power consumption than competing 7-nanometer and 16-nanometer platforms. Everything is available now, except the 7020HR4, which ships in early 2027. The speeds and feeds always make headlines, but the implications of the launch point to where AI infrastructure is heading.

During a pre-briefing, Brendan Gibbs, Arista’s assistant vice president of product line management, argued that the forces driving training across multiple sites will have the same effect on inference. Gibbs also said that roughly 30% of Arista’s AI business is now scale-across, indicating that distributed AI is rapidly becoming commonplace.

Inference will be distributed for three reinforcing reasons:

The implication is that the front-end network, long treated as plumbing, now needs back-end attributes: deep buffers, traffic engineering, multi-tenancy, and encryption, because traffic now leaves the building.

This launch is the opposite of the descriptors we typically associate with Arista. Recent announcements focused on dense 800G, 1.6T, and liquid cooling. The products launched at SC26 are smaller and less expensive. Arista dominates big iron and is now rounding out its portfolio. Arista’s customers range from hyperscalers to neoclouds to enterprises building local AI. The front end needs rich features, not massive bandwidth, and Arista hasn’t had a viable option for that tier until now.

These routers are designed as entry-level but ship with 400G uplinks, which may seem like overkill today but offer investment protection. Gibbs said the goal is a 10-year life cycle, with customers swapping optics rather than chassis. No one knows what agents will do to traffic volumes, and I suspect companies that consider this overkill today will think differently in three or four years. Headroom is cheaper than a forklift upgrade at a remote site. Also notable: Arista co-designed the 7280R4 with a hyperscaler seeking a gray-to-coherent bridge, a sign that it’s building with its biggest customers.

The most intriguing product is the hardened 7020HR4, built for 5G and AI-RAN cell sites. Telcos have largely sat out the AI buildout, yet they own the last mile and real estate near users, exactly what low-latency inference requires. This gives a carrier the backbone to offer a managed AI factory.

My view is that this performs better outside the U.S., where enterprises don’t trust carriers beyond connectivity. In Europe and Asia-Pacific, managed services are far more common, and providers such as BT, NTT and Telstra have the footprint to make it work. With sovereignty requirements, the opportunity for telcos to move up the stack has never been better. Telcos have never been a core market for Arista, so any growth from that audience is additive to its already massive market.

Since 2019, Arista has reported a far lower CVE count than competitors, even after the surge in AI-assisted discovery following Anthropic’s Mythos. I’m skeptical of CVE comparisons because counts depend on testing rigor, installed base and reporting practices, and some vendors now bundle multiple issues into a single CVE.

The more relevant benefit is operational. Customers often don’t apply patches because upgrades cause downtime and break things. If they trust the software, they patch faster, and the risk window shrinks. With Mythos accelerating the retirement of end-of-support gear, quality and longevity become buying criteria, not nice-to-haves.

On the call, Gibbs agreed it’s hard to draw conclusions from CVE counts but explained that CVE counts were a measure of Arista’s software quality. This has been Arista’s calling card since it was a startup. While CVEs provide one metric, the bigger proof point is its historical track record of quality software.

Also, wire-speed MACsec and IPsec on every port is a differentiator because AI brings different security requirements. However, integrated security does not replace firewalls. I asked Gibbs about this, and he said that Arista has no intention of replacing firewalls and expects Palo Alto Networks Inc. to continue to sit behind it in the line. I’d like to see that formalized into validated designs for distributed inference, like what Nvidia Corp.-validated designs did for the back end.

The optical line system is a similar simplification play. Arista isn’t an optical company and is reselling these products, but offering dark fiber customers a turnkey, EOS-integrated way to move 25.6 Tbps across a metro network removes a real headache.

Customers have responded positively to Arista’s entry into this market. Douglas Fast Net Chief Technology Officer Jon Vradenburg said the company needs “a compact platform that supports the services our business and carrier customers rely on.” Takayuki Sakou of Japan’s STNet cited “higher throughput and improved power efficiency while maintaining the quality of the EOS software we trust.”

The back end of AI networking is largely a solved architecture at this point. The front end is not, and that’s where the next round of competition will play out. With R4, Arista is betting that its routing credibility, built quietly within hyperscaler backbones, can make it the default there as well. Given how much traffic agentic AI is likely to generate, that’s a bet that, like most Arista bets, will likely pay off.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5442. Five Signs a Seller Has Genuine Negotiating Flexibility

Redfin’s September analysis estimated that sellers outnumbered buyers by 57.9% nationally in August, the largest gap in its records dating to 2013. Nashville, Miami and Houston had more than twice as many sellers as buyers.

“Buyers hear that sellers are negotiating again and understandably want to know how much they can take off the price,” says Nick Nastos, real estate broker and founder of Chicago’s Property Shop. “Before we talk about a discount, I want to know what else they could buy. If there are only two suitable homes in their budget, they may have less leverage than the headline suggests.”

Nastos recommends checking five signs before deciding how aggressively to negotiate.

Similar homes are selling below their asking prices. Recent closed sales reveal what buyers actually paid. Compare properties with similar condition, size and location, and check whether sellers provided credits.

“A seller asking $500,000 is giving you their opening position,” Nastos says. “If comparable homes are closing at $470,000, you have something concrete to discuss.”

The listing is taking longer than its competitors. A home sitting beyond the typical selling time for comparable properties may offer an opening. However, buyers should investigate why it remains available, including repairs, unusual layouts or financing complications. Check the original listing date and any previous withdrawals or relistings, rather than relying only on the current days-on-market count.

Buyers have several realistic alternatives. More national inventory means little if the additional homes fall outside a buyer’s budget or requirements. Count suitable alternatives in the same neighborhood and price range.

“If you can genuinely walk away and choose another home, that changes the conversation,” Nastos notes. “Ten listings you would never buy do not give you the same leverage.”

The seller is already adjusting the offer. Repeated price reductions or advertised closing-cost assistance can signal flexibility. A reduction alone does not establish a bargain, particularly if the original price was inflated. Buyers should assess the revised price against recent sales and expected repair costs.

Price is not the seller’s only priority. A seller may value a dependable closing date, flexible possession or fewer logistical complications. Buyers can also ask about repair credits or closing-cost contributions, subject to lender rules.

“Ask what the seller needs before assuming every negotiation has to end with a lower price,” Nastos says. “Sometimes you can solve a timing problem for them and preserve cash for yourself.”

His final advice is to set a firm spending limit before negotiating. A competitive neighborhood may justify a stronger offer, but it does not make an unaffordable payment safer.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.
