#5441. EXCLUSIVE: Google Co-Founder Sergey Brin and Ex-Wife Nicole Shanahan List Malibu Home for $33 Million

The elegant Malibu estate that Google co-founder Sergey Brin purchased with his ex-wife, Nicole Shanahan, has hit the selling block for $33.5 million—months after it was listed as a rental.

Brin, 53, and Shanahan—who went on to join Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s short-lived presidential campaign—bought the "dreamy" Point Dume dwelling for $13.5 million in September 2020, just over a year before it was revealed that they had split after three years of marriage.

The details of their divorce settlement, which was finalized in 2023, were never fully revealed. However, reports suggest that Shanahan walked away with around $1 billion in assets, including shares in Alphabet, Google's parent company.

It has never been revealed how the former couple split their shared properties. Brin purchased another Malibu residence for $35 million just a few months after their separation, a move that many saw as a sign that Shanahan, 41, had kept their former marital home.

Property records viewed by Realtor.com® show that the five-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom dwelling is currently registered to a limited liability company in Nevada that is managed by Shanahan's family office. That LLC lists the same mailing address as her charitable organization, the Bia-Echo Foundation, which is named for the former couple's daughter, Echo.

While it's unclear whether Shanahan ever used the property as her primary residence, she revealed in an October 2025 interview with Frontier Magazine that she was living in a different California property: a mountaintop ranch where she was residing with her partner, Jacob Strumwasser.

Although the home was listed for rent for $175,000 a month in May, the property has now vanished from the rental market and is now available for purchase.

The listing, which is held by Michael Cunningham of Pinnacle Estate Properties, notes that it has undergone an extensive series of overhauls in recent months, describing it as a "newly completed estate."

"A long, private driveway leads to a secluded sanctuary surrounded by mature trees, lush landscaping, and beautiful ocean views, with the rare privilege of keyed access to Little Dume Beach. Meticulously designed with every detail reflects an uncompromising commitment to quality and sophistication," the listing notes.

The property comes with an array of upscale features and amenities, including "keyed access to Little Dume beach," a stunning stretch of sand that is known as one of Malibu's best areas for surfing.

The dwelling itself has plenty to offer, both inside and out. The 1.2-acre lot includes a dazzling swimming pool with a large spa and a pagoda-style area for shade.

The parcel is incredibly private, featuring a gated entrance, a long driveway, and tall trees surrounding the home.

The listing describes the home as the "epitome of 'quiet luxury,'" constructed with top-of-the-line materials and quality craftsmanship.

Upon entering the home, visitors are greeted with a spacious, airy foyer that opens to an elegant dining space and living room, where walls of windows flood the space with natural light. A curved ceiling elevates the room, while a fireplace keeps it cozy.

The dining area separates the living space from the enormous open-plan kitchen, which features a curved island and huge French doors that open to a private deck overlooking the grounds.

For those with a fondness for entertaining, a second meal prep area with its own stove and additional appliances will no doubt prove to be one of the most-used spaces in the dwelling.

Elsewhere on the main floor are a media room—which the listing notes could be turned into an office or library—as well as a generous gym and wellness suite.

"Designed with wellness and longevity in mind, the residence incorporates advanced clean-building technologies and carefully selected materials, including a state-of-the-art VRF climate system, copper and cast-iron plumbing, rigid metal HVAC ducting, sustainable denim insulation, and specialized wiring and shielding intended to reduce EMF exposure," the description adds.

Two more bedrooms can be found on this upper level, each with its own bathroom. Another bedroom is located in a separate apartment space with a private entrance, as well as an additional kitchen and living room.

In addition to Brin, the property has a history of A-list residents, having previously been owned by pop star Pink, who purchased it for $11.9 million in 2010 and used it as her primary residence until 2016, when she sold it for $12.5 million.

The property is located just a mile away from the Malibu home Brin bought for $35 million in April 2022, just a few months after it was revealed that he and Shanahan had split.

He has since expanded his Malibu holdings with another pricier property that he picked up for $49.7 million in July 2025.

However, Brin has recently joined the growing list of billionaires pulling their fortunes out of California amid the threat of Proposition 40, a one-time, 5% wealth tax on residents worth over $1 billion—a proposal that has since been rejected.

The Google co-founder has been an outspoken critic of the tax, likening California to the Soviet Union when asked why he left the state.

"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place," he told The New York Times in April.

California voters rejected Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth, with most proceeds earmarked for healthcare. Opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argued that the measure could drive wealthy residents out of the state and reduce future tax revenue.

Brin has, quite literally, put his money where his mouth is, snapping up several properties outside of California in anticipation of the tax, including a $42 million mansion on the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe and a $51 million Miami Beach dwelling that he bought from LVMH CEO Michael Burke at the start of the year.

The Miami property is located on the exclusive Allison Island, a 35-acre stretch of land that sits in the Biscayne Bay, between La Gorce and Miami Beach. The 24/7 guard-gated island is home to fewer than 50 single-family homes.

It was custom-built for Burke and his wife, Brigitte Burke, in 2019, five years after they purchased the 1-acre plot of land on which the home now sits for $11.7 million.

The spectacular property spans 10,000 square feet and has seven bedrooms, 8.5 bathrooms, a waterfront pool, and a private dock. The modernist design includes two separate wings of the home connected by a central walk-through area.

It's unclear whether Brin has any plans to offload either of his Malibu homes in the wake of his move from California. Neither dwelling is currently listed on the multiple listing service.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5439. Buyers Need Cheaper Homes. Airbnb Is Putting $1 Million Toward Finding New Solutions.

For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach.

Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that.

The company announced a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes. It plans to distribute one award per year over a five-year period.

The $1 million prizes are intended for U.S.-based companies and nonprofits with ideas that are already in the works but need funding to succeed. These may include factory-built homes, faster construction sides, expedited permitting, or easier financing for new homes.

“Airbnb started as a way to help my co-founders pay their rent. Today millions of people do the same. Now we are helping to finance the building of housing in communities nationwide. We want to encourage others, through this prize, to think more creatively and ambitiously about home building and delivering affordability. Necessity is the mother of invention,” said Nathan Blecharczyk, Airbnb’s co-founder and chief strategy officer, in a recent press release.

While Airbnb’s efforts are a step in the right direction, experts agree that addressing the affordability crisis as a whole requires more funding, innovation, and collaboration across the industry.

Airbnb's initiative brings renewed attention to the need for more housing in the U.S., and finding ways to build it more efficiently and affordably is becoming increasingly important.

Realtor.com® data shows how serious the housing supply gap has become.

In 2025, new-home construction fell short of household formations, pushing the U.S. housing supply gap to an estimated 4.03 million homes. This demonstrates the need for new solutions that can make it easier and more efficient to build homes.

Addressing the shortage will also require evaluating and changing policies and regulations that may slow down construction and raise costs. That’s where the Realtor.com Let America Build initiative comes in.

It strives to encourage discussions and solutions on the U.S. home inventory and affordability crisis.

Several factors are slowing down homebuilding and driving up construction costs in the U.S., and initiatives like Airbnb’s could help.

“Builders cite slow permit processes, increased material expenses, and lack of skilled labor as the main factors raising construction costs,” says Michael Pearson, senior vice president of business development at A&D Mortgage LLC in Ft. Lauderdale, FL.

Additionally, with expenses on the rise and the pressure to keep homes marketable and affordable, margins for contractors and developers are very low.

Innovations for factory-built or modular homes, for example, could improve the situation. These homes are traditionally built homes assembled off site and delivered to a plot of land.

“While modular homes are more economical, as you don’t have to ship supplies and workers to a site build and you can better control costs and material overages, they come with logistical concerns, primarily getting the modular home on site. Innovation may find a solution that so far has not shown itself,” adds Pearson.

Gay Cororaton, chief economist at MIAMI Realtors + RWorld in Miami, points out that modular homes are simply more attainable for more households.

“The average price of a new manufactured home is less than $150,000, which could go up to, say, $300,000 for a double-wide home. At today's mortgage rates, for a household with $100,000 in income, that’s more affordable than a traditional home,” Cororaton explains.

Still, while the Airbnb Housing Innovation Prize could turn promising ideas into realities, Pearson believes $1 million prizes won’t be enough and innovations must be part of a greater strategy where we highlight issues, communicate ideas, and have demonstrable progress. It’s also important for other organizations to jump on board.

“I’d like to see more companies, nonprofits, and government agencies get involved with this kind of action. Housing safety and affordability is this issue of this generation, and together we can find solutions,” says Pearson.

Robert Trent, CEO and principal at Builders Capital in Puyallup, WA, agrees with Pearson and believes the success of Airbnb’s initiative will depend on what gets built after the award.

“The best-case scenario is quality homes people can afford, delivered at a lower total cost, with results that can be replicated across different communities,” Trent adds.

#5438. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

#5437. Dell puts a single gateway between enterprise AI agents and the data they crave

Data intelligence is becoming the deciding layer of the enterprise AI factory as companies learn that racks of graphics processing units deliver little value when agents lack trusted, governed context.

Neocloud providers built the first wave of large-scale AI systems, and core enterprise customers now want the same capabilities inside their own organizations. Dell Technologies Inc. recently extended its AI Data Platform with semantic and knowledge graph features aimed at that market shift. But both the challenge and the opportunity lie in pairing structured and unstructured data so agents get full context while maintaining guardrails and human oversight, according to Srinath Alapati (pictured, right), senior director of product marketing for AI Data Platform at Dell.

“The bottom line is if you feed the wrong data, you get the wrong outcomes,” Alapati said. “What we’ve found is in our own testing — by giving the right context — you can improve the accuracy from roughly 60% to like 94%.”

Alapati, Alison Biers (center), senior director of product marketing for compute, networking and global industries at Dell, and Adam Glick (left), senior director of AI solutions product marketing for compute at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is tying data, infrastructure management and validated designs together to move enterprise AI factories into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Enterprises can’t give agents unfettered access to their systems, which is where Dell’s newly announced Agentic Data Gateway fits. The gateway sits in the orchestration layer as a single point of control, backed by a Model Context Protocol server, Alapati explained. Storage intelligence tells customers what data they hold, who owns it and how large it is, while Dell’s new data intelligence capabilities track lineage and provenance. Hybrid workflows extend that model across the edge, the cloud and the data center, where companies can struggle to meet the data consolidation requirements of other data platform providers.

“They want you to bring all the data to wherever the platform is. That’s not always possible,” Alapati said. “Number one, it’s super expensive. Two is data is always being generated. It’s a never-ending game. You can’t always keep bringing in data, consolidating data. What we do is we only send metadata … That way your data stays where you want to be.”

On the infrastructure side, Dell OpenManage Rack Scale extends management beyond compute endpoints to the network fabric, power and cooling. That gives operators a single operational plane from day zero through day two, according to Biers. A rebuilt, intent-based Dell Fabric Manager replaces the company’s SmartFabric Manager, and Dell’s PowerRack systems treat the full rack as the unit of deployment.

“It is literally six hours from the time it hits your loading dock to full production,” Biers said. “Something that used to take maybe months and months [is] now cut in half, maybe even less.”

More than 6,500 customers now use the Dell AI Factory, and a growing share are core enterprises asking for help putting AI to work, Glick noted. Validated designs built with Nvidia Corp. and other partners cover both the hardware and the full software stack, and Dell is expanding its labs to keep pace with independent software companies joining the ecosystem. Compute still draws most of the attention, but that is only one part of a larger system.

“If you’ve got a factory, compute is your assembly line. It’s the important part,” Glick said. “It’s what you think of when you think of ‘factory’, but that assembly line doesn’t run if you don’t have a warehouse that’s feeding it the raw materials — that’s the data that goes into it.”

#5436. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5435. Exceeding Expectations Every Step of the Way

Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Starck Real Estate

Most important thing you learned this past year: The value of recognizing and drawing out the potential in others, sometimes before they even see it in themselves.

Who has most influenced your success? My father, Andy, who led the company for nearly 40 years. I consider it a privilege and a blessing to have been able to work and learn alongside him.

As a third-generation member of your family’s real estate firm, how do you honor the firm’s legacy while bringing your own perspective and ideas to the business?

We consider ourselves a family business made up of family businesses, so inherent in that is a sense of responsibility to the people and the families we serve. And so it’s a stewardship of what has been entrusted, not only to me, but to everyone in our company. The more we grow and find success, the more we’re able to invest in our agents and give in meaningful ways to charitable organizations and the communities we serve.

What is the most valuable lesson you’ve learned from the previous generations of your family who worked in the business?

The firm was founded by my grandparents on the values of service to others over ourselves and doing business with complete truth and integrity, which is part of the reputation we’ve worked hard to build over the last 66-plus years. While we firmly believe that good things happen when you treat others the way you would want to be treated, we take it above and beyond the Golden Rule to the Platinum Rule, which is treating others the way they want to be treated. Taking that one step further, our focus is on providing double platinum experiences—or exceeding expectations in order to treat others in a way they can’t even conceive.

What factor has the largest influence on the real estate industry today?

Distractions, particularly the technology in our pockets, which brings to mind the following Robin Sharma quote: “The enemy of mastery is not mediocrity. It is distractions. The addiction to distractions ruins many potentially awesome lives.” We’re privileged to work in this noble profession, which will always be a relationship-based business. Technology can be a wonderful tool when it’s used properly, but we believe that focusing on relationships and service is the best way to build a sustainable business that’s successful in any market.

How does your company make its agents’ jobs easier?

We operate on the belief that we only succeed as a company when our agents succeed, so we’re passionate about providing value and support so that their businesses and families can thrive. That means saving them time or making their jobs easier by taking things off their plate so that they can focus on doing the things only they can do. Another core thing we talk a lot about is the go-giver mindset, which is rooted in the idea that when you give and give and then give some more, good things happen.

As we approach the end of 2026 and head into a new year, what are you most looking forward to?

Our business is constantly changing, so it’s all about embracing that and looking forward to how we’re going to grow and get better while at the same time serving our agents better. It’s all about controlling what we can control. I’m optimistic about the future.

For more information, please visit https://www.BerkshireHathawayhs.com.

Paige Tepping is RISMedia’s senior managing editor.

#5434. Wisconsin Couple Seek To Enforce $1,350 Judgment Against Each of Their Neighbors in HOA Dispute

A neighborhood outside Green Bay, WI, is locked in a yearslong legal battle, as one couple is now taking legal action against their neighbors to collect a $200,000 settlement.

What began as a dispute over a backyard fence has turned into an ongoing series of lawsuits, with neighbors being forced to pay $1,350 each in a settlement—and those who haven’t are now being taken to court.

The case is centered around Michael and Lisa Newman and their five children, who reside in the Nazcr Trac neighborhood in De Pere, WI. After some of their children were diagnosed with autism, the Newmans wanted to build a fence around their backyard, as they wanted the children to be able to play outside safely.

Citing the children’s diagnoses and that two of their children “demonstrated significant risk of elopement,” according to a press release from the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council, the Newmans wrote to the Nazcr Trac Property Owners Association (NTPOA) to request an accommodation to the subdivision’s “no fence” rule.

Neither the initial request, sent in July 2019, nor a subsequent request in December 2020, which included information about the association’s legal obligation to consider an accommodation due to the children’s disabilities, were answered by the association.

In August 2021, the Newmans filed a lawsuit against the association in federal court, alleging that it had discriminated based on disability, a violation of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. A judge granted a preliminary injunction in May 2022 that prohibits the NTPOA from enforcing the rule, and the family built their fence in time for summer, three years after the initial request.

While the family got their wish, the battle was just beginning for other residents of Nazcr Trac.

In August 2024, a settlement was reached, requiring the NTPOA to pay the Newmans $200,000—a payment that would be passed on directly to each household in the association.

Following the settlement, each property in the neighborhood was looking at a $1,350 bill. Residents told WGBA that they were frustrated by the situation and many had been unaware of the dispute until they received the charge.

One anonymous resident told the local station that most residents would have had no issue with the fence, and a poll of members could have saved a lot of time and money.

“If the board had polled us as members, a large amount of the members would have said, 'Absolutely, let the family do what they need to do to take care of their family,’” the resident said during WGBA’s initial coverage in 2025.

At the time, Lisa Newman told the station that she felt “not great” about her neighbors being on the hook for the settlement payment.

“It's just a really unfortunate situation, I think, for everybody involved, and the board kind of made that decision for everybody,” she told WGBA.

However, in September, the Newmans filed a new lawsuit against the NTPOA and a number of homeowners who still owe on the settlement.

Sixty-nine homeowners settled following the initial lawsuit, the Newmans’ attorney, Victoria Davis Dávila, told WGBA. The rest are now facing legal troubles of their own.

“There’s an outstanding judgment," Davis Dávila told WGBA. "You had the opportunity to pay. You chose not to pay it."

In addition to the association, 33 residents are named in the new filing.

“The Newmans want just as bad as anybody else to put this behind them,” Davis Dávila said, adding that the NTPOA membership as a whole could potentially be held liable if the outstanding amount isn’t paid.

The new lawsuit is frustrating and stressful for many homeowners who thought the issue would be behind them by now.

“Why is this coming back to us? It’s so unfair,” an anonymous homeowners told WGBA.

An answer and affirmative defense was filed by the Property Owner’s Association on Nov. 16, but the contents of the document were not publicly available at the time of publication.

Realtor.com® reached out to the legal counsel of both the association and the Newmans, but received no response.

#5433. Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement

Microsoft Corp. today rolled out new generative artificial intelligence models and updates to Foundry, the company’s unified enterprise platform that helps developers and organizations ground, test and deploy AI applications and autonomous agents.

Updates to Foundry IQ, part of Microsoft IQ, now provide an enterprise knowledge graph out of the box, delivering a full estate of unstructured and application data to provide rich context for building applications and delivering on essential use cases.

Microsoft also said Foundry now uses existing transparency and observability capabilities to help customers create learning loops. Internal evaluations allow autonomous agents to establish baselines for quality, safety, latency and cost, enabling continuous behavioral improvements.

This includes human annotations, now in preview, that allow experts to rate and comment on agent traces based on business judgment. It feeds back into an improvement loop. It’s combined with optimization tests against evaluations and comparisons against real-world results. Foundry now also has new capabilities to adapt to supported models with organizational data to apply reinforcement learning while Foundry runs compute.

Each improvement becomes the next baseline and teams can continue measuring results and test changes, allowing them to improve quality.

Microsoft today announced Decision-1.1 is generally available. It’s a fast, cost-effective model designed to make reliable decisions in software at scale.

The generative AI model can make decisions dynamically at low cost, rather than relying on hard-coded rules, while offering superior decision-making capabilities compared with large language models. LLMs spend a lot of time making decisions in routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control by “thinking it through,” which is unnecessary. Decision models are designed to reach answers quickly within constrained definitions and provide calibrated confidence scores, allowing applications to defer when uncertainty is high.

The new model builds on the previous generation, Microsoft-Decision-1, released in October. The new model delivers a significant improvement in intelligence and speed at a competitive price.

The company said it’s built on a new base, Google LLC’s Gemma 4 26B A4, adding multimodal support so it can analyze images in instructions.

Microsoft also extended its MAI, a Microsoft AI first-party family of models added to Foundry for enterprise trust.

These models include the new MAI-Code-2, which can handle demanding agentic coding work; MAI-Code-2-Flash supports high-volume, everyday coding, so developers can choose between performance and cost. Both are now generally available on GitHub, with Code-2-Flash in private preview in Foundry.

MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash are now in preview and offer sharper editing and more consistent image generation. These will help brands maintain a consistent look across campaigns at a lower cost.

In cybersecurity, MAI-Cyber-2-Flash is a purpose-built model for cyber efforts and available in preview in Codename MDASH – the company’s agentic code security system in preview for eligible organizations.

Microsoft Foundry itself now has an expanded model pool featuring the top 50 models, supporting a model router and AI Gateway for intelligence model selection. The Foundry also offers more than 11,000 models from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc., Mistral AI SAS, the open-source community and others.

The company said supported models can be evaluated and deployed in Foundry as part of the same continuous improvement workflow used for agents.

#5432. Stronger Together: HomeServices of America Celebrates Top Agents, Fuels Future Growth

Above: HomeServices of America President and CEO Chris Kelly addresses the crowd at the company’s “Stronger Together” Conference

While real estate success is often measured individually—with an emphasis on closed transactions, milestones achieved and accolades earned—some of the greatest opportunities for growth present themselves when real estate professionals come together.

That philosophy was at the heart of HomeServices of America’s 4th Annual “Stronger Together” Conference, held Oct. 26 – 29 at the Fontainebleau Miami Beach. The oceanside event brought together more than 400 agents from the HomeServices’ owned brokerage companies to celebrate the professionals whose achievements earned them a place among the company’s best—each invited on the strength of their success.

Collectively, these agents rank in the top 1.5% of approximately 1.4 million Realtors® nationwide—averaging seven times the sales volume of the national average and three times more transactions. Generating $10.2 billion in annual sales volume, Stronger Together agent attendees are responsible for helping 16,483 families move each year.

“Our agents earned their place at Stronger Together, and we wanted every moment to reflect how much we value them,” HomeServices of America President and CEO Chris Kelly said in a release.

The mastermind behind the reinvigoration of the organization, Kelly has led HomeServices of America’s transformation from a quiet holding company into a bold parent company focused on providing strategic direction, cohesion and resources across its family of brokerage, mortgage, insurance and title services.

Central to that vision is a commitment to investing in people, performance and long-term growth that extends throughout the organization—a commitment reflected in reflections and anecdotes shared with RISMedia after the event from both HomeServices of America executives and attendees alike.

Playing a key role in educating and elevating the performance of brokerage owners, operators, team leaders, office managers and the sales associates in the field each and every day, HomeServices of America Chief Coaching Officer Jimmy Burgess takes pride in seeing that work come together.

“I’ve been part of this event for a long time, and what still gets me is the room. Every person in it earned their seat, and they’re all generous with what they know,” says Burgess, who spent the week watching agents trade ideas between sessions as much as in them.

“It’s a privilege to say thank you to people who work this hard, and to send them home with a few new ideas and a few new friends,” he adds.

Reflecting the company’s commitment to delivering the complete real estate experience—a theme central to HomeServices of America’s strategy—this year’s event mirrored that philosophy by offering agents inspiration, practical insight and community in one setting. Newly introduced Super Sessions, which go beyond a traditional breakout or panel, and inspiring voices provided top-performing agents everything they need to keep winning in today’s market.

For clients, that complete experience is delivered through OnePoint, the integrated platform HomeServices of America launched earlier this year to provide a more streamlined, end-to-end experience to buyers and sellers alike.

“We changed a few things this year, including the Super Sessions and a main stage with three voices instead of one, because folks at this level already know their craft. What they want is room to keep growing,” explains Kelly.

“It’s the same thinking behind OnePoint: Give people what they need in one place, so they aren’t piecing it together alone,” he adds. “When our agents grow, their clients feel it.”

Providing agents the tools and motivation to keep succeeding, entrepreneur, investor and bestselling author Jesse Itzler kicked off the conference with a keynote presentation challenging attendees to redefine wealth through experiences, relationships, mindset, health and purpose.

In addition to Super Sessions designed to give agents the time and depth to explore a multitude of topics impacting the industry, attendees also heard shared perspectives on kindness, connection and determination. Another Stronger Together highlight was a live recording of the “Stay Paid” podcast with Kelly, Burgess and Prosperity Home Mortgage President and CEO Justin Messer.

“A gathering like this sets a standard for the industry,” says HomeServices of America Senior Vice President Lacey Conway. “With more than 400 agents in the top 1.5% nationally, the program had to match the people in the room, and it did.

“From the keynote to the ‘Super Sessions’ to the speakers on (the topic of) belonging, you could see the same things we see in these agents: Curiosity, discipline and a willingness to keep learning when they’re already at the top,” she says.

HomeServices of America is putting that same forward-thinking mindset into action across the board.

“What stands out about HomeServices is that it keeps building while it’s winning, and OnePoint is a good example. Bringing brokerage, mortgage, title and insurance together as one coordinated team is a real answer to what clients want,” says HomeServices of America Chief Marketing and Strategy Officer Brian Boero, who led one of the conference’s Super Sessions.

“The energy in the room at Stronger Together had that same appetite for what’s next…and that’s a sign of a company that plans to keep leading,” he adds.

The value of coming together: Ideas, connections and new perspectives

Attending HomeServices of America’s Stronger Together event along with 15 top-producing agents, Long Companies CEO Kevin Kaplan says that being able to bring together hundreds of the most successful real estate professionals from across the HomeServices network to learn, share ideas and build relationships is what ultimately makes the conference so valuable.

“What sets Stronger Together apart is that the focus goes beyond traditional sales skills and tactics. It’s about mindset, leadership, motivation and challenging yourself to think differently about your business and what’s possible,” says Kaplan, who believes that surrounding yourself with successful people who challenge and inspire you is one of the greatest opportunities for growth.

“Our agents came away energized, with new ideas, valuable connections and fresh perspectives on how to take their businesses to the next level,” he adds. “In my view, this was the best ‘Stronger Together’ event yet, and we’re already looking forward to 2027.”

For Elizabeth Nunan, president and CEO of Houlihan Lawrence, the conference was equally as powerful.

“Stronger Together was an outstanding conference from start to finish. The speakers were exceptional, the content was timely and relevant, and the opportunities to connect, network and share ideas made it even more valuable,” she says.

“Our agents left feeling inspired, energized and excited about what’s ahead. In fact, they’re already making plans for next year in Nashville. That’s always a pretty good indication of a great event,” adds Nunan.

For RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, what stood out most was the energy and the positive, can-do attitude throughout the event.

“I had the privilege of attending the 4th Annual Stronger Together conference, and watching the attendees connect with so many other passionate real estate professionals reminded me just how valuable it is to meet face-to-face and collaborate with industry leaders to share knowledge and techniques—and why it’s so important to success in our industry,” says Featherston, who applauded Kelly and his team for delivering an informative, meaningful and well-received experience for attendees.

“When you couple the industry talents educating attendees—from Jimmy Burgess’ coaching insights and Brian Boero’s informative, practical information—with incredible guests such as serial entrepreneur and best-selling author Jesse Itzler and award-winning singer, songwriter and author Nicolle Galyon along with several other incredible speakers—Stronger Together was a smashing success,” he adds.

“Congratulations to Chris and his team for a job well done!”

Paige Tepping is RISMedia’s senior managing editor.

Bitcoin price is entering a potentially decisive week as Wall Street prepares for three major events likely to reshape sentiment. Nvidia’s earnings, Anthropic’s enormous IPO, and an unprecedented Trump-Xi-Putin meeting are arriving almost simultaneously. Together, they could trigger a wave of capital rotation, putting pressure on crypto before potentially opening the door to a recovery.

Bitcoin price has already suffered a brutal correction, falling toward $65,000 after losing more than 20% over the past month. But the coming days could introduce a very different market dynamic. Institutional investors are preparing for one of the largest technology listings ever, bigger than SpaceX.

Anthropic upcoming IPO has likely become an enormous liquidity-absorption event, a butterfly effect across traditional markets and crypto. Claude developer has proposed selling 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each. The offering could raise between $57.75 billion and $64.35 billion, implying a fully diluted valuation of $1.4 trillion.

Anthropic has launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering: https://t.co/oE6TA0vt3ELegal disclaimer: A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the SEC but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold, nor may…

The capital ambitions are extending beyond the public offering. Anthropic has separately arranged a $26 billion private placement involving major technology companies, including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD and Broadcom. Combined proceeds could reach $84.6 billion to $93.7 billion.

That is an extraordinary amount of capital competing for investor attention. Reuters reported that institutional investors are already preparing for the IPO alongside Nvidia’s earnings, making both events major tests for an increasingly vulnerable AI trade.

Anthropic’s private-market valuation has also attracted speculative trading on platforms such as Hyperliquid, where pre-IPO exposure has traded at a premium, highlighting just how aggressively investors are positioning for its public debut.

The consequences extend beyond technology stocks. Bitcoin, with its around-the-clock liquidity, could become an unintended source of funding.

But what have we learned from this? Before the June SpaceX IPO, Bitcoin experienced a huge sell-off, falling nearly 20% during the 30-day pre-IPO period. Fast forward a couple of months, Bitcoin price grinded higher as SpaceX’s attention faded.

Now, Anthropic could be just another test. If its IPO absorbs substantial investment capital, Bitcoin could face additional selling pressure. Once allocations settle, however, that temporary competition for liquidity could ease, allowing investors to reconsider previously abandoned positions.

The expectations are enormous, particularly after Nvidia’s market valuation declined from $5.8 trillion in early October to $3.9 trillion. Investors are looking for evidence that AI infrastructure spending remains sustainable despite the company’s leadership transition.

A strong earnings report could nevertheless change the narrative. Higher revenue guidance, resilient data center demand, and confidence in future AI spending could help stabilize technology valuations. Nvidia has repeatedly beaten analyst expectations for 8 straight earnings reports.

Why does this matter for Bitcoin? Institutional risk appetite often moves across multiple asset classes. When investors become comfortable taking risks in equities, speculative assets like crypto can benefit from renewed capital allocation.

If Nvidia surprises positively, Bitcoin price could receive an unexpected boost just as the Anthropic IPO reaches its public debut.

#5430. Billy Joel–Linked Palm Beach Retreat Seeks $17.9 Million—With a Private Pool and Lavish Primary Suite

A recently renovated Palm Beach, FL, townhouse associated with Billy Joel has been listed for $17.9 million. It features a private pool, an elevator, and a primary suite complete with separate bathrooms and walk-in closets.

The four-bedroom property is being listed with Christian Angle of Christian Angle Real Estate. Its Mediterranean architecture and courtyard entrance set the scene for a residence that pairs formal entertaining rooms with outdoor spaces for dining and lounging.

The asking price puts the home well above its previous purchase price. According to Mansion Global, which cited PropertyShark records, the limited liability company that owns the townhouse paid $9.05 million in 2021.

A sale at the current asking price would represent an $8.85 million increase over that purchase, before accounting for renovation expenses, transaction costs, and other ownership expenses.

It would also put the closing price within striking distance of twice the amount paid five years ago. Joel’s association with the property has been reported through the company that holds its title. In 2022, Palm Beach Daily News reported the ownership connection.

Upon entering the residence, guests are greeted with a soaring foyer, where a staircase with iron detailing rises beneath a coffered ceiling.

The layout provides distinct spaces for hosting, working, and everyday meals, with a formal living room, a dining room, an office, and a breakfast nook adjoining the kitchen. A pecky cypress ceiling adds a wood accent to the cooking space.

The primary suite includes a Juliet balcony, along with its two bathrooms and two walk-in closets. Across the home, there are five full bathrooms and one half-bathroom.

The property, which was built in 2022, spans 4,956 square feet. A two-car garage and paved driveway round out the practical amenities.

Beyond the interiors, the pool is accompanied by an open patio, a built-in barbecue, and a sheltered area for outdoor meals. Worth Avenue, Mid-Town beach, and the Australian Docks are all within blocks, according to the listing.

The property adds another chapter to the musician’s extensive history of buying and selling homes in Florida.

The townhouse’s arrival on the market comes as Joel prepares for a public appearance in Boca Raton next month.

On Dec. 14, the songwriter is scheduled to take part in an event at Florida Atlantic University, where students will have the opportunity to ask him about his career and creative process, according to the Palm Beach Post.

Although the event’s title includes a reference to music, Joel’s representative clarified to the newspaper that the evening is intended as a conversation. Any playing would consist of short musical demonstrations to help explain his answers, with no band or prepared setlist.

The appearance follows a period in which Joel stepped away from his scheduled concerts after being diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus.

#5429. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5428. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.
