#5394. ZTO Reports Third Quarter 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

10.2 Billion Parcels Expanded Market Share to 20.1%Adjusted Net Income Increased to RMB2.6 Billion

SHANGHAI, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ZTO Express (Cayman) Inc. (NYSE: ZTO and SEHK: 2057), a leading and fast-growing express delivery company in China ("ZTO" or the "Company"), today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026[1]. The Company grew parcel volume by 7.0% year over year while maintaining high quality of service and customer satisfaction. Adjusted net income increased 2.6%[2] to RMB2.6 billion. Net cash generated from operating activities was RMB3.7 billion.

Operational Highlights for Third Quarter 2026

[1] An investor relations presentation accompanies this earnings release and can be found at http://zto.investorroom.com.

[2] Adjusted net income is a non-GAAP financial measure, which is defined as net income before share-based compensation expense and non-recurring items such as impairment of investments in equity investees, impairment of goodwill, gain/(loss) on disposal of equity investment and subsidiary and corresponding tax impact which management aims to better represent the underlying business operations.

[3] Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP financial measure, which is defined as net income before depreciation, amortization, interest expenses and income tax expenses, and further adjusted to exclude the shared-based compensation expense and non-recurring items such as impairment of investments in equity investees, impairment of goodwill, gain/(loss) on disposal of equity investment and subsidiary which management aims to better represent the underlying business operations.

[4] One ADS represents one Class A ordinary share.

[5] Adjusted basic and diluted earnings per American depositary share attributable to ordinary shareholders is a non-GAAP financial measure. It is defined as adjusted net income attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by weighted average number of basic and diluted American depositary shares, respectively.

Mr. Meisong Lai, Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of ZTO, commented, "In the third quarter of 2026, ZTO held to its strategic principle of high-quality service, high-quality market share and low end-to-end costs. Parcel volume reached 10.2 billion, up 7.0% year over year and 4.1 percentage points ahead of the industry average. Operating profit rose 23.8% to RMB2.98 billion, and adjusted net income was RMB2.6 billion. Daily average retail parcel volume grew 57% year over year and accelerated from the second quarter as higher-value services scaled up generating a favorable mix shift that lifted margin."

Mr. Lai added, "China's express-delivery industry continued to benefit from constructive regulation, and anti-involution has become an industry consensus rather than a policy slogan. Competition is more rational, pricing gradually recovered into the peak season, and competition shifted from a price focus to quality and value. ZTO's Quality-First approach, built on industry-leading efficiency and equitable network policies, is driving that shift into results. We are not trading long-term quality for short-term market share, and we are not buying volume at any price. Rooted in Shared Success culture, we help our partners and couriers earn more while keeping reasonable profit for the company. This is how we are able to sail through any industry and economic cycles."

Ms. Huiping Yan, Chief Financial Officer of ZTO, commented, "For the third quarter this year, our core express ASP rose 13.7% year over year, which was supported by an improved revenue mix from higher-value key-accounts, including rapidly expanding reverse-logistics business. Despite cost pressure from high oil prices, combined unit sorting and transportation costs decreased by 2 cents, thanks to end-to-end digitization and lean operations. SG&A, excluding SBC, was approximately 4.2% of revenue, down from 5.3% in the same period last year. Adjusted net income grew 20.7% year over year taking into consideration of RMB376 million tax refund received in the same quarter last year. Operating cash flow was RMB3.7 billion, and capital expenditure totaled RMB1.3 billion."

Ms. Yan added, "Our results reflected our simple but consistent financial discipline: we seek profitable growth through scale leverage without sacrificing fair price, optimize asset utilization and rely on technological innovations to stay cost competitive. With volume growth decelerated, we are directing focus and effort on building last mile cost advantage and strengthening earnings by our franchise partners and couriers. With that, we are maintaining our parcel-volume growth guidance for the year, and are well positioned to further expand our industry volume leadership."

Third Quarter 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

Total Revenues were RMB14,361.6 million (US$2,142.1 million), increased 21.0% from RMB11,864.7 million in the same period of 2025. Revenue from the core express delivery business increased by 21.6% compared to the same period of 2025 as a result of a 7.0% growth in parcel volume and a 13.7% increase in parcel unit price. Within core express delivery revenue, key account revenue, generated by direct sales organizations, increased by 68.3% mainly driven by increase in e-commerce return parcels. Revenue from freight forwarding services decreased by 8.1% compared to the same period of 2025. Revenue from sales of accessories, largely consisted of sales of thermal paper for digital waybills, increased by 2.8%. Other revenues were mainly derived from financing services.

Total cost of revenues was RMB10,829.3 million (US$1,615.2 million), an increase of 21.6% from RMB8,908.7 million in the same period last year.

Line-haul transportation cost was RMB3,327.7 million (US$496.3 million), increased 0.8% from RMB3,302.0 million in the same period last year. The unit transportation cost decreased 5.9% or 2 cents mainly attributable to better economies of scale and improved load rate through more effective route planning offsetting higher diesel prices.

Sorting hub operating cost was RMB2,595.9 million (US$387.2 million), increased 8.4% from RMB2,394.1 million in the same period last year. The increase primarily consisted of (i) RMB110.8 million (US$16.5 million) increase in labor-associated costs partially offset by automation-driven efficiency improvements, and (ii) RMB66.0 million (US$9.8 million) increase in depreciation and amortization costs associated with automation facilities and equipment upgrades. As of September 30, 2026, there were 805 sets of automated sorting equipment in service, compared to 761 sets as of September 30, 2025.

Cost of accessories sold was RMB139.9 million (US$20.9 million), increased by 3.2% compared with RMB135.6 million in the same period last year.

Other costs were RMB4,570.4 million (US$681.7 million), increased 59.1% from RMB2,872.2 million in the same period last year, which was mainly due to an increase of RMB1,665.7 million (US$248.4 million) for pickup and dispatching costs paid to network partners associated with serving key account customers, primarily for handling e-commerce return parcels.

Gross Profit was RMB3,532.4 million (US$ 526.9 million), increased by 19.5% from RMB2,956.0 million in the same period last year. Gross margin rate was 24.6% compared to 24.9% in the same period last year.

Total Operating Expenses were RMB555.9 million (US$82.9 million), compared to RMB550.9 million in the same period last year.

Selling, general and administrative expenses were RMB599.3 million (US$89.4 million), decreased by 5.3% from RMB632.6 million in the same period last year, mainly due to (i) RMB13.3 million (US$2.0 million) increase in compensation and benefit expenses, offset by (ii) RMB44.6 million (US$6.7 million) decrease in depreciation and amortization costs associated with administrative facilities and equipment.

Other operating income, net was RMB43.4 million (US$6.5 million), compared to RMB81.7 million in the same period last year. Other operating income mainly consisted of (i) RMB106.6 million (US$15.9 million) in losses on disposal and impairment of fixed assets, (ii) RMB94.7 million (US$14.1 million) of government subsidies and tax rebates, and (iii) RMB55.3 million (US$8.2 million) of rental and other income.

Income from operations was RMB2,976.5 million (US$444.0 million), increased 23.8% from RMB2,405.0 million for the same period last year. The operating margin rate increased to 20.7% from 20.3% in the same period last year.

Interest income was RMB103.1 million (US$15.4 million), compared with RMB185.2 million in the same period last year.

Interest expenses was RMB48.0 million (US$7.2 million), compared with RMB54.4 million in the same period last year.

Gain from fair value changes of financial instruments was RMB103.5 million (US$15.4 million), compared with a gain of RMB102.3 million in the same period last year. The Company uses EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net income, adjusted net income attributable to ordinary shareholders, and adjusted basic and diluted earnings per American depositary share attributable to ordinary shareholders, each a non-GAAP financial measure, in evaluating ZTO's operating results and for financial and operational decision-making purposes.

Reconciliations of the Company's non-GAAP financial measures to its U.S. GAAP financial measures are shown in tables at the end of this earnings release, which provide more details about the non-GAAP financial measures.

The Company believes that such non-GAAP measures help identify underlying trends in the Company's business that could otherwise be distorted by the effect of the related expenses and gains that the Company includes in income from operations and net income, and provide useful information about its operating results, enhance the overall understanding of its past performance and future prospects and allow for greater visibility with respect to key metrics used by the Company's management in its financial and operational decision-making.

EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net income, adjusted net income attributable to ordinary shareholders and adjusted basic and diluted earnings per American depositary share attributable to ordinary shareholders should not be considered in isolation or construed as an alternative to net income or any other measure of performance or as an indicator of the Company's operating performance. Other companies may calculate similarly titled measures differently, limiting their usefulness as comparative measures to ZTO's data. ZTO encourages investors and others to review the Company's financial information in its entirety and not rely on a single financial measure.

ZTO Express (Cayman) Inc. (NYSE: ZTO and SEHK: 2057) ("ZTO" or the "Company") is a leading and fast-growing express delivery company in China. ZTO provides express delivery service as well as other value-added logistics services through its extensive and reliable nationwide network coverage in China.

ZTO operates a highly scalable network partner model, which the Company believes is best suited to support the significant growth of e-commerce in China. The Company leverages its network partners to provide pickup and last-mile delivery services, while controlling the mission-critical line-haul transportation and sorting network within the express delivery service value chain.

#5393. Mamdani’s NYC public housing rebuild plan skirts DSA rebuke

Delegates debated and ultimately rejected a resolution opposing redevelopment at two Manhattan public housing properties. Critics cite privatization concerns tied to a shift to project-based Section 8, while the city argues rebuild costs less than renovation.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s quest to replace aging public housing with new buildings faced a potential political reckoning this past weekend. But Mamdani survived a challenge from like-minded Democratic Socialists.

Delegates to the city’s Democratic Socialists of America convention on Saturday voted down a resolution to oppose the city’s plan to demolish and rebuild two Manhattan public housing developments. It was the only one of nine resolutions to fail at a convention attended by more than 430 delegates.

Mamdani, who didn’t attend the convention, won a year ago on his vow to make New York more affordable. Delivering on that promise has meant sometimes walking a fine line. By proceeding with a plan developed under Eric Adams, a mayor critics accused of being in developers’ pockets, he risks being lumped in with his predecessor.

Democratic socialists now face similar choices elsewhere. In Los Angeles, DSA member Nithya Raman ousted outgoing Mayor Karen Bass on a pledge to build more homes faster. She will likely draw fire from neighborhood advocates opposed to higher density and zoning changes required by new state laws.

The plan is to demolish 2,056 public housing apartments in Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea Houses and rebuild them, with the New York City Housing Authority still owning them. Private developers would then add about 3,500 mixed-income apartments. Current tenants would get new apartments under private management, with rent held at 30% of income.

Had the DSA resolution passed, Mamdani could have faced stiffer backlash against a multi-billion project than he was already facing from tenant rights groups. Instead, Mamdani hopes the project stands as a model for rebuilding other decaying public housing properties elsewhere in the city.

Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea’s 18 buildings were built in phases from 1945 to 1965. Construction largely occurred under Robert Moses’ tenure as the city’s powerful unelected master builder.

Moses supported tall buildings, parks, highways and slum clearance to ease the path, including the site now being redeveloped. He dubbed the area’s tenements and factories blight.

But like public housing across the country, flawed maintenance policies left years of issues unresolved. Pruitt-Igoe in St. Louis began deteriorating within years of the 1954 completion of its 33 towers. The city demolished them by 1976.

Mamdani and DSA members in his administration say the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea buildings are in such bad shape that tearing them down costs less than renovating them. This approach also adapts to shrinking federal money for public housing.

The administration says NYCHA faces about $78 billion in repair needs. Conversion cash flow is one of the few ways to pay for them.

“Too many leaders have walked away from public housing,” Matt Rauschenbach, a Mamdani spokesman, said in a statement last month. “We are not going to.”

Cea Weaver, who leads the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants and is a DSA member, told Gothamist that leaving the housing in its current disrepair is unacceptable given her socialist values.

The fix has been circulating for years, first under former Mayor Bill de Blasio. Under Adams, NYCHA announced in December 2021 that resident leaders had selected Related Companies and Essence Development as its development partners. Related is best known for Hudson Yards, the 28-acre Manhattan megaproject it built with Oxford Properties.

NYCHA began issuing relocation notices in July 2025, and two buildings are designated for demolition in the first phase.

Critics, including the tenants’ DSA resolution, point to Hudson Yards as evidence that a for-profit firm has no place managing public housing.

“Related Companies is scheduled to make hundreds of millions of dollars from federal funding as well as rents through this project, while we, as socialists, know that a billion-dollar company like Related has no business anywhere near our city’s public housing,” the DSA resolution states.

The resolution says residents have called the project a “land grab.”

Three tenants joined DSA and were elected delegates with the backing of the chapter’s Tenant Organizing Working Group. They argue the plan privatizes public housing. The buildings would move from the federal Section 9 program to project-based Section 8, in which the government subsidizes rent through vouchers.

“We have no interest in being privatized,” Celines Miranda, one of the new delegates, told Gothamist last week. “We have no interest in being demolished.”

The resolution called the buildings structurally sound and criticized developer Related Companies for withholding structural analyses. More than two dozen families, including many seniors, are refusing to move.

Tenants and neighbors also tried to stop the project in court. In July, a state appeals court upheld rulings that denied their requests for preliminary injunctions. The court determined that their challenge was filed after the four-month deadline that began when NYCHA issued its July 2025 decision to proceed.

The court also ruled that relocation, while “inconvenient and difficult,” especially for seniors, did not amount to irreparable harm.

Weaver said the activists do not speak for all residents and that many tenants want the project to proceed.

Only 37% of delegates backed the resolution in a pre-convention survey. It won 44% on the floor, suggesting tenants flipped some votes but not enough to win.

The Docusign plugin for ChatGPT helps sellers prepare for renewals, spot opportunities to grow accounts, and move deals forward.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Docusign today announced new ways for sales teams to use the Docusign plugin through ChatGPT for Sales, so customers can see what was agreed to in a contract and act on that information in the same conversation. Sellers can prepare for a renewal, create a sales contract, or start a request with Legal directly in ChatGPT.

Docusign provides the agreement intelligence layer for these workflows. It brings signed terms, renewal deadlines, and commitments together with account context from a connected CRM like Salesforce. Sellers can spend less time tracking down contract details and more time talking with customers about what comes next.

"Every signed contract tells you what the customer bought, what you promised to deliver, and when it's time to talk about what's next," said Allan Thygesen, CEO of Docusign. "With Docusign in OpenAI's new ChatGPT for Sales, sellers can use that information to prepare for a renewal, draft the next agreement, or get Legal involved. Wherever people and AI work, Docusign provides the agreement intelligence to make informed decisions and the workflows to act on them."

With the Docusign plugin for ChatGPT, sales teams can:

The Docusign MCP server and the agreement layerThe Docusign Model Context Protocol (MCP) server powers the plugin, connecting ChatGPT to Docusign agreement intelligence and workflows. It shows what a headless agreement platform makes possible. Sellers can start agreement work in the tools they already use, while Docusign provides the underlying contract context, templates, and approval workflows.

The Docusign plugin for ChatGPT is available today for download. The Docusign plugin is available in ChatGPT for Sales and also works with the OpenAI Sales plugin. For more information about Docusign MCP connectors visit: https://www.docusign.com/products/mcp.

#5391. Promise Robotics raises $25M to scale automated homebuilding

Promise Robotics closed a $25M Series B after landing a multiyear D.R. Horton agreement. Its strategy focuses on platform investment and portable production to reduce fixed cost exposure that hurt prior industrialized builders.  AI Summary

Any way you look at it, homebuilding comes down to three things: how many homes a company can produce and sell, how much it costs to produce them, and how consistently the business can turn those homes into positive net margins. There’s no getting around throughput.

Homebuilding leaders who do those three things well rarely have qualms about finding ways to do them even better. Innovation, however, is another matter. Homebuilders like innovation. Many believe it’s necessary, even inevitable. But do they have to embrace it? Do they have to change how they operate to adopt and integrate it? Do they dare risk what works, warts and all, for what hasn’t yet proven to solve the throughput riddle economically?

Evidence suggests that if innovation were a necessity rather than a choice, or a known rather than a leap into a chasm of unknowns, more of the dozens of companies launched over the past decade with promises to transform homebuilding, lower costs and make homes more attainable would still be in business today.

Which brings us to Promise Robotics, a company whose name might as well be its business plan: Say what you’re going to do, and then do what you say.

Fresh off a multiyear commercial agreement with D.R. Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder, Promise Robotics today announced a $25 million Series B financing round led by White Star Capital, with participation from Horizons Ventures, Radical Ventures and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

The financing follows Promise’s agreement to support the production of more than 1,250 homes for D.R. Horton as the company prepares to bring its first U.S. manufacturing facility online in Phoenix in 2027. Promise already operates production facilities in Calgary and Nisku, Alberta, and reports more than 2,000 housing units under contract across three markets.

For Promise co-founder and CEO Ramtin Attar, the latest investment adrenaline shot is an opportunity to show that the company has figured out how to turn advanced robotics, artificial intelligence and factory-built construction into a sustainable business capable of weathering homebuilding’s inevitable ups and downs, which, by the way, are now mostly downs.

That’s where this homebuilding innovation’s never-ending story takes a turn.

Because the history of industrialized homebuilding is littered with companies that developed impressive technologies, attracted enthusiastic investors, and secured commitments from builders, only to discover that the economics of operating their businesses – and the critical factor of the time value of money in a stubbornly high cost of money backdrop – were far less forgiving than the promise of their innovations.

Attar is all too familiar with that history. So are his investors.

“Every investor’s question often starts by asking what went wrong with Katerra, what went wrong with X and Y and Z,” Attar told HousingWire TBD in an exclusive interview.

His determination is to transform Promise Robotics into a fundamentally different kind of construction technology business, one that uses venture capital to develop its technology platform while seeking lower-cost financing to scale its physical production capacity.

“We have been very clear about what we want to use this funding for,” Attar said. “It’s not for funding factories; it’s for funding the platform.”

Attar’s laser clarity on how the strategy will be operationalized may prove more important to Promise’s long-term prospects than the robots themselves. The distinction goes directly to the problem that has defeated so many would-be homebuilding innovators: scaling manufacturing capacity without accumulating fixed costs that become unsustainable when housing demand weakens.

One of the more revealing details from Attar’s latest interview concerns what Promise calls a factory. The company’s Phoenix operation is being set up in a 16,000-square-foot warehouse with existing electrical infrastructure and a loading bay. Attar said the facility requires almost no tenant improvements and is under a relatively short-term lease.

Importantly, the robotic equipment itself can be ported from market to market.

“It was the same two robots that were producing homes in Calgary,” Attar said. “We just moved them to Phoenix two weeks ago. They’re already set up. We’re just hiring, and we’re going to start producing.”

Portability is central to Promise’s effort to avoid the fixed-cost exposure associated with large, purpose-built manufacturing facilities. The company can theoretically deploy equipment in markets where customer demand supports production, rather than making a substantial permanent investment in each market before securing sufficient orders.

The model still depends on reliable demand, efficient material handling, trained workers, and economical installation. But it offers more flexibility to respond to changing market conditions. Attar also described an operational improvement that provides a clearer view of the company’s economic progress.

When Promise initially relied on outside contractors to install its prefabricated components, installation costs averaged about C$9 per square foot. After developing its own installation workforce, the company reduced that figure to about C$4.50.

That 50% reduction is significant, though it applies to installation costs rather than to total home construction costs. For Attar, it shows that the opportunity to improve construction economics extends beyond robotic manufacturing.

“There are still tremendous gains to be made on the human side of things,” he said.

The company’s recursive learning process increasingly involves understanding labor requirements, installation sequencing, material logistics and how production crews work alongside existing trades. Those improvements and the ongoing learning may prove as important as advances in robotic speed or capability.

Promise’s agreement with D.R. Horton establishes a prominent commercial relationship, serves as a lever for inroads among other operators and provides an opportunity to demonstrate its capabilities within one of homebuilding’s most sophisticated production organizations.

The multiyear agreement calls for Promise to support the production of more than 1,250 homes. For D.R. Horton, the attraction is access to automated manufacturing capacity without the expense and operational complexity of owning the infrastructure.

For Promise, the relationship offers the prospect of production volume, operating experience and elevated credibility with other builders. Attar said interest from additional homebuilders has increased following the announcement.

What’s more, the vibe around Promise has extended beyond potential new customers. Committed production volume could also help Promise secure financing for equipment and facilities at lower costs than venture equity.

“If you’ve got commitment, you can start to get creative about accessing [capital],” Attar said. “Using equity to build factories is the most expensive way to go about it.”

He believes that once individual manufacturing operations achieve sustainable economics, they can attract conventional financing. That remains an objective rather than an established financing model across Promise’s network. The company has not publicly disclosed factory-level profitability, capital requirements per deployment, or the utilization rates needed to support debt repayment.

Those measures will be important tests of its ability to expand without continually returning to venture investors for more capital.

According to Attar, Promise’s current production capabilities cover roughly 15% to 20% of construction activity, depending on the market and the components included. The company is working to increase that share to about 40% by incorporating more building systems into its manufacturing process.

In Canada, Promise already produces structural components that can include windows, doors and openings for mechanical systems. It has begun projects involving HVAC and plumbing, with electrical work, insulation, and drywall next.

Builders can begin with familiar framing components, build confidence in the manufacturing process, and gradually move additional work into the factory. That approach accounts for the effort required to change an industry whose production process depends on established relationships among independent trades.

“We’ve got to work alongside trades. We’ve got to work alongside the existing supply chain,” Attar said.

It also creates another challenge. Manufacturing more complete building assemblies can improve efficiency, but those benefits depend on local building codes, inspection requirements, and the ability to coordinate factory production with construction-site schedules.

Promise will need to show that greater factory completion lowers total costs and speeds home deliveries, rather than simply shifting work and complexity from one location to another.

The timing of Promise’s financing introduces another important test. Homebuilders face weak affordability, elevated financing costs, and persistent uncertainty about consumer demand. At the same time, labor availability remains a structural constraint, and immigration enforcement is further disrupting construction workforces in some markets.

That combination creates both opportunity and risk for automated construction.

Builders have stronger reasons to secure reliable production capacity and reduce their exposure to labor shortages. But they also have limited tolerance for new expenses, operational disruption, or technology that takes a long time to deliver measurable returns.

Promise’s model attempts to address that contradiction by allowing builders to purchase output without making upfront investments in robotic equipment.

Attar said the company is also developing installation partnerships to establish clear labor costs, quality expectations and operating standards.

Rather than necessarily employing every installation worker directly, Promise intends to use its platform to coordinate qualified installation teams across markets.

The company is preparing for two additional factory deployments in 2028, with the ambition to reach a pace of one new deployment per quarter by early 2029.

Those targets represent a substantial increase in operational complexity. Technology that works reliably in a small number of facilities must eventually support geographically dispersed teams, different builders, varying local regulations, and multiple supply chains.

Attar identifies workforce development and organizational culture as major challenges in that transition.

“At some point, technology scales really fast. It’s very controllable. It’s very measurable,” he said. “But how do you continue to grasp and build a culture, an environment that people thrive, they’re committed?”

For a business whose ultimate performance depends on the interaction among software, machinery, materials and people, that question looms large.

White Star Capital general partner Sanjay Zimmermann describes Promise as an opportunity to build a new production infrastructure platform for homebuilding.

“Just as impressive is how well this team executes across builders, projects, and markets, with their recent multi-year agreement with D.R. Horton a powerful proof point,” Zimmermann said in the financing announcement.

White Star’s investment thesis rests in part on the expectation that Promise’s production network will become more valuable as it expands.

More factories could generate additional operating data, purchasing opportunities, and production experience. These advantages could improve costs and performance across the network. But the economics must ultimately be demonstrated at the level of individual projects and facilities.

The company’s reported 2,000-plus housing units under contract demonstrate commercial traction, though that figure should not be confused with completed production or recognized revenue.

Likewise, the ability to reduce installation costs or shorten framing schedules does not automatically translate into lower total construction costs for customers. The evidence investors and builders will need includes sustained factory utilization, positive operating cash flow, reliable delivery performance, and measurable improvements in homebuilding economics. These practical measures will test Promise’s claims.

The $25 million Series B gives Promise Robotics more capital to develop its technology and pursue the expansion opportunities created by its growing commercial relationships. The D.R. Horton agreement gives it an important customer relationship and a proving ground for its operating model.

The difficult history of industrialized construction demonstrates that technological sophistication, investor enthusiasm and even strong initial customer interest won’t substitute for sustainable unit economics.

Attar’s approach reflects an appreciation for and hard-earned lessons from that history. Promise is concentrating on established construction activity, minimizing permanent factory investments, developing repeatable operating processes, and seeking financing structures that better match the economics of manufacturing.

Its most important advances may ultimately come from reducing installation costs, improving logistics, increasing utilization, and learning to integrate with builders’ existing operations.

That is a less glamorous story than robots transforming homebuilding overnight. It is also a more credible path to making industrialized construction an enduring part of the industry’s production system.

For an industry that needs more affordable homes but cannot rely on stronger demand, abundant labor or easier financing to solve its problems, Promise represents a potentially valuable experiment in doing more with the resources available.

The next two years will begin to show whether that experiment can become a durable business. And that is the real promise behind Promise Robotics’ latest round of financing: not simply developing a better way to build, but proving that the business of building better can survive long enough to change the industry.

#5390. OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday work

OpenAI Group PBC today announced the launch of GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier artificial intelligence model for complex professional work that is claimed to outperform its predecessor at less than a third of the cost, along with an updated version of its everyday model, GPT-6.2 Sol.

The new models are aimed at businesses and developers looking for frontier performance at a cost that works at scale, with both said to deliver better results on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens.

According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new high on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multistep professional work, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra while costing under a third as much. It is claimed to have finished 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

OpenAI is positioning GPT-6.2 Astra as the best model in the world for scientists, with the model scoring 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a benchmark for scientific work carried out in a terminal. On Harvey LAB-AA, a test of legal assignments, the model more than doubled the pass rate of Fable 5.2 at about one-sixth of the cost.

Along with improved benchmark scores, GPT-6.2 Astra was trained to create slides, spreadsheets and documents that more closely follow the conventions used by professionals in fields such as law, sales, finance and accounting. The model can match a slide template from an original file or a screenshot, including layout, colors and typography down to the exact font size.

Early testers of the model include accounting AI startup Basis, which said that its average time for long-horizon accounting work fell by 50%, with the time for its most complex work falling by up to 73%.

Described by OpenAI as its go-to model for everyday work, GPT-6.2 Sol is claimed to let users complete more tasks on the same paid plan than GPT-6.1 Sol did. According to OpenAI, the model came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI Inc.’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at about one-fifth of the cost.

GPT-6.2 Astra comes less than two months after OpenAI called off the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after internal testing found the model fell short on staying within scope and authorization. The decision was announced the day before the company’s DevDay event in September, where GPT-6.1 Sol launched on its own.

Like GPT-6 Astra, both GPT-6.2 models meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, and their increased capabilities have led the company to launch them with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance that are also said to restrict some legitimate vulnerability research. The company said it will work to bring the GPT-6.2 models to Daybreak, its program for vetted cyber defenders.

GPT-6.2 Astra is also the first externally released OpenAI model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement, a measure of a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. OpenAI tracks the capability because models that help build future AI systems could outpace safeguards and human oversight, and earlier this month it disclosed Control Room, a system already deployed across its research infrastructure that can halt model output when intervention is needed.

The company noted that in two of its alignment tests, the new models were more likely than GPT-6 Astra to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file. OpenAI said it has added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce the omissions and is continuing to investigate the behavior.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available starting today to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Enterprise and Edu access requiring a workspace admin to enable it. Developers can also access both models through the OpenAI API. API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is $8 per million input tokens, 40 cents for cached input and $40 per million output tokens, a 20% discount on input and output tokens compared with GPT-6 Astra. GPT-6.2 Sol carries forward GPT-6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

#5388. Mortgage rates jump to 7.58% as inflation lifts bond yields

Mortgage rates rose sharply last week, with 30-year conforming loans at 7.58% and jumbo loans at 7.87%. Hot inflation data and higher yields pushed Fed hike expectations above 93%, while builders continued offering rate incentives for new homes.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates skyrocketed last week on the back of rising inflation and bond yields, erasing some of the recent affordability gains for potential homebuyers.

At HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.58%, up 23 basis points from one week ago. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans jumped 31 bps to average 7.87%, while rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) rose 15 bps to 7.37%.

HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote over the weekend that “last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market” due to hawkish statements from Federal Reserve officials and hot inflation data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Additionally, the U.S. conflict with Iran and potential tariff increases against Mexico propelled long-term Treasury rates and mortgage rates upward.

Interest rate traders took notice. According to the CME Group‘s FedWatch tool, more than 93% expect benchmark rates to increase by 25 bps at next month’s Fed meeting. That’s up from 76% one month ago. It would be the second hike of the year by the Fed and put the federal funds rate at a range of 4% to 4.25%.

Kyle Bass, business production manager at Refi.com, pointed to Mortgage Bankers Association application data showing that recent downward moves in rates had positive impacts on loan demand. But with visible volatility in rates on a day-to-day basis, he said, preparation between loan officers and borrowers is needed to lock in the lowest possible rate and get lower monthly payments.

“Borrowers who benefit are the ones who prepared before the number moved. A shadow application, with income documents, statements and credit in order, lets a homeowner ask what their current mortgage could do for them the day rates cooperate. Waiting for a better number only works if you are ready when it arrives,” Bass said.

A report released Tuesday by Realtor.com shows that the new-home segment is giving the typical buyer lower rates and better affordability than existing homes. Homebuilders, who are also under financial pressure, continue to offer rate buydowns and other incentives as they seek to offload their inventory.

Realtor.com reported that the average mortgage rate for a new-home buyer in the third quarter was 5.01%, more than a full percentage point lower than the 6.15% rate for an existing-home buyer. That translates to a difference of $258 in monthly payments for someone buying a $400,000 home with a 10% down payment.

“Builders have adjusted to a market where affordability is still a major hurdle, but that adjustment isn’t always visible in the listing price,” Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. “Reduced mortgage rates can help make a new home more affordable for buyers while allowing builders to hold asking prices relatively steady.”

The report noted that reduced rates are often temporary and only last for the first few years after origination. But even when comparing 30-year fixed rates, those who bought a new home in the third quarter saved, with average rates of 6.19% compared to 6.68% for existing home-buyers. On the same $400,000 purchase with 10% down, the new-home buyer saves about $117 per month in interest.

“Mortgage-rate incentives can make a meaningful difference in what a buyer pays each month, but it’s important to understand how long the lower rate lasts,” Berner said. “A temporary buydown can provide relief early on, while a lower rate fixed for the life of the loan offers a different kind of savings.”

Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, said in a statement that tariff-driven increases to building materials are putting pressure on the new-home segment. In turn, this winds up being felt by consumers through higher home purchase prices. Regardless of the type of home being purchased, rising insurance premiums and property taxes are also straining budgets.

“For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market,” Hepp said.” Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner.”

While housing market professionals continue to grapple with fewer home sales and lower mortgage origination volumes, the U.S. economy as a whole continues to show resilience to inflation, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty.

Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage, pointed to last week’s Producer Price Index (PPI), which showed 6.5% inflation on an annualized basis in October. It was the largest year-over-year increase since November 2022. That came only days after the Consumer Price Index showed monthly inflation of 0.4%.

“Unfortunately, the CPI number that we got earlier this week has set off bond yields, and bond yields were probably up almost 25 basis points from where they were at the end of the previous week,” Cohn said Friday in a statement. “It’s not just because of the CPI number, but because of expectations about the Fed, where members are saying, ‘Well, we’re definitely going to have to hike rates.’ We know that the market’s expecting it.

“All of the benefit that we got in mortgage rates over the course of the past three weeks was basically just thrown out the window again, because mortgage rates are really tied to the rate of inflation. We’re back on the inflation wagon.”

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh offered some forward-looking remarks on Monday during a jobs and productivity conference in San Francisco, saying that the central bank continues to look closely at the development of “super intelligence” and its impacts on the global and national economies.

“At the Fed, our role in all this is neither advocacy nor opposition. Our responsibility is to recognize that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road,” Warsh said.

#5386. Renting as a financial strategy, what real estate agents should know

Entrata’s Virginia Love says renters are making intentional tradeoffs, prioritizing savings, debt reduction, and flexibility. Agents can better serve renters by discussing full ownership costs, budget comfort, and timelines without assuming buying is the next step.  AI Summary

Renting isn’t always a stepping stone to homeownership. Multifamily expert Virginia Love of Entrata explains how financial priorities, flexibility and the true cost of ownership are reshaping renters’ decisions.

The story we’re telling ourselves about renters is outdated, Virginia Love, industry principal at Entrata, told me recently.

Entrata is a property management operating system built to improve operational efficiency at multifamily communities. In its recent “Resident Pulse” survey, conducted in partnership with YouGov, the company asked renters about their financial priorities, attitudes toward homeownership, definitions of success and other lifestyle factors.

That gives Love a bird’s-eye view of the state of renting and, by extension, homeownership.

“I feel like people think that renters are less-than,” she said. “I think the real story is, people are trying to do what’s right for them and what’s right for their family.”

With homeownership increasingly out of reach for people of all ages, it’s time that real estate agents rethink the role of renters in the housing market. Entrata’s insights can help.

Love said that renters are prioritizing healthy financial hygiene and making decisions based on a more complex economic environment, reducing their existing financial obligations before pursuing longer-term financial goals.

“They are eating out less, they’re shopping less, they’re spending less, they’re switching to cheaper brands,” she said, with the goal of prioritizing emergency savings, debt reduction and other budgetary line items.

For previous generations, the initial barrier to homeownership was a down payment, Love said. Now, it’s the rising costs of everything that comes after the initial upfront purchase price: the mortgage payment at today’s higher rates, insurance, maintenance, repairs and other expenses. Managing the unexpected requires greater levels of financial stability.

“It’s then I have insurance, then I gotta take care of the yard. Then what if the tree falls on the driveway?” Love said.

Beyond the cost of rent vs. buy, maintenance, amenities and the ability to relocate can have real value for renters, especially when they’re working to pay down debt, pursuing educational goals, navigating career shifts or deciding where and when they’re ready to settle down. What they’re paying for, Love said, is freedom.

Love describes Gen Z in particular as pragmatic about money and more willing to take a gradual path toward major financial milestones.

For those who plan to buy, “they’re absolutely fine with starter homes,” Love said. “And I don’t think that that is something that we’ve seen for a while. Everybody kind of wanted to go from zero to 60, and this is a generation that’s willing to take those steps.”

She explains that some renters are working toward a purchase while others prefer to invest, maintain flexibility or avoid being tied to one address.

Real estate agents often approach renters with an ingrained belief in the superiority of homeownership, but it’s not right for everyone. Spend time upfront with renters to find out what matters to them, and don’t just push them toward homeownership automatically, Love said.

Stop assuming buying is the client’s next step: Renters aren’t necessarily buyers who simply haven’t saved up a down payment yet. They may have other financial priorities, like paying down student loans, building an emergency fund, investing for retirement or prioritizing flexibility. Ask what a client’s financial priorities are before assuming homeownership is the goal.

Talk about the full cost of homeownership: Down payments aren’t the whole story here. Monthly payments, rising insurance and repair costs, home maintenance and other expenses can affect whether, and when, buying makes sense. Make sure you’re sharing updated costs of ownership along with the upfront costs, and be realistic about affordability.

Ask what payment feels comfortable, not just what a lender will approve: A client’s maximum purchasing power isn’t necessarily the same as their target budget. Understand the buying budget that matches their comfort level, other financial considerations and personal priorities before locking in on a price range.

Understand that delay isn’t the same as giving up: Some renters may aspire to own a home, but they’re not necessarily in a rush. Maintain relationships over the long haul without turning every conversation into a homebuying pitch.

Recognize that renting has value beyond the monthly payment: The benefits of renting — maintenance support, amenities, flexibility and freedom — may outweigh those of homeownership, even though they don’t build equity for the renter. Understand what the renter values before presenting ownership as an obvious upgrade or superior choice.

“I think the real story is, people are trying to do what’s right for them and what’s right for their family,” Love said. By understanding timing, goals and price sensitivities, agents can help potential clients evaluate their options without prescribing the outcome ahead of time.

Troy Palmquist is the founder of HomeCode Advisors.

#5384. Prophetic unveils SiteAI Drafter for homebuilder land teams

Prophetic has launched SiteAI Drafter, a new feature for its SiteAI platform that lets land acquisition teams draw high-precision, compliant subdivision site plans and see lot yields update in real time. With added CAD export, both automated and drafted plans can move directly into detailed civil engineering, therefore cutting feasibility time and early design costs.  AI Summary

Prophetic has launched SiteAI Drafter, a tool that lets land teams draw high-precision, compliant subdivision site plans in minutes and export them directly to CAD.

The company, which describes itself as the operating system for land acquisition, introduced SiteAI Drafter on Tuesday as a new feature designed to help residential land teams move from site concept to engineering faster and at lower upfront cost, according to its announcement.

SiteAI Drafter is now available to all SiteAI users and adds manual, CAD-ready drafting to a platform that has focused primarily on automated layouts and early-stage feasibility analysis.

SiteAI generates subdivision site plans with lot and unit yield that account for setbacks, wetlands, flood zones, open spaces and stormwater ponds. Builders and developers use the system to run feasibility studies in seconds instead of weeks, replacing initial engineering reports that can cost from $3,000 to more than $10,000.

The platform’s automated layouts estimate maximum theoretical yield and quickly screen large numbers of parcels. Because SiteAI incorporates site constraints at the outset, it can flag issues that might not surface until much later in a traditional workflow, when engineering work is further along and sunk costs are higher.

For acquisition and development teams working in a competitive land market, this kind of early, standardized analysis is used to compare sites on a level playing field and decide which deals to advance before ordering surveys or full design work.

While automated layouts help screen many parcels at once, land teams often have a preferred concept for a specific site based on local jurisdiction standards, topography and planned product types. Under traditional processes, testing that concept typically requires drafting in CAD or waiting for an engineer, which can slow decisions and tie up billable time.

SiteAI Drafter allows users to draw their own road network and configure lots while the system enforces basic subdivision rules in the background. The tool understands roads and rights of way, lot dimensions and product mix so users can experiment with different layouts while staying within buildable constraints.

According to Prophetic, SiteAI Drafter enables land teams to:

The result is a customizable subdivision plan that can reflect the specific community a builder wants to take to a seller, investment committee or municipal review, while still providing a defensible yield number.

Beyond drafting, Prophetic is adding CAD export so that plans created either by SiteAI’s automated engine or by SiteAI Drafter can be used as a starting point for detailed civil engineering design.

This is intended to shift engineers and planners away from redrawing concepts from scratch and toward refining the land team’s preferred layout. Prophetic said the export capability also opens the platform to civil engineers, planners and land developers who want to generate quick concepts before full design or to show builders what a site can hold before a first meeting.

“Every land team plans a site a little differently,” said Oliver Alexander, founder and CEO of Prophetic. “Sometimes you want an answer in seconds across dozens of parcels. Sometimes you already know exactly where the entry and the main road go, and you want to see what your plan yields. SiteAI now works however you do. And with CAD export, the plan doesn’t stop with the land team. It goes to the engineer as a starting point, not a sketch to redraw. That’s what an operating system for land acquisition should do: carry the work forward and help our users win more deals.”

As higher rates and tighter capital make land bets more costly, builders, developers and their capital partners are under pressure to vet more sites with fewer people and less time. Early engineering work is expensive, and using consultants for preliminary concepts can slow down offers in competitive bid situations.

Tools that combine automated yield analysis with guided drafting give acquisition leaders a way to pressure-test their preferred community design before committing to full engineering fees. For homebuilders and land developers, the ability to walk into a seller or investment committee meeting with a concept plan, yield range and CAD-ready file can help shorten decision cycles and reduce the risk of surprises later in entitlement or design.

#5382. Token sticker shock pushes enterprises from frontier labs toward open-weight AI factories

Enterprises have spent the AI boom racing to secure GPUs, but the harder decisions now sit above the hardware. Token bills, data sovereignty and model choice increasingly decide which AI pilots reach production, a shift on display at the SC26 supercomputing conference.

Dell Technologies Inc. has spent the past year pushing its AI Factory beyond servers and storage. Customers now want a full-stack outcome that covers software, open-source tools, models and operations, according to Brad Maltz (pictured), senior director of AI solutions at Dell.

“The hardware’s key, because that drives the tokens,” Maltz said. “You really, truly need a full-stack AI factory view above and beyond just the hardware stack.”

Maltz spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how token bills and data sovereignty are steering enterprises toward open-weight models and a full-stack AI Factory. The interview came as Dell rolled out AI Factory updates at the conference. (* Disclosure below.)

Many enterprises are still stuck in pilot mode, and coding assistants are often the easiest place to start. Employees have already tried tools from Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, so teams want to apply that experience to business use cases. Once those pilots grow, the bill arrives, Maltz explained.

“The token spend right now in the frontier labs and the hyperscalers. That’s a little more than we expected,” Maltz said. “We didn’t expect to spend $10,000, $20,000 per person per month.”

Cost is only one trigger. Data sovereignty, intellectual property leakage, security and governance all have to be addressed before a pilot goes live. That is steering many enterprises toward open-weight models they can fine-tune and run on-premises, including U.S. options such as Nvidia Corp.’s Nemotron, according to Maltz.

“There will always be frontier labs. There will always be open-weight models,” Maltz said. “The question is going to be, do we have enough diversity with the open weights to meet the enterprise use cases?”

To keep pace, Dell launched its AI Ecosystem Program to validate software partners on its AI Factory. About 60 more partners have applied or are under evaluation, and each addition lets Dell solve 10 to 30 more customer problems, Maltz noted. For sovereign deployments, that often means disconnected, on-premises systems that keep models next to the GPUs and data enterprises already control.

“People understand data is the lifeblood of AI,” Maltz said. “It’s the thing that trains the models. It’s the thing the models operate against. It comes from your enterprise business applications.”

#5381. How reverse mortgage LOs can help borrowers to self-service

Reverse mortgage servicers are investing in borrower portals, mobile apps and smarter phone systems to reduce call volumes. Celink is launching ReverseLink soon, while Onity is expanding digital draw requests and emphasizing closing checklist steps for loan officers.  AI Summary

Reverse mortgage servicers are investing in portals, mobile applications and smarter phone systems so borrowers can manage their loans without contacting a human customer service representative. Servicing executives say that loan officers can play a key role in whether these tools actually work.

Gail Balettie, senior vice president of client satisfaction at Celink, and Ryan McIntire, director of reverse mortgage servicing controls at Onity Mortgage, outlined their companies’ self-service offerings during a panel discussion moderated by Chris Downey of CrossCountry Mortgage at last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo.

“In today’s world, where we are conditioned to some extent to be able to go online, get immediate satisfaction, to do things without talking to somebody, the more we can do that, the better we can reach our customers,” McIntire said.

Balettie announced at NRMLA Annual that her company’s mobile app, ReverseLink, will be launching “in the next few weeks.” Its design is similar to Celink’s website and borrowers will receive an invitation to download it. The company is the largest independent subservicer of reverse mortgages and has an estimated market share of about 75% across federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) and proprietary loans.

McIntire told the audience that Onity‘s servicing app is already available on iPhone and Android devices and mirrors its borrower portal. He stressed the importance of providing familiar technology to senior homeowners so “they don’t feel like they’re having to learn something all over again.”

Celink’s soon-to-be-released app will allow clients to accomplish multiple tasks, Balettie said. They’ll be able to request payoff quotes, make voluntary payments, upload forms and download up to two years of statements. The app automatically generates confirmation that an uploaded form has been received, cutting down the number of calls needed for this purpose.

“They can request a line-of-credit draw, and if they do so, they’re going to get their funds a day or two faster than the typical five-day turn time, because it comes in an automated fashion,” she added.

ReverseLink also has a number of FAQs and educational videos, covering subjects like how to manage the account online, what happens to the reverse mortgage when the borrower dies, how to shop for insurance coverage and how to file a claim, and how to find help with small home repairs.

Onity’s portal ties into the company’s system of record, McIntire said. It shows three months of transactions and includes an introduction package that’s tailored to the structure of the loan — for example, any funds set aside for required repairs. Onity is also in the process of building fully digital draw request forms. Today, borrowers have to download and complete these forms before returning it via email or fax, but the goal is to process e-signed draw requests within a few business days, McIntire said.

“Obviously, information that’s available to the borrower via this site is very sensitive. We obviously, as servicers, have to be very cognizant and mindful of fraud. So it does have multifactor authentication that just helps provide that additional sense of security,” he added.

Borrowers commonly contact their loan officer, rather than their servicer, when they have questions about their loan. Balettie said that LOs can take an “ABCD” role to approach to providing assistance in this area.

Making sure a servicer has the correct contact information for a borrower may seem obvious, but it doesn’t happen with perfect uniformity. “We get about 70% of our loans that board with an email address. I want to see that be 100%,” Balettie said. “I don’t know very many people who don’t have an email address in this day and age.”

Balettie sought to distinguish between the alternate contact on the loan application and an authorized third party. The latter may discuss the account but cannot change contact information or request a draw or payoff. Conversely, servicers use the alternate contact only when they cannot reach the borrower, she said.

A power of attorney can act for a living borrower, but legal authority ends at death, the panelists noted. Downey urged originators to execute the authorized party form at closing and warned that without it, payoffs for a borrower “can be a nightmare.” Having this information on file removes the need to hire an attorney to search for heirs after the borrower dies.

Balettie said originators should collect a canceled check and the direct deposit form at closing. Borrowers without a check can provide a redacted bank statement or bank letter with their account and routing numbers. Due to security concerns, servicers don’t allow bank details to be added online, but they’ll accept faxed or emailed documents, and closing is the best time to gather them.

#5380. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5379. ELEGOO Showcases New Solutions Across Resin Printing, FDM Printing and 3D Scanning at Formnext 2026

FRANKFURT, Germany, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ELEGOO, a rapidly developing brand in the global smart manufacturing industry, kicked off its participation at Formnext 2026 today, showcasing its latest product developments and offering visitors an exclusive first look at upcoming innovations. At booth 12.0-C02, ELEGOO brought together live product demonstrations, new innovation previews, and creator-led sessions, highlighting its continued exploration of resin printing, multi-material FDM printing, and connected creative workflows.

Kevin Wang, Co-founder and Vice President of ELEGOO, said, "We're continuously exploring new possibilities across different technologies to bring more versatile tools and solutions to creators. At Formnext this year, we're excited to share a preview of our upcoming developments in resin and FDM printing, alongside our latest 3D scanning solutions. The show also gives us a great opportunity to connect with creators and industry partners, exchange ideas, and be part of the conversations shaping the industry."

A First Look at What's Next in Resin and FDM Printing

Among the highlights, ELEGOO presented the Saturn 5 Ultra, its upcoming resin 3D printer. Designed as an all-round desktop resin printer, it combines high-precision performance and improved durability with enhanced productivity and ease of use. Its intelligent resin management system automates resin monitoring and replenishment, while design improvements simplify setup, maintenance, and operation. The Saturn 5 Ultra is currently planned for an early Q1 2027 launch.

ELEGOO also gave visitors an exclusive first look at the Centauri X Ultra, marking a significant milestone in the evolution of the Centauri series with its move into multi-printhead technology. Featuring four independent printheads, this upcoming FDM 3D printer explores new possibilities in multi-color and multi-material printing. Quick printhead switching helps minimize material waste during color changes, while compatibility with rigid and flexible materials enables a wider range of functional and creative applications. Its unexpected debut at Formnext drew visitors to the ELEGOO booth, sparking curiosity about the new addition to the Centauri series.

Experiencing the 3D Scanning Workflow with M1 Ultra

Another key highlight at the booth is the M1 Ultra, ELEGOO's first all-in-one smart 3D scanner. Through live demonstrations, visitors can experience its scanning capabilities and explore a complete workflow, from capturing physical objects to processing digital models with ELEGOOSCAN software. With metrology-grade accuracy of up to 0.02 mm and multiple scanning modes for different object sizes, surfaces, and levels of detail, the M1 Ultra supports applications ranging from reverse engineering and product development to digital archiving and 3D printing.

Connecting with Creators and the Global 3D Printing Community

Beyond product demonstrations, ELEGOO is hosting daily creator workshops at around 4:00 p.m., featuring experienced 3D printing creators who share practical insights, creative applications, and firsthand experiences with ELEGOO products. #5378. Lighter Halts Crypto Withdrawals After $15.5M Security Breach as LIT Falls

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Lighter has suspended crypto withdrawals after a suspected security breach drained $15.5 million from two market-maker accounts. Its LIT token fell more than 15% as traders assessed the damage.

The decentralized perpetual futures exchange halted withdrawals and new liquidity pool creation on November 16. The incident reportedly involved compromised API keys belonging to two market makers, rather than a vulnerability in Lighter’s core smart contracts.

Update: Our investigation indicates that today’s incident was caused by a leaked API key for a specific trader's account. The Lighter protocol and smart contracts are unaffected.As a precaution, we have enabled Guardian mode on our smart contract. Our main priority is to… https://t.co/LUuFiY5cK0

On-chain investigators identified a $10.39 million USDC withdrawal from Lighter’s Ethereum settlement contract. Another $5.09 million loss was reported from a second account, although investigators had not independently verified that amount leaving the platform.

The incident has raised fresh questions about security across decentralized derivatives platforms, particularly how exchanges protect large trading accounts and their liquidity infrastructure.

The suspected attacker reportedly gained access to API keys associated with two market-maker accounts. These credentials allegedly provided enough permissions to manipulate their trading positions and liquidity pool activity.

The reported losses were split between two accounts, with $10.39 million and $5.09 million in USDC taken from their respective balances. The alleged attack involved closing existing positions before creating a zero-fee liquidity pool under a compromised account. Attacker purchased nearly all its shares, transferred the victim’s funds into the pool, and redeemed those shares.

Bitquery independently tracked the first major withdrawal through Ethereum. The attacker converted $10.36 million in USDC into ETH within four minutes.

LIVE: tracking the Lighter hack walletAs of 11:36 UTC, 16 Nov:• 10.39M USDC out of @Lighter_xyz → 5,764 ETH• 10 payments of 160 ETH → Hyperliquid → 5,583 XMR1• 4,165 ETH still in the walletWe update as it moves:https://t.co/NZvBlmMEeP https://t.co/JcD3AOQ8Bs

The wallet received 5,764 ETH, subsequently distributing 960 ETH across six fresh wallets. Those wallets moved funds through Hyperliquid and purchased XMR1, while approximately 4,805 ETH remained in the original wallet during Bitquery’s investigation.

Lighter initially described this crypto incident as involving a compromised external party. It suspended withdrawals and new liquidity pool creation while investigating the breach.

The team subsequently clarified that its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. Instead, the incident reportedly originated from a leaked API key belonging to a specific trader.

As of now, Lighter activated Guardian mode on its smart contracts and announced plans to upgrade its contracts through its Security Committee. The exchange also identified recovering funds associated with additional withdrawal attempts as a priority. Its stated target was completing the upgrade and restoring withdrawals by the end of November 16.

LIT traders now face another question: whether the exchange can restore withdrawals quickly enough to prevent a prolonged confidence crisis.

Lighter builds its derivatives ecosystem around Ethereum, while ASTER taps into BNB Chain and Hyperliquid operates its own blockchain. Bitcoin, meanwhile, still has considerable room to develop its decentralized derivatives infrastructure.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning its Layer 2 network around that opportunity, combining Bitcoin’s settlement infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) execution for faster transactions and lower fees.

The idea is to bring more sophisticated DeFi applications to Bitcoin, potentially including decentralized perpetual futures trading. Rather than relying exclusively on Ethereum-based liquidity or another standalone derivatives chain, the project aims to connect Bitcoin’s liquidity with high-speed execution.

Its presale has raised more than $33.2 million. The current advertised token price stands at $0.0136, with buyers offered a 35% annual percentage yield (APY) through its staking program.

The project also has a live testnet featuring a bridge, faucet, explorer, and wallet infrastructure. Its roadmap targets further development of its Bitcoin bridge and DeFi ecosystem.

November 26 is the presale closing date, putting the token’s next major launch milestone just days away. So, for those watching the next generation of decentralized derivatives, Bitcoin’s potential role in that market remains an interesting opportunity.

Bitcoin Hyper is betting that combining Bitcoin’s liquidity with Solana-style execution can help establish that missing infrastructure.

Lighter’s immediate challenge is restoring withdrawals and demonstrating that its security upgrades address the vulnerabilities exposed by the incident. The $15.5 million loss is big, but the bigger issue is whether users and market makers remain comfortable keeping capital on the platform.

The coming sessions could prove decisive as traders monitor withdrawal availability, recovery efforts, and further disclosures from the exchange.

#5377. Dark Matter, ServiceLink add automated closing to Empower

Dark Matter Technologies integrated ServiceLink Accelerated Close into its Empower LOS, automating title, valuation and closing orders through Exchange. ServiceLink data shows 82% of borrowers expect refis to close in under one month and 87% value self-scheduling.   AI Summary

Dark Matter Technologies and ServiceLink have partnered to bring automated title, valuation and closing services to lenders using Dark Matter’s Empower loan origination system.

The partnership integrates ServiceLink’s Accelerated Close platform, powered by its NowIntelligence technology, into Empower. The service automates title and valuation orders, as well as closing orders, and allows lenders or borrowers to schedule appraisals and closings.

Using loan data, Accelerated Close automatically determines whether a loan qualifies for an expedited workflow. NowIntelligence evaluates eligibility using real-time market intelligence, including public and proprietary data, vendor information and market analytics.

For eligible loans, Empower automatically places title and valuation orders with ServiceLink through Exchange, Dark Matter’s partner marketplace. Once a loan reaches clear-to-close status, closing orders are also placed automatically through Empower.

The companies said the integration reduces manual work for lender operations teams and can shorten the time between underwriting approval and a scheduled closing.

Borrower expectations are also driving demand for faster and more flexible closing processes. According to ServiceLink’s 2026 State of Homebuying Report, 82% of borrowers believe a refinance should take less than a month to close, while 87% said the ability to schedule their own appraisal or closing would influence their choice of lender.

“Borrowers judge their lender by how fast and frictionless the process feels, and knowing when their appraisal and closing will happen matters a great deal,” said Vikas Rao, CEO of Dark Matter Technologies. “Accelerated Close takes routine ordering off lenders’ plates and, if desired, puts scheduling in borrowers’ hands, so loans close faster and borrowers feel in control of one of the biggest financial decisions of their lives.”

ServiceLink CEO Chris Azur said the integration is intended to help lenders shorten cycle times, improve pull-through rates and provide borrowers with a more streamlined experience.

For lenders, shorter cycle times could also reduce costs associated with extended rate locks. Orders placed through ServiceLink will continue to use the existing Exchange workflow for order status updates, documents and messaging.

Lenders can enable Accelerated Close through their Dark Matter or ServiceLink account managers, through self-service configuration or as part of a new Empower implementation, the companies’ release stated.
