#5359. Voltage Energy Unveils Microgrid System and New EBOS Solutions at RE+ 2026

New offerings support rapid deployment and better energy economics for mission-critical power while improving installation efficiency and project flexibility in utility-scale solar.

TIMBERLAKE, N.C., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Voltage Energy Group ("Voltage Energy"), a leading global provider of mission-critical power architecture solutions for utility-scale solar, BESS, and data center segments,  today unveiled its Microgrid System (MGS) and introduced two new electrical balance of system (EBOS) products, the Load Break Disconnect Box (LBD) and Combiner Box (CBX), at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.

The new offerings highlight two areas of innovation: rapidly deployable off-grid power for mission-critical applications and an expanding EBOS portfolio for utility-scale solar projects. Together, they demonstrate Voltage Energy's engineering expertise in delivering practical, reliable power infrastructure solutions across diverse energy applications.

Rapidly Deployable Power for Mission-Critical Applications

Making its debut at RE+ 2026, Voltage Energy's Microgrid System (MGS) combines solar generation and battery storage in a modular off-grid system. It features foldable PV racking and a pre-assembled Power Skid that integrates the inverter, batteries, junction equipment, and backup diesel generators. Factory pre-wiring simplifies on-site connections, while foldable PV racking supports faster installation and redeployment. Adjustable screw-jack legs accommodate slopes and uneven terrain.

Designed for rapid deployment, a 64 kW MGS system can be installed by a three-person team in 24 hours under suitable installation conditions. An illustrative energy cost comparison also indicates approximately 40% lower energy costs than on-site diesel generation, depending on operating assumptions.

MGS supports temporary and mission-critical power needs across utility-scale solar construction, data center construction, disaster relief, and mining site. From powering construction activities to providing electricity for time-sensitive emergency operations after natural disasters, the system delivers reliable off-grid power when and where it matters most.

Expanding EBOS Solutions with New LBD and CBX

Alongside MGS, Voltage Energy introduced its new LBD and CBX, further expanding its EBOS portfolio for utility-scale solar projects. Supporting both Trunk Bus and Multi-String architectures, these products give developers and EPCs greater flexibility in selecting DC collection solutions tailored to their project layouts, electrical requirements, and installation plans.

For Trunk Bus architecture, LYNX PLUS provides a modular solution that aggregates power from multiple PV strings along a shared trunk. The new LBD adds a defined disconnect point, allowing electrical isolation of sections of the DC power system. For Multi-String architecture, IBEX PLUS and IBEX solutions group PV strings into customized harness assemblies for flexible routing across varied project layouts. The new CBX combines up to 16 PV string inputs into a single output toward the inverter, while supporting parallel output conductors and maintaining access to fuses for O&M.

Founded in North Carolina in 2016, Voltage Energy continues to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint while building on its engineering expertise. Its Voltage Power Ranch in Timberlake, North Carolina, entered the pilot-run stage in October 2026, with a planned capacity ramp through 2027. The facility reinforces the company's commitment to engineering quality and reliable project execution for domestic energy infrastructure.

From mission-critical off-grid power to engineered EBOS solutions for utility-scale solar, Voltage Energy draws on its engineering expertise and manufacturing capabilities to meet today's project needs and support tomorrow's energy demands. Visitors can explore Voltage Energy's latest solutions at Booths N936 and N736 during RE+ 2026, November 17â19, in Las Vegas.

About Voltage Energy GroupFounded in 2016, Voltage Energy Group ("Voltage Energy") is a leading global provider of utility-scale solar EBOS and mission-critical power infrastructure solutions, with global headquarters in Timberlake, North Carolina. Voltage Energy delivers innovative, value-engineered technologies and services that improve installation efficiency, enhance safety, and optimize long-term system performance.We are a group of innovative people who sincerely care about the renewable industry. Learn more at the company's new website, www.voltageenergy.com.

#5358. Regaining U.S. measles-free status takes 12 months without continuous spread

Free daily briefing on global business news.

U.S. measles elimination status hinges on keeping any one virus lineage from spreading continuously for 12 months or more, and these 10 factors show what regaining it requires

Measles elimination is not the same as eradication. When the U.S. was declared free of endemic measles in 2000, the virus did not vanish from the country. Travelers $TRV could still bring it in from abroad. What changed was that no chain of transmission was sustaining itself inside U.S. borders.

That distinction sits at the center of U.S. measles elimination status. The World Health Organization and the Pan American Health Organization apply the same standard. A country keeps elimination as long as no single measles virus lineage spreads continuously for 12 months or more. The country also has to show its surveillance is strong enough to catch cases if they occur.

Events in 2025 put that standard to the test in North America. A large outbreak began in West Texas in January of that year. Two unvaccinated children in Texas died. A third 2025 death was reported in New Mexico.

Canada's experience showed how the rules work in practice. Canada lost its measles elimination status in November 2025. That loss also cost the Americas their regional elimination status.

Regaining status follows a defined sequence. Health agencies first have to interrupt every active chain of transmission. They then have to show 12 months without continuous spread. A regional verification commission reviews the documented evidence before status is restored.

Meeting those conditions depends on three connected pillars. The first is vaccination. Measles is among the most contagious viruses known. Public health agencies commonly cite about 95% two-dose coverage with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine as the level needed to block sustained spread. National averages can hide local pockets where coverage is lower.

The second pillar is outbreak response. That means fast case detection, lab confirmation, genotyping, contact tracing and isolation of cases. Post-exposure MMR shots and immune globulin can protect some contacts when given within set time windows. The third pillar is verification. It rests on surveillance strong enough to show the virus has stopped circulating, not just gone unreported.

The 10 slides that follow walk through each piece, from the definition of elimination to the review that decides whether a country meets the standard again.

Measles elimination status means a country has gone 12 months or more without the same measles virus lineage spreading continuously within its borders. Under the World Health Organization and Pan American Health Organization standard, that record counts only if surveillance is strong enough to detect cases.

The definition does not require zero cases. A country can record measles infections every year and still hold elimination status. What matters is whether those infections come from a chain of transmission that has taken root at home.

That distinction separates endemic measles from imported measles. Endemic measles circulates within a population on its own. It passes from person to person without needing new introductions from outside. Imported measles arrives with a traveler who caught the virus in another country.

An imported case can still spark local infections among unvaccinated people. Elimination status holds as long as public health workers break that chain before the same lineage runs unbroken for a year.

The U.S. was declared free of endemic measles in 2000. Under the definition, later imported cases do not cancel that status on their own. The question for each is whether the lineage it brings in goes on to spread continuously at home for 12 months or more.

The two agencies play distinct roles. WHO sets the global framework for measles elimination. PAHO is WHO's regional office for the Americas. It oversees how countries across North, Central and South America and the Caribbean document their status.

The surveillance condition ties the definition to evidence. A year without continuous spread has to be one the health system was equipped to see. Otherwise, missed infections could pass for a stopped virus.

For the U.S., the definition sets the terms of any return to measles-free status. Officials would need to show that no lineage circulated unbroken for 12 months, and that surveillance could support that finding.

The 12-month rule decides measles elimination status. A country loses it when the same measles virus lineage keeps spreading inside its borders, without a break, for a year or longer. That one-year threshold is part of the standard used by the World Health Organization and the Pan American Health Organization.

The rule is narrower than many people assume. It does not require a country to report zero cases. Travelers $TRV can carry the virus across borders, and local outbreaks can follow. A country can face several separate introductions and still meet the standard. Each chain of transmission has to end before it reaches the 12-month mark.

What the rule measures is persistence, not volume. Health officials follow the virus by its lineage, which is its genetic family. If one lineage keeps passing from person to person for a full year, the virus is treated as circulating locally. At that point it no longer counts as an import.

That is why one long outbreak can matter more than many short ones. A single sustained chain can cost a country its status, whatever the totals from other outbreaks look like. Several brief outbreaks of different lineages do not add together. The clock applies to each chain on its own.

The clock also does not reset just because an outbreak moves. A chain that starts in one state and continues in another is still one chain if the lineage is the same and transmission never breaks. Crossing county or state lines does not split an outbreak into separate events.

The large West Texas outbreak of 2025 shows how the standard becomes a practical question. Officials have to establish whether later cases in other places belong to the same lineage or come from unrelated introductions. That answer decides whether the spread counts as one continuous chain or several separate ones.

The same yardstick works in reverse. A country that has lost status cannot win it back by cutting case numbers alone. The test is whether continuous spread has ended and stayed ended for the full period.

The herd immunity target for measles commonly cited by public health agencies is about 95% two-dose MMR coverage. The bar sits that high for two reasons. Measles spreads with unusual ease, and the vaccine does not protect every person who receives it.

Transmission is the first reason. A single infected person can pass measles to most of the unvaccinated people around them. A virus that moves that easily keeps finding new hosts unless nearly everyone nearby is immune.

Vaccine performance is the second. One dose of the MMR vaccine is about 93% effective against measles, according to CDC. A second dose raises that protection to about 97%.

Put another way, roughly three of every 100 people who finish the two-dose series remain unprotected. After a single dose, about seven in 100 are left without protection.

For any one person, those odds are small. Across a classroom, a city or a country, they add up to a pool of people the virus can still reach.

The 95% target accounts for that pool. At that level of two-dose coverage, few enough susceptible people remain that an imported case tends to run out of new hosts. The chain of infection ends before it can stretch into lasting community spread.

Falling short of the target does not guarantee an outbreak. It does widen the openings the virus needs. Those openings matter most where unvaccinated people cluster together instead of being scattered across a wider population.

The same math explains the weight placed on the second dose. Going from one dose to two cuts the unprotected share among vaccinated people by more than half.

Some people cannot rely on their own immunity at all. Babies who are too young for a first MMR dose have no vaccine protection of their own. They depend on the immunity of the people around them.

For the U.S., 95% serves as a practical benchmark rather than a formal test for elimination status. It describes the level of protection that makes ending each chain of transmission realistic.

Exemptions and uneven vaccine uptake leave pockets of unvaccinated kindergartners, even when the national rate looks close to target. CDC reported national kindergarten MMR coverage of 92.5% for the 2024-25 school year, with exemptions at 3.6%.

The kindergarten year works as a checkpoint for measles protection. The MMR schedule puts the first dose at 12 to 15 months and the second at four to six years. That second dose lands around the age children start school. Kindergarten figures show how well young children are protected as they begin sharing classrooms every day.

The 2024-25 national figure sits about 2.5 percentage points below the two-dose coverage level that public health agencies commonly cite for blocking sustained spread. That gap is a national number. It does not show where the unvaccinated children are.

Coverage varies widely by state, by county and by school. A state's average can mask counties that sit well below it. A county's average can mask individual schools with even lower rates. Each layer of averaging hides the places where unvaccinated children cluster.

The 3.6% exemption rate works the same way. It is one figure for the whole country. It says nothing about where exempted children live or which schools they attend. Exemptions also do not explain the whole gap. The coverage rate and the exemption rate do not add up to 100%. Some kindergartners lack full MMR protection without holding any formal exemption.

Those clusters matter because measles needs only a small opening. A school or community with low coverage can give one imported case enough susceptible people to start a chain of transmission. A strong statewide average does not change the odds inside a school where many children are unvaccinated. Those local chains are what elimination rules track.

For measles-free status, the coverage target therefore works at the local level as much as the national one. Lifting the national average to the target would still leave risk in place if low-coverage schools and counties stayed where they are. School-level and county-level coverage data shows where those gaps sit.

Rapid case detection is the first step in stopping a measles outbreak. A suspected case that is spotted, confirmed in a laboratory and isolated quickly gives the virus fewer chances to reach new people.

Timing drives everything that follows. Every day a case goes unrecognized is another day of possible exposures in homes, clinics, schools and waiting rooms. An infected person who keeps going to work or school can expose many unvaccinated people before anyone suspects measles.

Detection starts with suspicion. A clinician, an emergency department or a local health department has to consider measles as a possible diagnosis and report it. That report sets the public health response in motion. Without it, an outbreak can grow before any agency knows it exists.

Lab confirmation turns a suspected case into a confirmed one. A positive result tells health officials the illness is measles and not something that only looks similar. That certainty lets agencies commit staff and resources to a full response.

The laboratory step has a second use. Samples from a confirmed case can also be sent for genotyping. That later work helps officials see how separate cases relate to one another.

Isolation follows confirmation. A person with measles is kept apart from others who could catch the virus. Isolation stops that person from adding new links to the transmission chain. It runs alongside the separate work of finding people who were already exposed.

Imported cases need the same quick response. A patient who recently returned from international travel and has symptoms consistent with measles gives clinicians a clear reason to test. Catching that first case quickly can keep a single introduction from turning into a local chain.

Prevention for travelers belongs to the same effort. Early doses are recommended for infants traveling internationally. Many of those babies are not yet old enough for their first routine dose. An early dose lowers the chance that a child picks up the virus abroad and brings it home.

Each of these steps shortens the time a case can spread before it is contained. A chain that is caught early stays short. Ending every chain is the first condition for measles-free status.

Genomic sequencing tells health officials whether new measles cases belong to one ongoing chain of transmission or to separate introductions of the virus. That distinction shapes how a country's measles-free status is judged. A single lineage that keeps circulating counts against it, while unrelated arrivals that die out do not.

The work begins after a laboratory confirms a case. Public health labs then genotype the virus taken from patient samples. The genotype places the infection within a known group of measles viruses.

Sequencing adds finer detail. It reads enough of the virus's genetic code to compare one patient's sample with another's. Two samples that closely match suggest the cases may share a source. Samples that clearly differ point to separate routes of entry.

That comparison is how officials separate imported measles from continuous spread. A traveler can carry the virus home from a country where it still circulates. That case, and any small cluster around it, does not by itself mean measles has re-established itself. A lineage passing from person to person and community to community is a different matter.

Sequencing data helps officials judge how long one lineage has been moving through the population. Without it, two unrelated outbreaks in different places could look like one long chain. The reverse error is also possible. One long chain could be mistaken for several short, unconnected ones. Either mistake would distort the picture of whether transmission has been interrupted.

The question becomes practical when cases surface in more than one state. Investigators can compare samples across state lines to see whether separate clusters stem from one chain or from separate importations.

The results also steer the response on the ground. A new cluster that matches an existing lineage sends investigators looking for a missed link in that chain, such as an unreported case. A cluster that does not match points them toward a fresh introduction. That tells them where to focus contact tracing and vaccination outreach.

Sequencing results also become part of the record a country builds over time. Laboratory data showing that later cases do not descend from earlier ones helps document that a chain was broken.

Contact tracing finds the people exposed to a confirmed measles case so health workers can protect them before the virus moves further. The two main tools are an MMR shot given within 72 hours of exposure and, for some contacts, immune globulin given within six days.

Tracing begins once a case is identified. Health departments work out where the infected person went and who shared that space. A household, a classroom, a clinic waiting room or a church service can each produce a list of names.

Each name is then checked against vaccination records. People with documented immunity need little follow-up. People without it become the focus of the response.

The 72-hour window shapes everything that follows. A post-exposure MMR dose has to reach an exposed person inside that period to do its job. That makes speed the deciding factor in tracing. A contact list finished on day four arrives too late for the shot to serve as post-exposure protection.

Immune globulin gives health workers a second option. It supplies ready-made antibodies instead of prompting the body to build its own. It is recommended for some contacts rather than all of them. Its six-day window also leaves room to reach people the first sweep missed. A contact reached on day five, after the MMR window has closed, may still be a candidate for immune globulin.

Quarantine handles the contacts tracing could not protect in time. It differs from isolation, which applies to people already confirmed to have measles. Exposed people who lack immunity and were not protected in time may be asked to stay home and watch for symptoms. If one of them falls ill at home, the virus has fewer people to reach.

Each contact reached in time removes a link from the chain of infection. When enough links break, the outbreak ends. Ending every active chain is the starting point for regaining measles-free status.

A country cannot claim measles elimination just because it reports few cases. The World Health Organization and Pan American Health Organization standard also requires surveillance strong enough to detect cases. Without that capacity, a quiet year is not evidence that the virus is gone.

The standard has two parts that work together. One is the absence of any measles virus lineage spreading continuously for 12 months or more. The other is a monitoring system capable of catching infections when they occur. A claim resting on the first part alone is incomplete.

An absence of reported cases can mean two different things. It can mean the virus is not circulating. It can also mean infections are happening but no one is finding, testing or reporting them. A functioning surveillance system is what lets health officials tell those situations apart.

That logic applies directly to the U.S. effort to win back measles-free status. A count of zero continuous chains only matters if the system producing that count would have caught a chain that was there. The burden falls on showing the result, not assuming it.

Surveillance depends on clinicians recognizing suspected cases and sending samples for laboratory confirmation. Genetic testing of the virus adds another layer. It shows whether cases in different places belong to one chain or reflect unrelated importations.

That distinction matters under the standard. An imported case that never produces 12 months of continuous spread does not by itself end elimination. Showing that a chain has stopped takes the same detection and testing capacity that found it in the first place.

Each confirmed case and each sequencing result becomes part of the documented record a country submits for review. Missing tests or incomplete reporting leave holes in that record.

The biology of measles makes any blind spot costly. The virus ranks among the most contagious known. One infected person can pass it to most unvaccinated people nearby. A single missed case can start a chain of infections before anyone recognizes it.

Measles-free status does not return on its own once case numbers fall. A country regains it only after the regional verification commission completes a documented review showing that continuous spread has stopped.

The review is the final step in regaining status, not a replacement for the earlier ones. Health agencies first have to break every active transmission chain. Only after that can a country build the record the commission needs to see.

The commission measures a country against the elimination standard shared by the World Health Organization and PAHO. That standard has two parts. No measles virus lineage may spread continuously for 12 months or more. Surveillance must also be strong enough to detect cases.

Each part calls for its own evidence. Showing that no lineage has spread continuously for 12 months depends on laboratory records. Lab confirmation establishes that a suspected case is measles. Genotyping then identifies which lineage caused it.

Lineage data lets reviewers separate two situations that can look alike in raw case counts. A country may record several imported cases in a year and still meet the standard. What it cannot have is one lineage sustaining a chain that lasts 12 months.

The second part of the standard concerns detection capacity. A quiet year tells reviewers little if the surveillance system could have missed cases. The evidence has to show that cases would have been caught, not only that few were reported.

The word documented matters in this process. Restoring status rests on recorded evidence that the commission can examine, not on a declaration by national health officials that spread has ended.

The same route applies to the U.S. Any future verification of U.S. measles-free status runs through documented review by the regional commission. That review cannot shorten the timeline. The 12 months without continuous spread have to pass before the commission can confirm them.

Canada lost its measles elimination status in November 2025, and the Americas lost their regional status as a result. Sustained spread inside one country was enough to end the measles-free standing of the whole region.

The Canadian outbreak illustrates a point that case totals can obscure. Status does not hinge on how many cases a country records in a year. It hinges on whether a single chain of transmission keeps going past the 12-month mark.

The regional loss follows from that structure. A region's standing depends on the standing of the countries in it. When Canada no longer met the standard, the Americas no longer qualified as a measles-free region. No single country can restore the regional standing on its own.

For the U.S., the long shared border and regular travel between the two countries matter. Measles moves easily between people who lack immunity. A case that crosses the border in either direction can seed a new chain wherever vaccination coverage is low.

Imported cases do not by themselves cost a country its status. What counts is whether health officials stop the chains those cases start. The test is whether any one lineage reaches 12 months of continuous spread.

That makes each border crossing a test of a country's outbreak response rather than an automatic threat to its standing. A quickly contained importation leaves status intact. An importation that settles into a community with low coverage can become the long chain that decides the outcome.

Canada now faces the same recovery requirements that apply to any country in the region. Its status depends on its own record, measured against the same 12-month standard that ended it.

The region's measles-free standing is tied to vaccination and outbreak response inside each member country, including the U.S. and Canada. A gap in either country affects the record of the region as a whole.

#5357. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5356. /C O R R E C T I O N - Finzly/

In the news release, Finzly Appoints Former Early Warning Services CEO Paul Finch to Its Board of Directors, issued 16-Nov-2026 by Finzly over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

Finch helped launch Zelle and brings extensive experience scaling bank-led payments as Finzly accelerates adoption of BankOS.

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Finzly, a leader in modern banking technology, today announced the appointment of Paul Finch, former Chief Executive Officer of Early Warning Services and a key architect behind the launch of Zelle, to its Board of Directors.

Finch brings decades of experience helping financial institutions bring new services to market at scale. As a Finzly director, he will provide strategic guidance as the company expands adoption of BankOS, its modern bank operating system that enables banks to modernize payments and introduce new banking capabilities alongside their existing core systems.

As CEO of Early Warning Services from 2003 to 2019, Finch led the expansion of the bank-owned company's capabilities in payments, fraud prevention, and identity verification. Under his leadership, Early Warning worked with leading U.S. financial institutions to launch Zelle in 2017, making real-time payments available to millions of Americans through their banks.

"Paul has already helped transform how America moves money. Now, we have an opportunity to transform how America banks," said Booshan Rengachari, Founder and CEO of Finzly. "Paul understands what it takes to earn banks' trust, build industry-wide collaboration, and bring new services to market at scale. His experience will be invaluable as we bring BankOS to more financial institutions, helping them innovate faster and deliver next-generation banking experiences without being constrained by legacy technology."

Finzly is advancing its strategy to enable banks of all sizes to rapidly introduce new products, connect to emerging payment networks, seamlessly integrate acquired businesses, harness AI capabilities, and deliver differentiated financial experiences while maintaining control of their infrastructure and customer relationships.

"The financial services industry is entering a new era of transformation, and banks need the freedom to innovate without being held back by legacy infrastructure," said Paul Finch, incoming member of Finzly's Board of Directors. "Booshan and the Finzly team have built a compelling platform that addresses this challenge. BankOS allows banks to modernize progressively while preserving their existing investments and accelerating innovation. I'm excited to join the board and help Finzly scale its impact across the banking industry."

"Finzly has built a strong foundation for its next chapter of growth," said Shamit Mehta, a member of Finzly's Board of Directors and Partner at TZP Group. "Paul's experience in building and scaling one of America's most successful payment networks brings invaluable expertise and industry perspective to our Board. I believe the combination of Finzly's technology, entrepreneurial drive, and Paul's industry leadership positions the company to play an increasingly important role in shaping the future of banking."

Finzly is a banking technology company on a mission to modernize the financial infrastructure that powers banks and credit unions. Its flagship platform, BankOS, is an AI-native, API-first, event-driven bank operating system enabling financial institutions to progressively modernize legacy systems and rapidly introduce new banking capabilities.

Through its modular platform spanning payments, accounts, digital banking, foreign exchange, tokenized deposits, and agentic AI, Finzly enables financial institutions to innovate faster, operate more efficiently, and grow through mergers and acquisitions without technology becoming a barrier to their strategic ambitions.

Headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, Finzly is helping shape the future of banking with secure, scalable, and interoperable infrastructure.

For more information, visit www.finzly.com.

#5355. 12 inches of rushing water can carry away most cars, the NWS says

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How much water it takes to sweep away a car, along with National Weather Service depth thresholds and road signs to know before approaching a flooded road

Flooding kills more people each year than any other thunderstorm-related hazard, according to the National Weather Service. That puts floodwater ahead of lightning, tornadoes and every other danger a thunderstorm can produce.

The National Weather Service is the U.S. federal agency responsible for weather forecasts and warnings. It sits within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Its flood safety guidance is built around a four-word phrase: Turn Around Don't Drown.

The phrase tells drivers to turn back rather than enter a flooded road. The agency backs that message with specific depths. None of them exceeds 2 feet.

The short answer to how much water it takes to sweep away a car is 12 inches of rushing water for most cars, according to the weather service.

This slideshow covers five pieces of that guidance. Three are depth thresholds. The first is the depth at which fast-moving water can knock over an adult. The second is the depth that can carry away most cars, and the third is the depth that can carry off SUVs and trucks. The thresholds climb from a person on foot to passenger cars to larger vehicles.

The other two items deal with the road itself. One explains why the weather service warns drivers never to go around barriers on a flooded road. The other describes the two road signs that carry the Turn Around Don't Drown message. One is a yellow permanent warning sign, and the other is a pink temporary incident sign.

One detail applies to every number in this piece. The weather service ties its depth thresholds to fast-moving or rushing water. It does not attach a specific current speed to them. The figures describe what moving water can do at those depths.

The guidance covers people on foot as well as people in vehicles. The first threshold below concerns a pedestrian rather than a car. The slides that follow move to passenger cars, then larger vehicles, then the barriers and signs placed on flooded roads.

Six inches of fast-moving flood water can knock an adult off their feet, according to the National Weather Service. The agency gives this depth for a person on foot, not for a vehicle.

Walking into or near flood waters accounts for the second-largest share of flood deaths, the weather service reports. Only deaths tied to driving into flood water make up a bigger share.

That category is broader than wading. It covers people who are near flood water as well as those who walk into it.

Just 12 inches of rushing water is enough to sweep away most cars, according to the National Weather Service. The figure applies to most cars, not to every vehicle on the road.

Larger vehicles have their own, higher threshold in the agency's guidance. The 12-inch mark is the one for ordinary cars.

The NWS says people underestimate the force of moving water. Its warning about cars is framed around water in motion, not around depth alone.

The agency cites the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the circumstances of flood drownings. The CDC reports that over half of flood-related drownings occur when someone drives a vehicle into dangerous flood water.

By that measure, entering flood water in a vehicle accounts for more flood-related drownings than all other circumstances combined.

Never drive around a barrier that closes off a flooded road, the National Weather Service warns. The road beneath the water may have collapsed.

That possible collapse is the reason the agency gives for the rule. Floodwater hides the surface underneath it. A stretch of road that looks intact from behind the barrier may no longer be there.

The NWS guidance also applies to roads without barriers. The agency states that driving into flood waters is never safe. That rule holds on any flooded road, whether or not a crew has closed it.

The warning covers people on foot as well. The NWS says walking into flood waters is never safe either. Leaving a car to cross a flooded stretch on foot falls under the same warning.

Read together, the two points link a depth to a behavior. The 12-inch threshold describes what rushing water can do to a car. The CDC figure shows how often a flood drowning involves a driver who entered dangerous water.

The National Weather Service says 2 feet of rushing water can carry off SUVs and trucks.

Many flood deaths involve vehicles that moving water carries downstream, according to the National Weather Service. The agency describes many of these drownings as preventable.

Guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that floodwater of sufficient depth can carry away sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks. The same guidance explains what happens to a vehicle after it drives into floodwater.

At first, the vehicle floats. Air trapped inside the cab holds it up. Water then comes in through the doors. The vehicle grows heavier as it fills, and then it sinks.

A sunken vehicle creates another problem for anyone still inside. Under water, the pressure outside the cab differs from the pressure inside it. That difference makes the doors impossible to open.

The agency treats a barrier on a flooded road as a place to stop, not an obstacle to steer around. Its message at that point matches its campaign name: turn around.

Two road sign designs carry the "Turn Around Don't Drown" message: a yellow permanent warning sign and a pink temporary incident sign. The National Weather Service describes where each one belongs and what it looks like.

The yellow sign reads "When Flooded, Turn Around Don't Drown." It meets Federal Highway Administration standards. It is designed to stay in place as a permanent road sign.

The NWS lists three kinds of locations where the yellow sign belongs. One is a spot where flooding happens often. Another is a spot where flooding begins quickly. The third is a place where crews cannot realistically put up incident signs in time.

The yellow sign has a black legend and a black border on a yellow background. The NWS specifies the yellow as RGB 255:208:69, or Pantone 116. Warning signs are covered in Chapter 2C of the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, known as the MUTCD.

The pink sign reads "Flooding Ahead Turn Around Don't Drown." Through a Letter of Support, the Federal Highway Administration has encouraged its use as an official incident management sign.

Incident management signs are one type of Temporary Traffic Control sign. They are used for short-term events. The NWS gives accidents, natural disasters and hazardous material spills as examples.

The pink sign is meant for places where stream water running across a road makes passage dangerous. One example is a road that dips down to the level of a stream channel. Another is a bridge or culvert that cannot handle high flows.

The pink sign goes on temporary sign holders. It is not meant to be mounted on construction barricades.

The two designs split the job by timing. The yellow sign stays up at locations with a frequent or fast-developing flood risk. The pink sign is a temporary tool, set up for a specific event where water is crossing the road.

#5354. AI phishing emails: how cloned voices, deepfakes and clean grammar fool readers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

AI phishing emails no longer carry the typos and clumsy wording that once exposed them, and these 10 changes show what to watch for and which defenses still work

For years, the standard advice on phishing came down to one test: read the message closely and look for mistakes. A misspelled company name, a clumsy greeting or a sentence no native speaker would write was often enough to expose a scam. That test was never perfect, but it caught a lot of crude fraud.

Generative AI has weakened it. Large language models produce fluent, correctly spelled text in seconds. They can write in a formal register or a casual one, and in many languages. A scammer who once struggled with grammar can now send a message that reads like it came from a payroll department, a supplier or a senior executive. The errors that used to expose a fake are much easier to remove.

The change goes beyond polish. The same tools make it cheaper to tailor a lure to one person using details from a public profile. They can copy the tone of a colleague and produce many different versions of a single message. They can also help build the fake pages that sit behind a link. Voice cloning and deepfake video add another layer. A request that starts in an inbox can be followed by a phone call or a video meeting that seems to confirm it.

For anyone who handles payments, passwords or sensitive data, this shifts where attention needs to go. AI phishing emails are hard to judge by how they look or sound. They are easier to judge by what they ask the reader to do. A request to change bank details, approve an urgent transfer or sign in through an emailed link carries the same risk whether the writing is polished or clumsy.

This list covers 10 specific ways AI changes phishing, from cleaner grammar and automated spear phishing to cloned voices and convincing fake login pages. It is a selection of changes, not a complete catalogue. It includes two real fraud cases in which synthetic audio and video were used to persuade staff to send money. It also names criminal-market chatbots that security researchers found advertised on underground forums. The final slide turns to defenses that do not depend on spotting a bad sentence. These include verifying requests through a separate channel and checking the real sender domain. Passkeys and security keys also help. They will not release credentials to a lookalike site.

A phishing email with perfect spelling and polished grammar is no longer unusual. Chatbots draft clean, error-free copy on request. That leaves the old advice to hunt for clumsy wording with little value as a test.

For years, security awareness training leaned on that advice. Misspelled brand names, odd capitalization, broken idioms and stiff phrasing were treated as the giveaway. The logic was simple. Many scammers wrote in a second or third language, and few took the time to proofread.

Generative AI removes most of that friction. A rough prompt can become a finished message in seconds. The tool can tidy the punctuation, line breaks and sign-off that once looked off. It can hold a consistent tone from the subject line to the closing, whether the message poses as an invoice reminder, an IT alert or a note from HR.

Revision is cheap, too. A scammer who dislikes a draft can ask for a shorter version, a more formal one or one that sounds more rushed. Each rewrite takes seconds rather than the time a human writer would need.

The test was never perfect in the other direction either. Legitimate companies send emails with typos, and real colleagues often dash off hurried, error-filled notes. Polish was always a weak signal of trust. Now it is close to no signal at all.

The more reliable clues sit in the action a message wants. An email that pushes the reader to move money, enter a password on a linked page, open an unexpected attachment or hand over personal details deserves a second look. That is true whether the prose is clumsy or flawless.

Pressure is a second clue that AI does not remove. Phishing depends on a fast reaction before the reader stops to think. Deadlines measured in hours, warnings that an account will be locked and requests to keep a matter confidential are built to cut that pause short.

Tone can carry pressure as well. A note that flatters, scolds or invokes a senior executive's authority is trying to shift the reader from checking to complying. A language model can strike any of those tones on request.

A message can read as though a professional editor wrote it and still be a scam. Judging an email by its request and its urgency, rather than its grammar, reflects how attackers now work.

Generative AI lets a scammer turn a target's public details into a tailored phishing email in seconds. That closes the old gap between cheap mass phishing and labor-intensive spear phishing. Personalized lures can now reach far more people.

Phishing has long come in two broad forms. Mass phishing sends the same generic message to huge lists of addresses, such as a fake delivery notice or a password-reset warning. Spear phishing targets a specific person with a message built around who they are and what they do.

The trade-off used to be cost. A convincing spear-phishing email required someone to research each target by hand. That meant reading profiles, finding the right colleague's name and writing a message that fit the person's role. The effort limited how many people an attacker could reach.

Large language models remove much of that labor. A scammer can paste in a person's job title, employer and a recent public post. A model then drafts a message that references those details. A fresh version can be generated for the next name on the list.

The raw material is often easy to find. Professional networking profiles list roles, managers and past employers. Company websites publish staff directories, press releases and event schedules. Conference speaker pages and personal social media accounts fill in projects, travel plans and recent achievements.

Those details let a lure mention a real vendor, a real deadline or a real event the recipient attended. A finance employee might get a note about an invoice tied to a supplier the company uses. A new hire might get a message that appears to come from their onboarding team.

This undercuts a check many people rely on. A message that names your manager, your current project or last week's industry conference once suggested the sender knew you. Today, that knowledge may have come from a quick scrape of public pages.

The practical lesson is narrow. Familiar details in an email show only that the sender could find them. They do not show who the sender is. They do not confirm that a request is genuine.

Large language models let criminals write fluent phishing emails in languages they do not speak. That removes a clear warning sign for readers in smaller language markets. They could once dismiss a message in their own language that read as though a clumsy translator had produced it.

Europol, the European Union's law enforcement agency, flagged this risk in a 2023 report on ChatGPT and law enforcement. The report noted that language models can help criminals produce convincing text in languages they do not know. A target's native language is no longer much of a barrier to an attacker.

For years, the language gap worked in defenders' favor. Scammers targeting readers in Finnish, Hungarian, Czech or Korean often relied on older machine translation or their own limited skills. The results tended to be stiff, overly literal or simply wrong. Native speakers could often spot a fake within a sentence or two.

That gap has narrowed. A scammer can now draft a lure once and ask a model to render it in another language. The output can match the tone of a bank notice, a delivery update or a letter from a tax office. The same model can then adapt it for a second country in minutes.

Translation is only part of the shift. Many languages build politeness directly into their grammar. German distinguishes the formal Sie from the informal du. French has vous and tu. Japanese business writing depends on keigo, a layered system of honorific speech. Getting these wrong once marked a message as foreign. A model can be told to use the register a real company would choose.

Local conventions are easier to imitate as well. Date formats, currency symbols, the phrasing of a sign-off and the names of familiar national services all give a message a local feel. An attacker no longer needs a native-speaking accomplice to get those details right.

For readers outside the English-speaking world, the old shortcut no longer works. A natural-sounding message in a less widely spoken language once suggested a sender who actually lived and worked there. It no longer carries that meaning. Polished wording, in any language, now says little about who wrote the email.

A language model can copy the way a specific manager, colleague or supplier writes after seeing only a few of their emails. When an attacker controls a real mailbox, that borrowed voice can appear inside an existing reply thread. The target already trusts that conversation.

Every regular correspondent has habits. Some sign off with a single initial. Some skip greetings entirely. Others write in clipped fragments from a phone. Those quirks used to be hard for an outsider to fake. A model given a handful of past messages can reproduce them, including vocabulary, sentence length and level of formality.

The risk grows once an attacker gets inside a genuine account. Stolen passwords and earlier phishing messages are common routes into a mailbox. From there, the intruder can read months of real correspondence. That archive shows who pays whom, which invoices are pending and how each person normally phrases a request.

A hijacked thread removes several checks a careful reader would normally apply. The sender address is genuine. The subject line matches an ongoing project. The earlier messages quoted below the new reply are real. The fraudulent message only has to sound like the person who wrote the previous ones. A model can supply that voice.

Attackers also use versions of the technique without full access to the target's own account. A message can arrive from a lookalike address while continuing a thread copied from a compromised mailbox elsewhere. In a crowded inbox, it can pass as a normal reply in a familiar chain.

Mailbox intruders often add inbox rules that forward, hide or delete certain messages. Those rules can keep the real account owner from seeing replies that would expose the fraud.

The warning sign in these cases is rarely the language. It is the request itself. A new bank account for a known supplier deserves scrutiny. So does a sudden change to payment instructions, a request to keep a deal confidential or a push to skip a usual approval step. That holds even when the wording sounds exactly like the person who normally writes.

WormGPT and FraudGPT are AI chatbots that were advertised on underground forums in 2023 as tools for writing phishing and business email compromise messages. Security researchers, including the firm SlashNext, reported the listings that year.

A scammer using such a tool does not need to write a convincing lure from scratch. The scammer also does not need the skills to set up and run a language model. The forum listings pitched fraud-ready text generation as something that could simply be bought.

Business email compromise, often shortened to BEC, is the type of fraud these tools were marketed for. In a BEC scheme, the attacker poses as someone the target already deals with. That might be a chief executive, a finance director, a supplier or an outside lawyer.

The message usually asks for something specific. It might be a wire transfer, a change to the bank account on file for an invoice, or sensitive records such as payroll data. The request is framed as routine business.

Many BEC emails carry no malicious attachment and no link. They rely on wording alone. That leaves fewer technical traces for security software to catch. It also makes the writing the main tool of the scheme. Writing is exactly what a text generator produces.

The researchers' reports described the advertisements and what the sellers pitched the tools for. A sales listing on a criminal forum shows what was offered to buyers, not how well the product worked.

Mainstream chatbots such as ChatGPT run under safety rules. Those rules are designed to refuse requests for scam emails or malicious code. They can sometimes be evaded.

One method is a jailbreak prompt. It reframes a harmful request as fiction, role play or a hypothetical exercise. Another approach splits a request into harmless-looking pieces.

A BEC request can also look harmless on its own. An email asking an accountant to confirm a vendor's new bank details reads like ordinary office work. A chatbot may find little in that wording to refuse. Scammers are therefore not limited to tools sold on criminal forums.

Generative AI can rewrite one phishing lure into many distinct versions, each with different wording, structure and subject lines. That variety weakens email filters that work by matching known phrases or by spotting identical message bodies sent to many inboxes.

Many traditional spam defenses depend on repetition. When a campaign sends the same text to a long list of addresses, a filter can learn that text once and block every copy. Some systems create a fingerprint of a message body. They then compare it against fingerprints of messages already flagged as malicious. Other systems score each message on words and phrases that commonly appear in fraud.

A language model undercuts both methods. An attacker can ask for the same request — reset your password, approve this invoice, open this shared file — written dozens of different ways. The underlying instruction stays the same. The sentences, greetings, sign-offs and subject lines all change. Each version can read like an ordinary business email and share no fingerprint with the others.

Scammers tried to vary their messages long before generative AI. They swapped words in and out of templates or inserted random characters to break up matching. Those older tricks often produced awkward or garbled text. A careful reader or a well-tuned filter could catch that. Model-written variants usually keep their grammar intact. The variation itself no longer leaves an obvious trail.

Email security tools have answered by looking less at what a message says and more at where it comes from and what it does. Sender reputation weighs signals such as how long a sending domain has existed. It also considers whether that domain has a history of legitimate mail. Link analysis follows where a URL actually leads, including any redirects, instead of trusting the visible text.

Anomaly detection asks whether a message fits the normal pattern for a recipient or an organization. A first-time sender asking for a payment can raise a flag. So can a reply-to address that differs from the sender address, or a request arriving at an unusual hour. None of these signals depends on how the message is worded.

An email that reaches the inbox has not been certified safe. Getting past the filter means only that the message did not match what the filter was built to catch.

A phone call that sounds exactly like the boss no longer confirms an email request. Voice cloning lets fraudsters pair a written payment demand with a synthetic voice that matches the supposed sender. A single suspicious message then feels like a verified instruction.

The technique works by training a speech model on recordings of a real person. Executives are convenient targets. Their voices are often public. Earnings calls, conference keynotes, podcast interviews and company videos all supply usable audio.

A widely reported case predates today's consumer chatbots. In 2019, the Wall Street Journal reported that criminals had used a cloned voice to defraud a U.K. energy firm. The voice imitated the chief executive of the firm's parent company. It persuaded the head of the U.K. firm to transfer €220,000, according to the newspaper.

In a phishing scheme, the voice often plays a supporting role rather than the lead. An email arrives first. It asks for a wire transfer, a change to a supplier's bank details or a set of login credentials. A call or voice note follows, apparently from the same person, repeating the request. That second contact is designed to settle the doubts the email raised.

The sequence exploits a familiar piece of security advice. Employees are often told to confirm unusual requests by phone. If the attacker places that call, the check happens inside the scam.

A call that comes from the requester proves nothing. Caller ID can be spoofed. A familiar name or number on the screen is not evidence of who is speaking. Voice notes sent through messaging apps carry the same risk. The attacker either controls the account or chooses the recording.

Listening for robotic delivery is not a reliable test either. A short call, a poor connection or background noise can hide flaws in a synthetic voice. Attackers also tend to add urgency. That leaves less time to notice anything odd.

The safer pattern reverses the direction of contact. The recipient ends the call and rings the person back on a number taken from a company directory or an earlier trusted record — not from the email, the signature block or the incoming call. Some finance teams also require a second approver for any payment change. Under that rule, one convincing voice cannot move money on its own.

Deepfake video calls let scammers stage a whole meeting of fake colleagues to back up a payment request. In early 2024, Hong Kong police described a case in which an employee of a multinational firm sent roughly $25 million after joining a video call with deepfaked coworkers.

Arup confirmed in May 2024 that it was the company involved. Arup is a British engineering and design firm with offices in many countries.

The fraud did not begin with the video call. It began with a message that the employee initially suspected. The employee joined the call with the deepfaked colleagues after that and then sent the money.

That order of events matters. A cautious recipient who doubts an email will often look for some form of confirmation. In this case, the confirmation was itself fake.

A call with several participants works differently from a single cloned voice on the phone. Each face on screen appears to agree with the others. The request seems to come from a group rather than from one person. The employee is no longer weighing one sender's word but what looks like a room of colleagues.

Deepfake video tools build a synthetic face and voice from existing footage of a real person. Senior executives often appear in recorded presentations, interviews and conference talks. That public material gives attackers something to work from.

The Arup case shows that a familiar face on a screen does not prove who is behind it. A video call that the requester arranges is part of the scheme, not an independent check.

Companies can reduce this risk by tying large payments to fixed internal controls rather than to a conversation. One example is a rule that big transfers need sign-off from more than one person through the company's own payment system. Under that rule, the request still has to clear the usual approvals, however convincing the meeting looked.

The case also shows a pattern to watch for. A message that raises doubts, followed by a meeting meant to settle those doubts, is a reason to pause before any money moves.

Generative AI tools can produce a convincing copy of a bank, email or software login page in minutes, along with the text that surrounds it. The page behind a phishing link can now look as polished as the email that delivered it.

Fake sign-in pages are not new. Criminals have long copied logos, color schemes and layouts from real brands. They then host those copies on domains that look close to the original. AI changes the speed and finish of that work.

A scammer can ask a model to write the page's code, help text, error messages and password-reset prompts. The result has fewer of the broken layouts and odd phrases that once gave a copied page away.

The same tools can match the page to the lure. A message about a shared invoice can lead to a document-viewer login. A message about a missed delivery can lead to a form asking for card details. Each page can be written in the target's language and in the tone of the email that pointed to it.

When the page itself looks clean, the address bar carries the most reliable evidence. The part of a web address that identifies the owner sits directly before the ending, such as .com or .co.uk. In an address like "login.yourbank.com.account-check.net," the real domain is account-check.net, not the bank.

Lookalike domains rely on small substitutions. Common ones include "rn" standing in for "m," a zero in place of the letter O, or an extra word such as "secure" attached with a hyphen. Some use characters from other alphabets that look identical to Latin letters. This technique is known as a homograph attack.

The padlock icon does not settle the question. It shows that the connection is encrypted, not that the site belongs to the company it imitates. Basic security certificates are available free of charge. A phishing site can get one as easily as a legitimate business can.

On a computer, hovering over a link reveals its real destination before a click. On a phone, pressing and holding a link usually shows the address. The safer route skips the link entirely: type the company's address directly or open a saved bookmark.

Password managers add one more check. They fill in saved credentials only on the domain where those credentials were stored. A manager that offers nothing on a familiar-looking login page is a sign that the address does not match the real site.

The defenses that hold up against AI phishing do not depend on judging how a message reads. They check things an attacker cannot easily fake: a separate contact channel, the real sender domain and a sign-in method tied to the genuine website.

Out-of-band verification is the first layer. Any request to send money, change bank details or share login credentials gets confirmed through a channel the recipient already trusts. That means contact details from a company directory, a contract or a previous invoice. It never means a number or address supplied in the message itself. An organization can make this a written policy: no payment detail changes without confirmation through contact details already on file.

The second habit is reading the technical details rather than the display name. An email client shows a friendly name, such as a colleague's or a supplier's. The address behind that name can belong to anyone. The domain after the @ sign is the part that identifies the sender. A display name and the visible text of a link are both labels that the sender controls.

Phishing-resistant sign-in covers the gap that human attention leaves open. FIDO2 security keys and passkeys use public-key cryptography, and the private key stays with the user. Each credential is bound to the real website address it was created for. On a lookalike page, the browser will not offer that credential at all. A fake site has nothing to capture that it can replay on the real one.

Email authentication works at the domain level. SPF lets a domain owner publish which mail servers may send on its behalf. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature that receiving servers can check against the domain's published key. DMARC tells receiving servers what to do with messages that fail those checks. A domain owner can set that policy to none, quarantine or reject. DMARC also sends reports back to the domain owner.

Together, those three standards help block spoofing of an exact domain, such as a fake message claiming to come from a company's real address. They do not stop lookalike domains. Those are registered separately and can pass their own authentication checks. That limit is the reason the verification and sign-in habits still carry weight.

None of these measures asks anyone to spot a flaw in the writing. Each one moves the decision away from a message's tone and toward facts that a language model cannot alter.

#5353. ‘Water for life, not data’: Amazon data center plan draws Eastern Washington protests

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon’s plans to build a data center campus near the Columbia River in Eastern Washington drew pushback Monday at a meeting of the Walla Walla County commissioners.

Some attendees held handmade and printed signs reading “Amazon lies,” “Big tech is shady. No more data centers” and “Water for life, not data,” according to the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin and its photos of the event.

The majority of the roughly 56 public comments were opposed to or had concerns about data center development, including worries about groundwater supplies, effects on agriculture and wildlife, and a lack of transparency, the Union-Bulletin reported. Supporters pointed to potential benefits from job creation and economic development.

The meeting highlighted continued resistance to data centers from communities concerned about higher electricity bills, depleted freshwater supplies and other environmental and social repercussions. Over the past year, tech giants including Amazon and Microsoft have pledged to limit those impacts and invest in host communities, but those commitments have not ended the opposition.

Elected officials are increasingly considering legislation and local ordinances to set standards and require greater transparency — an approach some tech leaders say could help address public concerns.

“There is a role for good laws, and if laws emerge that require that everybody do this work in a responsible way, I think that might be part of the solution,” Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, recently told reporters at a company event.

Commissioners in Western Washington’s Skagit County last month adopted significant restrictions on data center development. The facilities are prohibited in unincorporated areas, with some exceptions, and new caps on size and electricity usage will limit the technology to small-scale operations.

The planned Walla Walla County campus is one of two projects that would mark Amazon’s first large-scale data center developments in its home state. The second is in West Richland, part of the Tri-Cities. Amazon already operates smaller data centers in Washington.

The Walla Walla County campus would occupy roughly 134 acres at Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. Its three proposed single-story data center buildings would create about 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

According to a company fact sheet, the campus would use roughly 14 million gallons of water from the public utility to cool its equipment during its first year of operation. Amazon says it is working with the port to build a system that would replace the utility-supplied cooling water with nonpotable water drawn from the Columbia River. Wastewater from the campus “will meet industrial reuse standards,” the company said.

The campus would also use about 6 million gallons of utility-supplied water annually for employee needs.

Amazon’s fact sheet says the company will cover the electricity costs associated with the data center and that the “expenses aren’t added to the bills of local residents or businesses.”

The company is also working with partners to develop a nuclear power plant using small modular nuclear reactors near the Tri-Cities. The proposed plant could begin operating in the 2030s and “will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said.

Despite Amazon’s assurances, many attendees at Monday’s meeting called for a one-year, countywide moratorium on new data center development, the Union-Bulletin reported. Commissioner Bertha Clayton said she would consider a pause on new applications to give officials time to draft an ordinance to better regulate the developments.

Clayton said zoning changes adopted now would be unlikely to affect the current phase of Amazon’s project. The other two commissioners have previously said they do not support a moratorium, according to the Union-Bulletin.

The proposal is undergoing an environmental review under Washington’s State Environmental Policy Act, or SEPA. The review will assess potential environmental impacts and identify measures to address them. It will also determine whether the project requires a more detailed environmental impact statement.
