#5348. 10 AI cybersecurity terms explained, from breakout time to deepfakes

Free daily briefing on global business news.

10 AI cybersecurity terms, from breakout time and agentic AI to deepfakes and prompt injection, defined in plain language with how each attack or risk works

Artificial intelligence sits on both sides of the security problem. Attackers use it as a tool to write convincing messages and imitate real voices. Defenders also have to protect it as a target. A model that reads email, writes code or answers customers can be manipulated like any other system.

That double role has produced a working vocabulary that matters well beyond security teams. A finance employee asked to approve a payment on a video call needs it. So does a manager deciding whether staff can use a chatbot, and a board reviewing an incident report. Without shared definitions, a warning about prompt injection or shadow AI can sound like jargon. In practice, each term points to a specific risk and a specific response.

Some of these AI cybersecurity terms are new. Agentic AI, prompt injection and data poisoning describe problems that arise from how machine learning models are built, trained and connected to other software. Others come from older security ideas. Breakout time measures how quickly an intruder spreads from one compromised machine to the rest of a network. CrowdStrike $CRWD popularized that metric in its annual threat reports. Red teaming comes from traditional security testing, and shadow AI echoes the older term shadow IT.

Organizations trying to manage these risks also have a formal reference point. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology published its AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 in January 2023. The framework is voluntary. It offers a shared structure for thinking about AI risk rather than a set of legal requirements.

The 10 terms below are a selection, not a complete glossary. Each slide defines one term in plain language and explains how the attack or practice works. Several of the terms sit close together. Prompt injection, jailbreaking and adversarial examples all involve manipulating what a model receives. Each one exploits a different weakness, though. Prompt injection overrides an application's instructions, and jailbreaking pushes a model past its own safety rules. Adversarial examples use small, deliberate changes to an input to make a model misclassify it. Reading the definitions side by side makes those distinctions easier to keep straight.

Breakout time is the time an attacker needs to move from the first compromised machine to other systems on the same network. It measures how long defenders have to spot and contain an intrusion before it spreads beyond its starting point.

CrowdStrike $CRWD, the U.S. cybersecurity company, popularized the metric in its annual threat reports. The term describes attacker behavior, not a single tool or exploit. It applies whether the first foothold came from a phishing email, a stolen password or an unpatched server.

The step that breakout time tracks is known as lateral movement. After gaining access to one laptop or server, an intruder typically looks for credentials, maps the network and searches for more valuable targets. Those targets often include domain controllers, which manage user accounts across a Windows network. File servers, databases and backup systems are common targets too. MITRE ATT&CK, the public knowledge base of attacker techniques maintained by the nonprofit MITRE, lists lateral movement as a tactic of its own.

Attackers often move sideways with legitimate tools already present on the network. Remote Desktop Protocol, PowerShell and administrator accounts can all serve that purpose. Security teams call this approach "living off the land." It can make malicious activity look like routine IT work. That makes early detection harder.

Breakout time differs from dwell time. Dwell time counts how long an attacker stays inside a network before being discovered. Breakout time covers only the first stretch, from initial access to the jump onto a second system.

The distinction matters for defense. An intrusion caught on a single machine can often be handled by isolating that device and resetting the stolen credentials. Once an attacker reaches many systems, the cleanup becomes a much larger investigation. Ransomware operators, for example, often spread across a network before encrypting files. That lets them lock as many systems as possible at once.

Defenders work against the clock on two fronts: faster detection and slower spread. Endpoint detection and response software watches individual devices for suspicious behavior and can cut a machine off from the network. Network segmentation and multifactor authentication make each sideways step harder. Both measures slow the attacker down.

Agentic AI refers to AI systems that pursue a goal by planning a sequence of steps, using software tools and taking actions with limited human input. That autonomy is the source of both their usefulness and their security risk.

A standard chatbot works in a simple loop. A person types a prompt, the model writes a reply, and the exchange ends there. Any action that follows is taken by the human who read the answer.

An AI agent closes that gap. Given a task such as booking travel, sorting an inbox or fixing a software bug, it breaks the goal into smaller steps. It then decides which tools to call, reads the results and adjusts its plan before moving on. Those tools can include a web browser, an email account, a file system, a calendar, a code repository or a company's internal software.

The security question follows directly from that access. An agent that can send email can send the wrong email. An agent that can edit files can delete or leak them. An agent that can write and run code can introduce changes no one reviewed.

Two broad failure modes concern security teams. The first is hijacking, where an attacker steers the agent toward a goal of their own. That can happen through malicious content the agent encounters while working. The second is misdirection, where no attacker is involved. The agent misreads its instructions or chains together steps that produce a harmful result. In both cases, the damage depends on whatever permissions the agent holds.

Agents act on behalf of a person or an organization. To do that, they typically carry real credentials, such as login sessions, API keys and access tokens. If an agent is compromised, those credentials are exposed along with it.

One defense draws on an older idea: the principle of least privilege. Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder described it in their 1975 paper "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems." It holds that every program and user should have only the access needed to do the job.

Applied to agents, that means narrow permissions scoped to a specific task. An agent that summarizes documents does not need the ability to send email. An agent that drafts code does not need permission to push that code into a live production system.

Other safeguards include requiring human approval before high-impact actions such as payments, deletions or outbound messages. Teams can also log every tool call. That record lets them reconstruct what an agent did and in what order. Keeping an agent's access separate from the wider corporate network limits how far a single error or compromise can spread.

A deepfake is an image, video or audio clip that artificial intelligence has generated or altered. In most cases, the result makes a real person appear to say or do something they never said or did. Deepfakes matter in security because they exploit the trust people place in seeing and hearing someone directly.

The word combines "deep learning," the branch of machine learning built on layered neural networks, with "fake." It entered wide use in late 2017. That year, a Reddit $RDDT user posting under the name "deepfakes" shared videos in which celebrities' faces had been swapped onto other people's bodies.

Several techniques sit under the label. Face swapping replaces one person's face with another's across a video. Lip-sync manipulation alters mouth movements to match new audio. Face reenactment transfers one person's expressions and head movements onto someone else's face. Some images contain no real person at all and show an entirely synthetic face.

Much of the early work relied on generative adversarial networks, or GANs. Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduced the method in 2014. A GAN pits two neural networks against each other. One generates fake samples, and the other tries to tell them apart from real ones. Each round of that contest pushes the generator toward more convincing output. Newer image and video tools also use diffusion models. These start from random noise and remove it step by step until an image emerges.

For attackers, the main appeal is impersonation. A fabricated video of a senior executive can be used to pressure staff into sharing passwords or granting system access. Deepfakes can also target identity verification. Banks and online services often ask new customers to take a selfie or short video and match it to a photo ID. A synthetic face can be used to try to pass those checks. So can a manipulated video fed directly into the camera stream.

Defenses fall into three broad categories. Detection tools look for visual inconsistencies such as unnatural lighting, blurred edges around the face or mismatched reflections. Each flaw a detector learns to spot is also a flaw that developers of generation tools can work to remove.

Provenance standards take a different approach. The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity is an industry group whose members include Adobe $ADBE and Microsoft $MSFT. It has developed a technical standard that attaches signed metadata to a file. That metadata records where a piece of media came from and how it was edited.

The third defense relies on process rather than technology. Companies can require that any unusual request made over video be confirmed through a separate, known channel before anyone acts on it.

Prompt injection is an attack that hides instructions inside text a large language model reads. The model then follows the attacker's instructions instead of the ones its user or developer intended.

The weakness comes from how these models handle input. A language model receives everything as one stream of text. The developer's setup instructions, the user's request and any outside content all arrive in the same form. The model has no reliable built-in way to tell a trusted command from a sentence that only looks like one.

The name echoes SQL injection, an older attack on databases. In that attack, someone slips database commands into a form field meant for ordinary data. Prompt injection works on the same principle of mixing data with commands. The difference is that a language model reads plain human language. That leaves no fixed syntax for a filter to catch.

The attack comes in two forms. Direct prompt injection happens when a user types the malicious instructions into the chat window. A user might tell a customer service bot to disregard its earlier instructions and reveal its configuration, for example.

Indirect prompt injection is harder to spot. The instructions are buried in content the model processes on someone's behalf, such as a web page, an email or a shared document. A person asks an assistant to summarize a page. Hidden text on that page tells the model to do something else. The user may never see the planted words. They can sit in white text on a white background, in comments or in metadata.

The stakes depend on what the model can reach. A model that only produces text can be pushed into giving false or misleading answers. A model allowed to call other tools could be steered into sending private data to an attacker or taking actions the user never requested.

OWASP, the nonprofit Open Worldwide Application Security Project, lists prompt injection first in its Top 10 for large language model applications. Common defenses include restricting what the model can access, treating its output as untrusted and requiring a person to approve sensitive actions. None of these measures fully removes the risk.

Data poisoning is an attack in which someone corrupts the data used to train or fine-tune an AI model. The finished model then behaves wrongly. The damage is built into the model itself and does not depend on what a user types later.

The attack works because a machine learning model learns its behavior from examples. If an attacker can slip altered or mislabeled examples into that collection, the model absorbs those patterns along with the legitimate ones. The bad records can be hard for engineers to find among a very large number of normal ones.

Poisoning produces two broad kinds of harm. The first is degraded accuracy. In this case the attacker wants the model to become less reliable overall — a spam filter that lets more junk through, or a fraud model that misses more fraud. The second is a hidden backdoor. A backdoored model works normally almost all the time. It switches behavior when it sees a specific trigger chosen by the attacker. That trigger might be a particular phrase, a small pattern in an image or an unusual string of characters.

Backdoors are the harder problem to catch. A backdoored model can perform well on standard accuracy tests. Those tests are unlikely to contain the attacker's trigger. The flaw stays dormant until someone who knows the trigger uses it.

One simple technique is label flipping. The attacker changes the labels on some training examples, for instance by marking malicious files as safe. Other methods leave the labels correct and alter the content in subtle ways instead. That makes the tampering harder to spot during review.

Timing separates data poisoning from attacks on a model that is already running. Poisoning happens before or during training. The attacker shapes what the model learns, rather than tricking a finished model later.

The training data supply chain is where that exposure begins. Many models learn from large datasets scraped from the public web, bought from third-party vendors or drawn from open-source collections. Each of those sources is a point where someone outside the organization could insert content. Fine-tuning carries the same exposure on a smaller scale. A company that adapts a model with customer records, support tickets or user feedback is trusting that data too.

Defenses focus on knowing where data came from and checking it before use. Teams track data provenance and restrict who can modify training sets. They filter for outliers and duplicates, and they test models against known trigger patterns. None of these steps guarantees a clean model. Fixing a poisoned model can require retraining it on verified data.

Jailbreaking is the practice of crafting prompts that get an AI model to ignore its built-in safety rules. The goal is to make a chatbot produce content its developer trained it to refuse, such as instructions for causing harm.

The term comes from an older practice. People jailbroke iPhones and other locked devices to remove manufacturer restrictions and install software the maker had not approved. With AI models, the restrictions being removed are behavioral rather than technical. Nothing in the model's code is changed. The attacker works entirely through the conversation.

Those restrictions come from how a model is built. Developers train large language models to decline certain requests. A common technique is reinforcement learning from human feedback, in which human ratings of responses are used to steer the model's behavior. That training shapes tendencies rather than enforcing fixed rules. A carefully worded prompt can sometimes push the model outside the behavior it was taught.

Jailbreak prompts take several familiar forms. One approach asks the model to play a character who has no rules. An early example aimed at ChatGPT circulated online as DAN, short for Do Anything Now. Other approaches wrap a forbidden request inside fiction, a hypothetical scenario or a claimed research purpose. Some split a request into harmless-looking pieces spread across a long conversation.

Jailbreaking and prompt injection are related, but they aim at different targets. A jailbreak goes after the model's own safety restrictions — the limits its developer trained into it. Prompt injection goes after the instructions an application gives the model. Those instructions might tell a customer service bot to discuss only its company's products. A single attack can involve both, but the weakness being exploited is different.

The distinction shapes who handles the defense. Resisting jailbreaks falls largely to model developers. They retrain their models and add filters that screen what goes in and what comes out. Guarding against injection falls more heavily on the companies building applications on top of those models.

For businesses, the risk is that a deployed chatbot can be talked into producing harmful, offensive or dangerous output under the company's name. A model that refuses a request in one phrasing may comply when the same request is reworded. Model updates can also change that behavior. A safeguard that held against one version of a model is not guaranteed to hold against the next.

Adversarial examples are inputs that have been changed in small, deliberate ways so that a machine learning model misclassifies them. Because the attack targets a model that is already in use, the technique is also known as an evasion attack.

The classic case involves an image. An attacker adjusts pixel values by amounts too small for a human to notice. A person looking at the altered picture sees the same object as before. The model assigns it a different label, sometimes with high confidence.

The weakness comes from how models learn. An image classifier does not recognize objects the way people do. It learns statistical patterns across many numerical features. Those patterns can respond sharply to changes that carry no meaning for a human eye. An attacker who understands that sensitivity can push an input across the boundary the model uses to separate one category from another.

Attacks are often described by how much the attacker knows. In a white-box attack, the attacker can see the model's internal structure and parameters. That access lets the attacker calculate which changes will have the most effect. In a black-box attack, the attacker can only submit inputs and observe outputs. That attacker must probe the model repeatedly to find a change that works. An adversarial example crafted against one model can sometimes fool a different model trained for the same task. Researchers call this property transferability.

Images are the textbook example, but the idea applies wherever a model makes a decision about an input. A malware file can be modified so that a machine learning detector scores it as harmless while the code still runs. Spam and phishing messages can be reworded to get past filters that rely on learned patterns. Audio can be altered so that a speech recognition system transcribes something other than what a listener hears.

Timing separates evasion from data poisoning. Poisoning corrupts a model while it is being trained. Evasion leaves the model untouched and manipulates the inputs it receives after deployment.

Defenses exist, but none is complete. One common approach, adversarial training, adds manipulated examples to the training data. The model then learns to classify those altered inputs correctly. Other measures screen incoming data for signs of tampering before the model sees it. A model's accuracy on ordinary test data does not show how it performs against an attacker deliberately searching for its blind spots.

Shadow AI is the use of AI tools by employees without approval from their company's IT or security team. The main risk is that confidential information, such as customer records, source code or contract terms, gets pasted into an outside service the company does not control.

The term borrows from shadow IT. That older phrase covers any software, cloud service or device that staff adopt on their own, outside official channels. A team that stored work files in a personal cloud account or tracked projects in an unvetted app was practicing shadow IT. Shadow AI applies the same idea to chatbots, writing assistants, coding helpers, transcription services and image generators.

The typical case is ordinary. An employee who wants a quick summary of a long report or a cleaner draft of an email may open a free chatbot in a browser tab. The issue is what goes into the prompt. Once text is submitted, it leaves the company's network. From that point it is handled under the provider's terms, not the employer's.

Those terms vary. Some consumer AI services retain conversations and may use them to improve their models unless a user opts out. Business and enterprise tiers from the same providers often come with different data-handling commitments. An employee signed in with a personal account may not know which set of rules applies.

Unapproved tools can cause problems on the way back in, too. Code written by an unvetted assistant may contain security flaws. A chatbot's answer may contain factual errors that end up in documents sent to customers. Browser extensions that add AI features can request broad permissions to read web pages, documents or email.

Companies typically respond with a mix of controls. Some block specific AI websites on corporate networks. Others license enterprise versions of AI tools with contractual data protections, giving employees a sanctioned alternative. Acceptable-use policies can spell out which categories of information may never be entered into an AI service. Data loss prevention software scans outbound traffic for sensitive patterns such as account numbers. It can be configured to cover AI prompts as well.

AI red teaming is the practice of deliberately attacking an AI system to find its weaknesses before real attackers do. Testers act as adversaries. They probe a model or an AI-powered product for ways it can be misused, tricked or pushed into causing harm.

The practice borrows its name and approach from traditional security red teaming. In that older discipline, a red team plays the attacker and tries to break into an organization's networks, buildings or processes. A blue team defends. The exercise shows where defenses fail under realistic pressure rather than on paper.

AI red teaming applies the same adversarial mindset to a different kind of target. A conventional red team might look for an unpatched server or a weak password. An AI red team looks for prompts, inputs and sequences of actions that make a model behave in ways its builders did not intend.

The scope is broad. Testers typically attempt jailbreaks and prompt injection against the system. They also hunt for harmful outputs. These include instructions that could help someone cause physical harm and responses that leak private information. Answers that reflect bias against particular groups count as failures too.

One feature sets AI testing apart from much of traditional security work. Language models produce probabilistic outputs. The same prompt can return different answers on different attempts. A single failed attack does not prove a system is safe. Testers often repeat and vary their attempts to gauge how reliably a weakness can be triggered.

Red teaming can target a model on its own or the full application built around it. An AI assistant connected to email, documents or company databases has more ways to fail than a model answering questions in isolation. Testing the whole system shows what an attacker could reach in practice.

The findings feed back into fixes. Developers may retrain or adjust a model, add filters on inputs and outputs, or narrow the permissions an AI tool holds. Models and the applications around them are updated over time. For that reason, red teaming is usually treated as a recurring exercise rather than a one-time check.

Voice cloning uses AI to copy a person's voice from recorded audio samples. Vishing is voice phishing — a scam carried out over a phone call. The pairing lets a caller sound like a specific relative, manager or colleague.

A cloning model learns the pitch, accent, rhythm and tone of a voice from existing recordings. It can then produce new speech in that voice. Some tools work from typed text. Others convert the scammer's own speech into the target voice as they talk. The source audio can come from anywhere a person's voice is public, such as social media videos, podcasts, conference talks or a voicemail greeting.

Vishing is older than AI cloning. The word joins "voice" and "phishing." The classic version relies on a caller posing as a bank, a government agency or a tech support desk. Scammers often pair it with caller ID spoofing, which makes a call appear to come from a trusted number. Cloning adds something the older scam lacked: a voice the target already knows.

At home, a common script is a family emergency. A call arrives in what sounds like a child's or grandchild's voice. The caller describes an arrest, an accident or a trip gone wrong. Then the caller asks for money quickly and asks the listener to keep it quiet. That pattern predates AI and is known as the grandparent scam.

At work, the impersonated voice usually belongs to someone with authority. A call that appears to come from a manager or finance chief may ask an employee to approve a wire transfer. It may also ask them to change a supplier's bank details or share login credentials. A call to an IT help desk that imitates an employee may seek a password reset or a new device enrolled for multifactor authentication.

Each version leans on the same levers: urgency, authority and secrecy. The aim is to rush the target past the checks they would normally apply. Requests for payment in forms that are hard to reverse, such as wire transfers, gift cards or cryptocurrency, are a common feature.

The defenses rely on verifying the request through a separate channel rather than judging the voice. Hanging up and calling back on a number already on file gets around a spoofed caller ID. Some families agree in advance on a code word that only a real relative would know. Companies can require a second approver for payments and a call-back step before any change to bank details. A familiar voice on its own is not proof of who is on the line.

#5347. XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

#5346. Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 1:16 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 1:16 pm

Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

#5345. Nvidia beat earnings estimates in first report since Jensen Huang's exit

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, excluding Data Center compute sales in China

Nvidia $NVDA reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier, in its first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. Earnings per diluted share were $2.70 on a GAAP basis and $2.68 on a non-GAAP basis.

Analysts expected revenue of $109.10 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.48 a share, according to CNBC.

Nvidia stock climbed by up to 4% in after-hours trading following the report. The company will hold a call with analysts and investors at 5 p.m. ET.

Net income was $65.3 billion, up 105% from a year earlier. Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier and up 21% from the prior quarter. GAAP gross margin was 74.8% and non-GAAP gross margin was 74.9%.

For the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, and the outlook excludes any Data Center compute revenue from China. The company expects GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins between 71.0% and 72.0%. The average analyst estimate for fourth-quarter revenue was $125.1 billion, according to CNBC.

Data Center shipments of Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the quarter, the company said.

"Our momentum is real," interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said in a statement. Nvidia said its Vera Rubin platform has begun shipping.

Nvidia said its supply commitments rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in the prior quarter, mainly because of multi-year memory procurement. The company also said its guarantees tied to the SB Energy data center campus in Ohio, which will host Nvidia infrastructure leased to OpenAI, are capped at $105 billion.

The company returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter through buybacks and dividends. Its board raised the repurchase authorization by $150 billion in September, leaving $227.3 billion available. Nvidia will pay a quarterly dividend of $0.25 per share on Dec. 23 to shareholders of record on Dec. 2.

Huang resigned last week after admitting to an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence officials suspect she is an agent of Beijing's spy agencies. Kress took over as interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and the board began a search for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia's board also took a governance step on Tuesday when it established a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance. Huang said in a statement Tuesday that he'd be "honored" to take back the chief executive role should directors conclude that doing so is "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America," according to The Wall Street Journal.

#5344. OfferUp co-founder sees ‘mini power plants’ in buildings full of EVs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or new power plants built to meet peak demand.

“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

“Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5343. How attackers turned IT management, red-team and VPN software against its users

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Security tools used as weapons, from the SolarWinds Orion backdoor to cracked Cobalt Strike copies, show how software built to manage or protect networks can become the way in

The software trusted with the deepest access to a network is also the software an attacker most wants to control. Network monitors, remote management consoles, VPN gateways and penetration-testing kits hold privileges that ordinary applications lack. When an intruder takes over that access, the defenses themselves carry the intrusion.

This selection of 10 cases looks at security tools used as weapons, along with the IT management and remote access software that sits beside them. It is not a ranking or a complete list. Nine of the cases trace a different route by which a protective or administrative tool ended up serving an attacker.

Some routes run through the supply chain. In supply chain attacks, intruders tamper with a trusted product or abuse the channel a vendor uses to reach its customers. A routine update or management command then delivers the payload. The SolarWinds Orion and Kaseya VSA incidents both followed versions of that path.

Other cases involve dual-use security software. Red teams use commercial frameworks such as Cobalt Strike and Brute Ratel C4 to imitate real adversaries. Cracked and stolen copies of those frameworks have reached ransomware crews and other malicious actors. Mimikatz was released to demonstrate weaknesses in how Windows handles credentials, and attackers later used it to steal them.

Attack tools reportedly built by governments can escape too. EternalBlue, an exploit widely reported to have been developed by the U.S. National Security Agency, was leaked by a group called the Shadow Brokers in 2017. It was then used in the WannaCry and NotPetya outbreaks.

Another group covers equipment at the edge of a network and software with standing access inside it. A flaw in a VPN gateway such as Ivanti Connect Secure can turn perimeter security gear into the entry point. Remote support platforms such as ConnectWise ScreenConnect draw attackers because they already hold broad legitimate access. Other attackers have loaded legitimately signed but vulnerable drivers to gain kernel-level access and switch off endpoint detection tools.

The final case is different in kind. The U.S. government restricted Kaspersky products, citing the risk of exploitation by the Russian government. Kaspersky has denied the allegations.

CrowdStrike $CRWD's faulty update in July 2024 is excluded. It was an error, not a weaponization. Every case here involves deliberate misuse by attackers or, for Kaspersky, a government's stated concern about potential misuse.

Attackers hid a backdoor, later named Sunburst, inside software updates for SolarWinds' Orion network management platform. SolarWinds said about 18,000 customers received the tampered update.

The backdoor was discovered in December 2020. By then, the tampered Orion update had already reached customer networks through the vendor's normal distribution channel.

Orion is network management software. Organizations run it to monitor and administer their networks. That role places it inside the environment it oversees, with access to the systems it watches.

The attackers did not need to break through each victim's defenses one at a time. The malicious code arrived inside an update from a vendor the customers already trusted. Installing a vendor update is ordinary maintenance work. In the Orion case, that ordinary step delivered the backdoor.

That is what makes the incident a supply chain attack. The target was the supplier, not each end organization. Once the Orion update had been tampered with, every customer that installed the affected release received the backdoor along with it.

The 18,000 figure counts customers who received the tampered update. It measures how widely the backdoor was distributed. It is not a count of organizations where the attackers took further action.

The U.S. government attributed the operation to the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service. That attribution is the U.S. government's conclusion about who ran the campaign.

Software updates exist to fix flaws and keep products current. In the Orion compromise, the update channel itself carried the intrusion into customer networks.

In July 2021, the REvil ransomware group exploited Kaseya's VSA remote management software and used it to push ransomware to the customers of managed service providers. Kaseya said fewer than 60 of its direct customers were affected. It put the number of downstream businesses hit at roughly 1,500.

VSA is IT management software. Managed service providers are the outside firms that run IT for other companies. They use tools of this kind to look after many clients' computers from a single console.

Through that console, a provider can install software, run scripts and push changes to machines it never physically touches. The same access that saves time on routine maintenance can deliver anything the operator chooses to send.

That made the Kaseya incident a case of a legitimate administration tool turned against the networks it was meant to look after. REvil did not have to break into each victim one at a time. It turned VSA itself into the means of distribution.

The ransomware reached victims by the route that ordinary IT work takes. To the affected machines, the instructions came from a trusted system they were set up to obey.

The two figures Kaseya gave show how that layering works. Its direct customers sat at one level. The businesses those service providers supported sat at the next.

An attack on the first level spread to the second. That is how an incident Kaseya measured in dozens of direct customers reached well over a thousand businesses further down the chain.

Most of the businesses hit were not Kaseya's own customers. Their exposure came through the service provider they had hired to run their IT. A single provider's console could carry the attack to the client machines it managed.

Software that holds administrative reach over many networks gathers that reach in one place. Whoever controls the console can use everything it was built to do.

Cobalt Strike is a commercial adversary-simulation tool that Raphael Mudge created for red teams. Cracked and stolen copies have since been widely used by ransomware crews and state-linked groups. A product built to test defenses became one used to defeat them.

Red teams are security staff or outside consultants hired to act like attackers. They try to break into an organization's network with its permission, then report what the defenders missed. Adversary-simulation software gives them a ready-made kit for that work. It lets testers mimic how real intruders behave instead of building every component themselves.

That design goal is the root of the problem. A tool built to reproduce real attacker behavior convincingly does the same job in an actual attack. The software has no way to tell an authorized tester from a criminal.

Mudge built Cobalt Strike as a commercial product meant for legitimate testers. Cracked copies are versions altered to get around the product's licensing controls. Stolen copies are genuine builds taken from the people entitled to use them. Either route puts the full toolkit in the hands of people the seller never meant to serve.

The tool's core component is Beacon, its payload. A payload is the software that runs on a machine after an intruder gets in. Beacon gives its operator a foothold on that machine. It checks back in with whoever controls it and waits for instructions. For a red team, that foothold shows how deep an attacker could reach. For a ransomware crew or a state-linked group, the same foothold is a working base inside the victim's network.

Defenders face a specific puzzle as a result. Spotting Cobalt Strike activity on a network does not, by itself, reveal whether an approved exercise or a real intrusion is underway. Security teams have to confirm whether anyone authorized a test before deciding how to respond.

The case also differs from attacks that depend on a software flaw or a tampered update. Nothing in Cobalt Strike had to break for it to be misused. The product did what it was designed to do. The only thing that changed was who was running it.

Mimikatz is a tool that pulls passwords and other authentication material out of a Windows computer's memory. Benjamin Delpy released it in 2011 to demonstrate weaknesses in how Windows handles credentials. Attackers later adopted it for credential theft and lateral movement.

The program targets something most Windows users never see. Passwords and other authentication material can sit in a computer's memory. Mimikatz extracts that material and hands it to whoever runs the tool.

Delpy's purpose was demonstration. The tool turned an abstract weakness in Windows credential handling into a concrete result. A defender running it on a machine could see what an intruder with the same access would be able to recover.

That visibility also made it useful to attackers. Intruders folded Mimikatz into their operations, where it served two purposes.

The first purpose is credential theft. A recovered password or piece of authentication material lets an intruder act as a legitimate user. Actions taken with valid credentials can look like ordinary activity on a network.

The second purpose is lateral movement. This is the process of spreading from one compromised computer to others on the same network. Credentials taken from the first machine can unlock the next one. Each new machine can then yield more credentials, and the cycle can repeat.

NotPetya used credential-harvesting techniques of this kind.

Mimikatz is an example of dual-use security software. The same output that shows a defender an exposure gives an attacker usable credentials. The tool did not create the weakness it exposed. It made that weakness straightforward to act on for anyone holding a copy.

EternalBlue is an exploit for a flaw in Microsoft $MSFT's SMB protocol, and it was widely reported to have been developed by the U.S. National Security Agency. A group called the Shadow Brokers leaked it in April 2017, and attackers used it in the WannaCry outbreak in May 2017 and later in NotPetya.

SMB, short for Server Message Block $SQ, is the protocol Windows computers use to share files and printers across a network. The flaw EternalBlue targets sits inside a service built for routine communication between machines.

EternalBlue moved from intelligence tool to publicly available attack code. Software written to break into systems did not stay with the people who built it. Once the Shadow Brokers released it, anyone with a copy of the leak could reuse it.

Microsoft had already issued a patch, MS17-010, in March 2017. The name is the bulletin number Microsoft assigned to its security update for the SMB flaw. That fix arrived about a month before the leak. Windows systems could therefore be patched before the exploit became public.

WannaCry spread roughly two months after the patch shipped. Computers that had applied MS17-010 were protected against this exploit. Computers that had not installed it remained exposed to the same flaw.

NotPetya later used EternalBlue as well. That made the exploit a shared component of two separate outbreaks. Each one depended on the same SMB flaw that MS17-010 had already addressed.

EternalBlue's origin sets it apart from tools sold commercially to security teams. It was not a product, a red-team framework or an IT management platform. It was an offensive capability, widely reported to originate with a government agency, that escaped into public circulation.

A patch protects only the systems that install it. The month between MS17-010 and the leak, and the weeks between the leak and WannaCry, formed the window that separated protected networks from exposed ones.

Brute Ratel C4 is a commercial command-and-control framework that Chetan Nair built for red teams. A cracked version circulated in 2022, and security researchers reported that malicious actors were using it in real attacks.

A command-and-control framework, often shortened to C2, is the software an operator uses to direct implants on compromised machines. It sends instructions and collects results. It also keeps the connection between the operator and those machines alive.

Red teams use this kind of tooling to play the part of an intruder. They do it during authorized tests of an organization's defenses, with the client's permission.

Brute Ratel was built to evade endpoint detection and response, or EDR, tools. EDR tools watch individual computers for suspicious behavior and alert defenders when they find it. For a red team, that evasion is the purpose of the product. A test only shows whether defenders can catch a skilled intruder if the simulated intruder behaves like one. A framework that slips past security products gives the client a realistic picture of its blind spots.

The same feature takes on a different meaning once the tool leaves licensed hands. A cracked version is a copy with its licensing protections stripped out. Anyone who obtains it can run it without paying for or registering it. The vendor then has no record of who holds that copy or what they use it for.

When a cracked copy of Brute Ratel circulated in 2022, its evasion features became available to people with no authorization to attack anyone. Those features did the same job in a real intrusion that they did in a sanctioned test.

Brute Ratel follows a pattern already seen with Cobalt Strike, another commercial red-team product whose cracked copies reached attackers. The two cases share one underlying tension. Software that convincingly imitates an attacker is, by design, useful to an actual attacker.

Bring your own vulnerable driver, or BYOVD, is a technique in which attackers load a legitimately signed but flawed driver onto a machine. The driver gives them kernel-level access, which they use to switch off endpoint detection tools.

A driver is software that lets an operating system talk to hardware or perform low-level tasks. On Windows, many drivers run in the kernel, the most privileged layer of the system. Code running there can see and change almost anything on the machine, including other security software.

That level of access is why Windows expects kernel drivers to carry a digital signature. The signature tells the operating system who published the code and that it has not been altered since. It does not tell the system whether the code contains a bug.

BYOVD exploits that gap. Rather than writing a malicious driver and trying to get it signed, an attacker brings along a real one that already passed the signing process. The file is genuine. The flaw inside it is what the attacker wants.

Once the vulnerable driver is loaded, the attacker abuses its weakness to carry out actions with kernel privileges. That can include shutting down the processes of endpoint detection and response products, often called EDR. Those tools are designed to resist being stopped by ordinary programs. Kernel access removes that protection.

Some of the drivers abused this way come from security and anti-malware products. A component built to help defend a computer becomes the means of blinding its defenses. That makes the technique a direct example of dual-use security software turned against the systems it was meant to protect.

BYOVD is usually not the first step of an intrusion. Loading a driver on Windows requires administrator rights. Attackers generally reach for it after they already have that foothold. Its job is to clear the way for whatever comes next, such as stealing data or deploying ransomware, while the monitoring tools are offline.

In January 2024, attackers exploited two vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure and Ivanti Policy Secure. Organizations use these products to control who gets into their networks. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887.

Connect Secure is a VPN product. It sits at the edge of a network and decides which remote users may reach internal systems. That position is what made the flaws serious. The device meant to keep intruders out became the way in.

Policy Secure handles a related job at the same boundary. Both products belong to the category of perimeter security equipment. This is the gear that faces the internet on an organization's behalf.

A zero-day is a flaw that attackers exploit before the vendor has shipped a fix. Defenders have no patch to apply when it is first used against them. For owners of Connect Secure and Policy Secure devices, that meant the exposure could not be closed at first by the routine step of installing an update.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, responded with Emergency Directive 24-01 on Jan. 19, 2024. The directive ordered federal civilian agencies to disconnect the affected Ivanti products.

That order reversed the usual direction of network defense. Agencies typically add security appliances to reduce risk. Under this directive, the required step was to take the security appliance offline.

Taking a VPN gateway offline also cuts off the remote connections it exists to provide. The directive required agencies to accept that loss rather than keep the exposed devices running.

The Ivanti case differs from attacks that tamper with a vendor's software updates or abuse a stolen testing framework. Here the weakness sat inside the product itself. Attackers did not need to slip code into a vendor's release. They targeted flaws in equipment that was already installed and trusted at the network boundary.

In February 2024, ConnectWise disclosed critical flaws in ScreenConnect, its remote access software, including an authentication bypass tracked as CVE-2024-1709. Attackers exploited the flaw after the disclosure. A tool built for IT support became a route into the networks it was meant to help manage.

An authentication bypass is a specific kind of failure. It lets someone reach parts of an application that should sit behind a login without supplying valid credentials. In most software, that is a serious problem. In remote access software, the stakes are higher. The login is the main barrier between an outsider and every system the tool can reach.

A bypass also differs from a stolen password. The attacker does not need to guess, phish or buy anyone's credentials. Strong passwords and careful account hygiene offer little protection when the check that should demand them is skipped.

ScreenConnect belongs to the category of remote support tools. Software of this kind lets a technician connect to a computer from another location to view the screen, take control of it and fix problems. That job requires broad, trusted access to the machines the tool serves. An attacker who gets past the login inherits that access instead of having to build it.

This is why remote support tools are a favored entry point for intruders. The access already exists, and an organization granted it on purpose. Sessions run through a remote support tool can look like routine IT work. That makes an intruder harder to tell apart from a legitimate technician.

In this case, attackers moved after ConnectWise made the flaws public, not before. A disclosure tells defenders what needs fixing. It also tells attackers where to look. The period that follows is a race. Any ScreenConnect server left unfixed stays open to anyone who has read the same advisory.

Nothing about ScreenConnect had to be altered or smuggled out. A flaw in how the software checked who was allowed in was enough. That flaw turned the product's own legitimate access against the organizations that relied on it.

The U.S. government has restricted Kaspersky security software in two stages, citing the risk that the Russian government could exploit it. Kaspersky denies the allegations, and no confirmed attack is part of this case.

The first restriction came in 2017. That year, the Department of Homeland Security ordered federal agencies to remove Kaspersky products. The order applied to the government's own systems. It did not cover private companies or households.

The second restriction reached further. In June 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department announced a ban on selling Kaspersky software in the U.S. That step carried the issue past federal computers and into the wider U.S. market.

Taken together, the two steps shifted the focus from the federal government as a buyer to Kaspersky as a seller.

Both actions rested on the same stated concern about exploitation by the Russian government.

That concern follows from the job security software is built to do. An antivirus or anti-malware product needs broad access to the machine it protects. It inspects files and running programs. It also receives regular updates from its maker. That reach is what makes such a product useful to defenders. The same reach is why the U.S. government treated possible outside influence over the vendor as a national security question.

The concern centered on the vendor, not on a specific flaw in the code. No disclosed vulnerability or patch is part of this case. A patch can close a flaw, but it cannot answer a question about who stands behind the software.

This sets the Kaspersky case apart from most examples of security tools used as weapons. In those cases, attackers tampered with, stole, cracked or exploited a legitimate tool. Here, the issue is a policy judgment about trust in a vendor. The U.S. actions describe a risk of misuse. They do not establish that Kaspersky software was turned against its users.

#5342. ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm

Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue…

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna said the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it plans to make to avoid similar outages.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”

We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Update, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.
